#9148. Wildlife Silhouettes and the Power of Shape

Wildlife Silhouettes and the Power of Shape

Explore how posture, shape, light, and composition can help wildlife photographers create striking backlit imagery that tells a powerful story.

Wildlife photography often emphasizes detail. Photographers work to capture the texture of feathers, patterns in an animal’s coat, expressions in its eyes, and the small features that reveal its character. Silhouette photography takes a different approach. Instead of relying on those details, it reduces an animal to its outline, using shape, posture, and positioning to communicate the subject. The result is a more graphic, interpretive image that asks viewers to recognize the animal through its form rather than its appearance.

Creating compelling wildlife silhouettes involves more than placing an animal in front of a bright sunset. The subject needs a recognizable outline, its posture should contribute to the image, and the background must provide enough contrast to make its shape clear. Composition and timing also matter more because small changes in an animal’s position can dramatically alter the photograph. Understanding these elements helps photographers recognize opportunities where removing detail can make a wildlife image more expressive.

A successful silhouette depends on how easily the viewer can identify the subject and interpret its position. Without visible detail, the outline becomes the primary source of information. Body proportions, head position, and distinctive anatomical features all contribute to whether an animal remains recognizable. A silhouette that communicates its subject immediately is generally more effective than one that leaves the viewer guessing.

Some animals and poses naturally lend themselves to this approach. An elk with clearly defined antlers, a fox with its ears raised, or a bird with its wings extended has a distinctive outline that remains identifiable even when rendered entirely dark. By contrast, an animal facing directly toward the camera may lose much of its recognizable shape. Its body can appear compressed, and important features may overlap.

A strong silhouette should also contribute something to the photograph beyond simply creating a dark subject. It might emphasize an animal’s scale against a large landscape, highlight a particular behavior, or simplify an otherwise busy scene. The most effective images use the silhouette as a deliberate storytelling choice rather than treating it as an exposure effect.

Before photographing an animal as a silhouette, consider which anatomical features make it recognizable. Different species have distinctive profiles, and understanding those features can help you anticipate the most effective shooting angle. For mammals, this might be the shape of the head, the length of the legs, the position of the ears, or features such as antlers and horns. For birds, the bill, neck, tail, and wing shape often provide the most important identifying characteristics.

The angle of the animal can change how these features appear. A broadside position often provides a recognizable profile because the body, head, and legs appear as separate shapes. A three-quarter angle can add depth, particularly when the animal turns its head toward the camera. Front-facing positions can also work, but they often rely on distinctive features to keep the outline from looking indistinct.

Birds offer a wide range of possibilities because their silhouettes change so dramatically with wing position. A bird in flight with its wings fully extended has a very different outline from one gliding with its wings angled downward. The shape of the wings can also help identify a species, with long, narrow wings, broad rounded wings, and separated flight feathers each creating different visual patterns.

Studying animal profiles and observing wildlife in the field can help you recognize these opportunities. Instead of focusing only on whether an animal is facing the right direction, look for positions that reveal its defining characteristics. A slight turn of the head or a change in ear position can be enough to transform an ordinary outline into a recognizable portrait.

When fine detail disappears, posture becomes one of the most important ways to communicate an animal’s character. A standing animal with its head lowered may create a relatively unremarkable shape, while the same animal raising its head, stretching, or interacting with another individual can produce a much more expressive image. The silhouette should ideally show something about the animal, not just document its presence.

Behavior can provide some of the most interesting opportunities. An elk bugling with its head raised, a bear standing on its hind legs, or a bird extending its wings during a display all create recognizable gestures. Even smaller movements can work well. A fox listening with its ears pointed forward, or a heron poised with its neck extended, can create a distinctive profile without requiring dramatic action.

Anticipating these moments is often more effective than reacting after they happen. Wildlife photographers already spend considerable time learning animal behavior to predict where subjects will move and when interesting activity might occur. The same preparation applies to silhouettes. If you know a bird is likely to take flight from a particular perch, or that an animal regularly pauses on an exposed ridge, you can prepare for the moment rather than scrambling to adjust your position after it begins.

Continuous shooting can help when the opportunity involves movement, but a burst of frames does not guarantee the strongest composition. Watch for the positions that communicate the behavior most clearly. For a bird in flight, that might mean waiting for the wings to reach full extension. For a mammal, it could be a moment when its head and limbs create a particularly expressive gesture. The goal is to capture the most meaningful position, not simply the most frames.

The simplicity of a silhouette makes compositional decisions especially noticeable. With fewer details competing for attention, the animal’s placement, direction, and relationship with the surrounding space carry much of the photograph’s visual weight.

Consider the direction in which the animal is looking or moving. Leaving open space in front of a subject can create a sense of movement and give the viewer somewhere to follow its gaze. A bird flying toward the open side of the frame, for example, generally feels less confined than one positioned directly against the edge. Similarly, an animal looking toward an open horizon can create a sense of anticipation or connection with the landscape.

The animal’s size within the frame also changes the story. A relatively large silhouette emphasizes anatomy and posture, making it easier to appreciate the subject’s shape. A smaller animal surrounded by open sky or landscape can communicate scale, distance, and isolation. This wider approach can be particularly effective when the environment is an important part of the photograph.

Natural lines can provide useful compositional structure. A ridgeline, shoreline, or distant tree line can anchor an animal within the scene and create a visual connection between the subject and its surroundings. Experiment with both tight and wide compositions when the situation allows. A tighter frame emphasizes the animal, while a wider image can reveal more about its place in the landscape.

Silhouette photography depends on contrast between the subject and its surroundings. Sunrise and sunset provide familiar opportunities because the sky is often much brighter than the landscape. Positioning an animal against a bright section of sky can create a dark outline while retaining the colors and tonal transitions of the surrounding light.

The sun does not necessarily need to be visible in the frame. A colorful band of light near the horizon, a bright opening between clouds, or a softly illuminated sky can all provide an effective background. Other lighting conditions can work as well. Bright overcast skies, open water, reflections, and distant illuminated areas of landscape may provide enough contrast to isolate an animal.

Think about the background as an active part of the composition rather than simply a source of brightness. A relatively uniform sky often works well because it allows the animal’s shape to stand out. More complex backgrounds can introduce atmosphere and context, but they may compete with the subject if they contain too many contrasting elements.

Light quality and direction change as the sun rises or sets, so the best background may be available only briefly. Identify promising positions before the animal reaches them, and watch how the light changes across the scene. A slight shift in the animal’s position or the sky’s color can produce a noticeably different result.

Even a distinctive animal can become difficult to identify when its outline merges with the surrounding environment. Branches, grasses, rocks, and other animals can obscure important features, particularly the legs, ears, antlers, and wings. Because a silhouette removes most internal detail, these overlaps matter more than they would in a conventional wildlife portrait.

Before taking the photograph, scan the entire outline. Check whether the animal’s legs are distinguishable, whether its head and ears are clearly defined, and whether important features are lost against nearby objects. With birds, pay particular attention to the wings and tail. A bird with its wings tucked tightly against its body may appear as a much simpler shape than one with its feathers spread.

Changing your position is often the easiest way to improve separation. Moving a short distance to one side can shift a branch out of the animal’s outline or create a gap between its legs. A lower shooting position may place the subject against the sky rather than vegetation, while a higher position can sometimes remove distracting foreground elements. These adjustments are especially useful in wetlands, grasslands, and wooded environments.

Multiple animals introduce another challenge. When individuals overlap, their silhouettes can merge into a single shape that is difficult to interpret. This does not mean you should always avoid groups. A group of birds in flight can create a compelling pattern, and animals gathered together may communicate social behavior. The important distinction is whether the arrangement remains visually understandable. Waiting for individuals to separate or for their positions to change can make the difference between a confusing cluster and a deliberate composition.

Exposing for a silhouette requires a different approach from a traditional wildlife portrait. Rather than preserving detail in the animal’s shadows, the goal is to retain important background information while letting the subject fall into darkness. This means exposing for the brighter surroundings instead of trying to balance the entire scene.

Automatic exposure modes can sometimes make this difficult. When a camera detects a large dark subject against a bright background, its metering system may attempt to brighten the scene. The result can be an animal with visible shadow detail instead of a solid silhouette. Exposure compensation provides a straightforward way to address this. Reducing exposure can keep the subject dark while preserving the sky’s colors and tonal information.

Manual exposure offers more control, particularly when the background brightness remains relatively consistent while the animal moves through the frame. You can establish an exposure based on the sky and maintain those settings rather than allowing the camera to continually adjust for changes in the composition. Spot or center-weighted metering can also help, depending on where you place the metering area and how your camera interprets the scene.

The histogram helps you evaluate exposure, especially when photographing colorful skies. Overexposing the brightest areas can remove the subtle color transitions that make the background interesting. Review the histogram and highlight warnings to determine whether you are retaining the tones you want. At the same time, don’t worry about preserving shadow detail in the animal if you intend to create a true silhouette.

Shutter speed remains important because wildlife behavior doesn’t become less unpredictable just because the subject is dark. A bird taking flight still needs a fast enough shutter speed to preserve the shape of its wings, and a running mammal may require a similarly fast exposure to prevent motion blur. If the animal is stationary, you may have more flexibility, but it is still worth accounting for small movements such as turning its head or shifting its weight.

Autofocus can become more challenging when the subject is dark against a bright background. Depending on the camera and scene, the autofocus system may have fewer visible details to identify. Tracking modes and subject detection can still help, but watch how reliably the camera follows the animal. In some situations, focusing on the subject before it moves into the brightest part of the background may be more effective. Continuous autofocus and burst shooting can help with unpredictable movement, but they work best when paired with an understanding of the animal’s likely path.

Although the animal itself is often rendered as a dark shape, the background can bring considerable color and atmosphere to a silhouette photograph. Sunrise and sunset provide familiar warm tones, but cooler twilight colors can work just as well. Deep blues, soft purples, and muted pastels can create a quieter mood, while reflections and layers of color can add depth without distracting from the subject.

Negative space gives the animal room to stand apart and allows the viewer to focus on its shape. This works especially well when photographing a small animal against a large sky or open landscape. The surrounding space becomes part of the story, communicating scale and emphasizing how the subject fits into its environment.

Minimalist compositions often work well because they reduce competing elements. A single bird against a colorful sky, an elk standing on a distant ridge, or a fox crossing an open field can create a strong image with very little visual information. However, minimalism does not mean every photograph needs only one subject. A small number of carefully arranged elements can create balance, rhythm, or visual contrast.

Reflections offer another way to add visual interest while keeping the composition simple. A bird standing in shallow water may produce a second shape beneath its body, creating symmetry or a repeating pattern. A calm lake can also provide a contrasting surface, depending on the direction of the light. These compositions can be particularly effective when the reflection remains recognizable and adds something to the overall arrangement.

Another way to use minimalism is to move in closer and create a tighter portrait, emphasizing the animal’s outline and the details that define its shape. At this distance, subtle textures and contours become more prominent, adding visual interest while keeping the composition simple. This is another time when I play with my exposure to decide if I want a flat silhouette or one with more information in the darkened areas.

Silhouettes, or backlit images, aren’t always the best approach for every wildlife encounter. Many situations require an animal’s coloration, markings, expression, or visible behavior to tell the story. A close portrait that reveals the texture of fur or the details of a bird’s plumage may communicate far more than a dark outline. Deciding whether to photograph a subject as a silhouette should come down to what the image is meant to convey.

When shape or gesture is the most interesting part of the scene, removing detail can strengthen the photograph. A bird spreading its wings against a sunset, an elk calling from a ridgeline, or a mammal looking toward an open horizon can communicate its presence through posture alone. The viewer does not need to see every detail to understand the moment. Instead, the simplified form encourages them to focus on the animal’s movement and relationship with the environment.

Most of all, silhouettes can add variety to a wildlife portfolio. Photographers naturally spend considerable time pursuing sharp, detailed images, particularly when working with long telephoto lenses and tracking fast-moving subjects. A silhouette offers a different visual approach, emphasizing composition and light over revealing every feature. It can help tell a broader story about an encounter or location, especially when paired with more traditional wildlife portraits.

When conditions allow, photograph a scene both ways. A traditional exposure may reveal the animal’s markings and expression, while a silhouette may create a more graphic, atmospheric interpretation of the same moment. Comparing the two approaches can help you decide which communicates the scene most effectively.

Ultimately, wildlife silhouette photography is about recognizing the visual strength of an animal’s shape. Distinctive anatomy, expressive posture, thoughtful composition, and suitable light all contribute to an image that remains compelling without the details normally associated with wildlife photography. Sometimes, revealing less about an animal allows its shape, movement, and place in the landscape to tell a more compelling story.

#9145. Samyang AF 60-180mm f/2.8 Review: A Trinity Completed

Samyang AF 60-180mm f/2.8 Review: A Trinity Completed

The two major third-party manufacturers from Japan have a complete trinity of full-frame professional f/2.8 zoom lenses. Sigma has long had a complete set, and Tamron has its excellent G2 series finalized. The Chinese companies are only now venturing into the autofocusing pro zoom lens market, but Samyang, out of Korea, has worked very hard — and quickly — to complete its full set, too. With the release of the new $1,099 Samyang X Schneider Kreuznach AF 60-180mm f/2.8, that goal is realized.This lens has some surprises up its sleeve, but the experience still feels lacking in features and refinement. PetaPixel Score 7/10 ProsVery sharp right to the cornersLightweight and compactBokeh has a pleasing rendering of backgroundsConsButtons and controls feel down-marketBasic and slower stepping autofocus motorNo optical stabilizationNo aperture ring This lens is being released for E-mount and L-mount cameras, and whether you should buy it will be highly dependent on that lens mount.

This lens has some surprises up its sleeve, but the experience still feels lacking in features and refinement.

I’m going to get this out of the way first: Samyang lenses, also sold under the Rokinon brand in North America, have always aimed at a budget price point and, as a result, rely heavily on plastic construction. Okay, lots of companies do, but Samyang lenses always just look and feel a little less refined and a little more basic than some of the others.

I’m not going to go so far as to say that this negatively impacts the build quality. I know many Rokinon users who have had years of reliable service out of their lenses. But the buttons and controls always feel a little flimsy and make obtrusive clicking noises when pressed. The plastic hood is basic and twists into place with a little bit of coercion.

The rubber rings feature two different textures, which Samyang usually likes to use. There is a custom button and an AF/MF switch, along with an unexpected locking switch for the zoom mechanism. The manual focus ring has a nice smoothness to it, but the zoom ring takes a bit of force to get moving and lacks refinement.

Flicking this will keep the zoom at the 60mm mark, but you do have to unlock it before zooming again. You will not find an aperture ring on this lens, but this is pretty standard at this price point. Samyang lenses do have some baffles and a little weather sealing incorporated into the lens mount.

With the 77mm filter threads on the front, this lens looks fairly hefty, but with an overall weight of 730 grams, it is actually lighter than the Tamron and Sigma alternatives. I also like that the lens doesn’t extend that far when zoomed to 180mm, and the point of balance doesn’t change much either. However, part of the lighter weight comes with a lack of optical image stabilization within the lens.

I was worried about the bokeh on this lens when I started with specular highlight tests. At the widest apertures, the highlights have a truncated look, which I do not prefer, and there are some slight onion rings present as well. However, at tighter apertures, the highlights are fairly round, and more importantly, the actual rendering of the out-of-focus areas of the images is quite smooth. I expected a harsher edge to the bokeh with a more distracting rendering, but the backgrounds looked soft and pleasant. Other than the distracting highlights, this lens presents shallow depth of field beautifully.

There is a little bit of flare present, which is something I found with the other Samyang f/2.8 lenses. At f/2.8, there is some green ghosting and a bit of veiled flare washing out the image. The green cast stays at tighter apertures but doesn’t get too obnoxious. Overall, the flare control is decent, and the hood will do a good job of blocking extraneous light. Speaking of color casts, expect a little bit of LoCA at the wider apertures. These longitudinal chromatic aberrations will present with a slight green and magenta split, but the effect is minimal and usually won’t cause much concern in the vast majority of your images.

Sharpness is where this lens excels, with excellent detail in the center of the image right from the start. I found the 180mm mark to be particularly good in the center at f/2.8, with slight improvement to be found at tighter apertures. The corners at the long end were also impressive, with more detail than I expected at f/2.8 and fairly low vignetting. Closing the aperture will improve things as usual, but I was impressed by how good the corner detail was overall. At the 60mm mark, the story is similar. The center sharpness is maybe slightly softer at this focal length, but still very acceptable. The corners were also similarly excellent, with far better-than-expected detail. This Samyang lens has the most consistent corners and overall detail compared to its third-party contemporaries.

The lack of lens-based image stabilization is unfortunate, although to be fair, the impact will largely depend on what camera body you are using. Clearly, the lack of a stabilizer keeps the cost down a bit and shaves off some weight. Another cost-cutting choice is the use of a more basic stepping motor for focus. Focusing is smooth and accurate, but the speed is noticeably slower than the competition. If you want to tackle faster sports and action, you might want to consider alternatives.

Kudos to Samyang for finalizing a trilogy of professional-grade f/2.8 full-frame zoom lenses. However, should you buy this set or even any of these lenses individually? Here is what we can say for certain: in my opinion, Samyang lenses are well-built but lack refinement, and tend to lack extra controls and aperture rings.

They always feel a little down-market in the hand to me, but the optical performance is formidable. This 60-180mm f/2.8 is both compact and frighteningly sharp. Its optical performance beyond that is certainly acceptable, but it doesn’t ever seem to shine in any other regard. Samyang has a 14-24mm and 24-60mm lens, both with f/2.8 apertures, and they are both capable of capturing great images. However, in a field of fierce competition, Samyang lenses may struggle to find a foothold.

Samyang AF 14-24mm f/2.8Buy new on B&HSamyang AF 14-24mm f/2.8Buy used on KEH.comSamyang AF 24-60mm f/2.8Buy new on B&HSamyang AF 24-60mm f/2.8Buy used on KEH.com

In Sony E-mount, this 60-180mm lens goes up against the Tamron 70-180mm f/2.8 Di III VC VXD G2, which almost exactly matches the $1,099 Samyang.

In L-mount, it only has to compete with the Sigma 70-200mm f/2.8 Sports and Panasonic S 70-200mm f/2.8, both of which are much larger and more expensive options. I’d probably go for the Tamron 70-180mm f/2.8 myself due to the faster AF experience and optical stabilization. However, if you value maximum sharpness and slightly less weight, and have a camera body with IBIS, or if you are looking for an excellent option in L-mount, the Samyang 60-180mm could be a sound choice.

Sigma 70-200mm f/2.8 SportsBuy new on B&HSigma 70-200mm f/2.8 SportsBuy used on KEH.comPanasonic Lumix S 70-200mm f/2.8Buy new on B&HPanasonic Lumix S 70-200mm f/2.8Buy used on KEH.com

Regardless of lens mount, the Sigma 70-200mm f/2.8 Sports is going to be much larger at a higher cost, and only makes sense if you want to use teleconverters. This is pretty much the same story for the Panasonic S 70-200mm f/2.8 as well. The Tamron does offer similar optical performance with better AF and stabilization, and is even more compact and manageable. The Samyang 60-180mm should put pressure on Sigma to make a better alternative, but Tamron has nothing to worry about.

Yes. This lens is still going to deliver excellent images at a good price and in a compact chassis. Whichever way you slice it, the Samyang is still a good tool for the dollar.

#9144. Budapest exhibition explores Van Gogh and Gauguin's artistic excursion to Montpellier

The portico of Budapest’s Museum of Fine Art

Adventures with Van Gogh is a weekly blog by Martin Bailey, The Art Newspaper's long-standing correspondent and expert on the Dutch painter. Published on Fridays, stories range from newsy items about this most intriguing artist, to scholarly pieces based on meticulous investigations and discoveries.

Explore all of Martin’s adventures with Van Gogh here.

After Paul Gauguin arrived in Arles in October 1888 to stay with his friend Van Gogh, the two artists would go out to paint together and then socialise and discuss art in the evenings over a glass of wine. Their very different personalities, however, soon led to tensions. Living together in the confines of the Yellow House and sharing a small room as a studio, they began to row. As winter approached, and the weather made it impossible to work outside, the situation only worsened.

In mid-December, in an attempt to clear the air, Gauguin suggested that they should make a trip to Montpellier, 70 km west of Arles. Their goal was to visit the Musée Fabre, renowned for its fine collection of paintings.

The artistic result of this trip forms a central part of a major exhibition on Gauguin which opened this week at Budapest’s Museum of Fine Arts. Bonjour Monsieur Gauguin: The Circles of Post-Impressionists and Symbolists (until 28 February 2027) provides a wide-ranging exploration of the art of Gauguin and his associates. The show’s title comes from a key painting by the artist inspired by the Montpellier visit, Bonjour Monsieur Gauguin (late 1889).

Paul Gauguin’s Bonjour Monsieur Gauguin (late 1889)

Hammer Museum, Los Angeles (photograph The Art Newspaper)

Van Gogh and Gauguin travelled from Arles to Montpellier by train, which took around four hours. Although it has long been assumed that they made a day trip on either 16 or 17 December 1888, it is arguably more likely that they spent the night there and stayed for both days. The Musée Fabre had over 800 paintings on display, so they would surely have wanted time to savour the works. Many of the finest pictures were French, given by Alfred Bruyas, a local collector and patron of Gustave Courbet.

Gustave Courbet’s Bonjour Monsieur Courbet (1854)

For Gauguin, the highlight of the museum was Courbet’s Bonjour Monsieur Courbet (1854). This landscape composition includes the figure of Courbet himself, laden with his equipment and holding a walking pole. He is greeting Bruyas, who is accompanied by a bowing servant.

Gustave Courbet’s Bonjour Monsieur Courbet and Gauguin’s Bonjour Monsieur Gauguin in the Budapest exhibition

Gauguin, who was impressed with the Courbet, painted a work in response, a year later, in the Brittany fishing village of Le Pouldu. The main figure in this work is Gauguin himself, facing a Breton woman on the other side of a gate.

Superficially, the Gauguin painting bears little resemblance to the Courbet. Stylistically, Courbet’s smoothly painted picture contrasts with Gauguin’s rough brushwork. The compositions appear to have little in common, other than showing an artist encountering other people—and being greeted with a “good day” (and, incidentally, both scenes also include a dog).

The moods seem very different. Courbet appears thrilled to greet his patron and friend. Gauguin’s encounter with the Breton woman, however, is fleeting, as they happen to pass each other at a gate. The Budapest exhibition’s lead curator, Judit Geskó, sees the Gauguin picture as representing “the artist as a solitary wanderer”.

But despite the differences, Gauguin’s decision to entitle his work as he did shows that he was directly acknowledging the source of his inspiration, the Courbet. Gauguin’s title is actually inscribed on the painting, in the lower-left corner.

Gauguin made two versions of his composition: the one on loan to Budapest from the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles and the other (which was unavailable for borrowing) at the National Gallery in Prague. The Hammer picture, which was the original, was created to display on the dining room door in the small inn where he was staying in Le Pouldu.

As for Van Gogh, the Dutchman was particularly struck in the Musée Fabre by the portraits by Courbet. These included a self-portrait, The Man with the Pipe (around 1849), which may well have inspired Van Gogh one month later to paint his Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear and Pipe (January 1889).

Bruyas was depicted by a range of artists and these portraits were also much admired by Van Gogh in the Montpellier museum. Vincent described Bruyas’ appearance to his brother Theo as “a gentleman with a beard, red hair, who looks damnably like you or me”.

Postcard of Musée Fabre, Montpellier (1905)

Both Gauguin and Van Gogh were great admirers of Courbet, who was very well represented in the Musée Fabre. Although they agreed about Courbet, their tastes for other artists were often rather different. Vincent wrote to Theo that their artistic discussions in Montpellier had been “excessively electric”. He explained: “We sometimes emerge from it with tired minds, like an electric battery after it’s run down.”

Despite these animated discussions, the inspirational visit seemed a success. Vincent reported back to Theo the day after their return that in the museum they had been “right in the midst of magic”. He added: “Gauguin said to me this morning, when I asked him how he felt: ‘that he could feel his old self coming back’, which gave me great pleasure.”

Sadly, the reconciliation did not last long: just four days later Van Gogh severely mutilated his ear. Although the trigger was probably news he had just received that Theo had become engaged (which Vincent feared would threaten his brother’s support), tensions with Gauguin were also a contributing factor.

Budapest’s Gauguin exhibition is ambitious, with 80 works by the French master and 70 by other artists. Although financial valuations for exhibitions are rarely revealed, The Art Newspaper can report that its total insurance value is €1.5bn.

Van Gogh’s Field with Irises near Arles (May 1888)

Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)

The show includes three works by Van Gogh: the landscape painting Field with Irises near Arles (May 1888, Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam) and two rarely-displayed drawings from the collection of the Budapest museum, The Parsonage Garden at Nuenen in Winter (March 1884) and Haystacks (July 1888).

Van Gogh’s The Parsonage Garden at Nuenen in Winter (March 1884) and Haystacks (July 1888)

The Budapest exhibition has two Gauguin paintings dating from his stay with Van Gogh in Arles: the landscape Les Alyscamps (October 1888, Musée d’Orsay, Paris) and the portrait Madame Roulin (November-December 1888, Saint Louis Art Museum). Both of these subjects were also tackled by Van Gogh.

Gauguin’s Les Alyscamps (October 1888) and Madame Roulin (November-December 1888)

Musée d’Orsay, Paris and Saint Louis Art Museum

Among the other Gauguin highlights in the show is Sunflowers on an Armchair (1901, Bührle Collection, on loan to the Kunsthaus Zurich). This is one of four still-life paintings inspired by Van Gogh’s favourite motif—sunflowers. Gauguin painted these in the Marquesas Islands (north of Tahiti), with flowers grown from seeds he was sent by a friend from Paris.

Gauguin’s Sunflowers on an Armchair (1901)

Bührle Collection, on loan to the Kunsthaus Zurich

The museum estimates that the Gauguin exhibition could see up to 350,000 visitors, a huge number for a medium-sized European capital. However, even this won’t match Geskó's Van Gogh show in 2006, which attracted 486,000 people to the museum to see the Dutch painter's works.

Martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

His other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

To contact Martin Bailey, please email vangogh@theartnewspaper.com

Please note that he does not undertake authentications.

#9142. How I Shot and Edited a Documentary About Bicycle Jousting In Under a Day

How I Shot and Edited a Documentary About Bicycle Jousting In Under a Day

Lime Bike Jousting was conceived by Cameron Carnegie-Brown (AKA Camtholomew the First) and Jack Carden, two London creatives who turned a joke about jousting on rental e-bikes into a viral performance art event.

The first joust, held earlier in October, drew hundreds to London Fields and racked up over four million Instagram views. Lime’s response was measured but clear: “While we appreciate the medieval spirit, safety must always come first. Lime bikes are designed for getting around the city, not for jousting. We discourage anyone from attempting similar events to help keep riders and those around them safe.”

The second event went ahead anyway, with thousands RSVPing online, the location released to the public only two hours beforehand to those registered, and initiatives taken to raise money for charity.

At that second Jousting event, on October 31st, 2026, I produced a short film, a mini-doc, coming in at 10 minutes, 33 seconds. It was a light-hearted event, taking place on the afternoon before Halloween, so plenty in the crowd were dressed up in various costumes, some themed, others a little less on-topic, and once the Joust concluded, they headed straight onward into their Halloween celebrations, to their house parties and trick-or-treating nights.

This was a fast turnaround production. I shot with a Nikon ZR and Tamron 28-75 (an ideal photojournalism-adjacent lens, although at one point I remember wishing I had my 15mm for some extreme wide when I was packed into the crowd). At the same time, Amanda Dombroski used a Panasonic camcorder for B-roll and alternate angles.

The ZR is ideal for run-and-gun cinema: incredibly compact, with phenomenal image quality and stabilization that doesn’t feel unnatural. For interviews at a moment's notice, the 28-75 is ideal, and the reach was basically fine for the action, although I could have used a little more at times.

Combined with the camcorder's extreme reach and versatility, I had plenty of material to choose from in the edit, and I think the mini-doc covers the community aspects of the event and context especially well. Amanda’s footage gave me great cut-ins, alternate perspectives of the joust, and overall flavor, all of which were really valuable to the finished short film.

Photographer Elliott Gunn (who previously featured in my first-ever feature-length film "Everything Happens All the Time") stepped in as a sort of presenter, offering the microphone to various "Squires," "Knights," and other attendees. We even briefly interviewed one of the Lime Bikes, which was clad in makeshift armor.

The event was scheduled to begin at 3:30 PM, although the location wasn't announced until a couple of hours before. I arrived at 2 PM, having walked from Colombia Road to London Fields, where an annual Day of the Dead celebration was taking place. This meant I could catch some quieter moments and interviews before crowds arrived, and warm up visually as different elements fell into place.

I left after the event had mostly wrapped up (although some spontaneous reveling unfolded after the main jousting concluded), around 4:45 PM, so Amanda and I had a relatively short window to record a total of 80 minutes of footage between us. I was working in N-RAW, and the camcorder doesn't support it, so the first hurdle in the edit was grading the footage consistently.

The wired microphone was tricky to work with in such fast conditions, and I got tangled in it a few times while draping it over my shoulders when not in use. While it's a non-brand, cheap thing, the ZR's built-in 32-bit float capabilities left plenty of room to refine the audio, and it sounds really quite good, in my opinion.

It was Elliott's first time as a "presenter," and I think he did well, although I do have some notes for him. One moment saw one armor-clad Knight chugging a can of the soft fruit drink he was there promoting, and Elliott held the mic so close it was almost ASMR; I think he handled it really well, and it was a great moment in the film. The Knight then slammed the empty can against his helmet until it crumpled flat.

The edit worked out at 10 minutes and 30 seconds, not too bad, all considered. It covers the event fairly well, although the jousting itself was the hardest part. As soon as the lances struck, other photographers, videographers, and influencers swarmed the downed Knight, and even as they cycled, some camera operators ran past, obscuring the action. At some points I gave up trying to push through other photographers and spent time on the edges shooting the crowd. If I were tackling this as a longer-term body of work, I would have had the energy to work harder on those aspects and outmaneuver the “competition.”

I think my take is less on the action itself and more on the community. I spoke with the lady who built the lances out of foam and soft wood; Elliott and I spoke with some of the Knights and passers-by; and we got a more in-depth look at the event overall, in a more traditional documentary approach.

It's a pure document of the event as best as I could manage, with depth beneath the surface from the diverse interviews and moments. It doesn't end as strongly, but it isn't a narrative arc; there wasn't much pacing or natural rhythm to edit to, so it was makeshift as best as possible. I didn’t want a highlight reel or a collection of disjointed moments, which is mostly what’s out on social media and mainstream platforms right now.

There’s been such a huge response to the jousting phenomenon as a whole, so I think the audience for this mini-doc is anyone who likes these fringe, seemingly spontaneous community events, and who wants to see a little more than what's been shown on the news or in shorter social media snippets. It's currently out on YouTube and Vimeo.

Unfortunately, I couldn't make it to the first Lime Bike Joust earlier in the month because of a prior commitment. Still, I think if I'd been able to make any recordings, I'd have kept that footage in reserve, kept shooting as events unfolded, and then put together something more substantial. Since it's “just” the second one, I think it made sense to treat it as standalone, because while the event itself is unique, it risks becoming “content saturated.”

I noticed some serious camera rigs in the crowd, and I wouldn't be surprised if someone came out with a more complete narrative film in a few months (or longer, depending on how many jousts are yet to take place, I’m keeping an eye on “TalesByTyler”). Without that level of commitment, it’s just a matter of showing up with a camera and a vague outline of an idea, and doing your best to apply your skill to the scenario, the same as I am used to with my documentary photography.

I used various presets and plugins to give the footage a sort of filmic glow and grain, which meant the ZR footage worked well alongside the camcorder. I didn't have a specific look in mind, but I like Lance Oppenheim's "Ren Faire," and I think there's a little taste of that in this. I used proxies in Premiere Pro to speed up render times and exported in 4K, which took quite a while with all those plugins.

Editing was from when I got home at around 6:30 PM, and then it was finished in the early hours of the following day, so taking into account dinner and distractions, I'd say it was a five-hour editing process. Luckily, I've been in a good creative flow, and it was fun to shoot, edit, and publish something like this in such a short amount of time. The whole thing reminded me that you don't need a perfect setup or a grand plan. Most of the time you just need to show up, pay attention, and let the story tell you what the production needs to be.

#9141. Sabine Marcelis takes a moment to reflect in first museum exhibition

Photography by Umberto Romito and Ivan Šuta

Sabine Marcelis has a knack for creating viral objects, from IKEA’s most-sold light to her mesmerising Candy Cube tables. Now, the designer is revealing the method behind her “magic” in an exhibition at Zürich‘s Museum für Gestaltung.

Light and Color is the first museum show dedicated entirely to Marcelis‘s work since she founded her studio 15 years ago.

In that time, the Rotterdam-based Kiwi has gone from being a student at the Design Academy Eindhoven to one of the most prolific and in-demand designers working today.

“This is the first time a museum has brought so much of my work together in one place,” Marcelis told Dezeen. “I’m always so preoccupied with what’s next that I don’t like to look back so much, but it’s amazing to have this moment to actually stop and look back for a minute.”

The show brings together 17 key pieces from the last decade and a half, going as far back as Tall Stripe – the first of many mirrors – and her signature resin Candy Cubes, which first catapulted the designer to international acclaim in 2014.

But Marcelis is adamant it should not be considered a retrospective.

“I didn’t want the show to feel like a retrospective in the sense of a chronological archive,” she said. “I wanted to select a variety of projects that each show a different way of working with light and colour.”

Rather than chronologically, the exhibits are arranged by colour, blending into each other like the soft gradients she favours in works like her curved glass chaise longues for the Barcelona Pavilion.

Her favourite materials – glass, resin and stone – recur throughout the exhibition, with carefully placed spotlights showing off the play of reflections and shadows the designer has learned to elicit through years of experimentation.

A prime example is her Lokum coffee table for Acerbis, stacked on top of each other on a curved wall to show the gradients of colour and water-like reflections created when the glass is seen at different angles and levels of illumination.

There are also two room-scale installations, reminiscent of Yayoi Kusama‘s Infinity Mirror Rooms, throwing back endless reflections of Marcelis’s viral IKEA “donut lamp” and the towering three-metre-tall Column lava lamp for Mathmos.

For the show’s curator Damian Fopp, these are less about Instagram bait and more about allowing visitors to experience the full visual effect of these objects in real life, rather than through a screen.

“Her work circulated widely as images, but no institution had looked at it as a whole,” he said. “This also made it interesting to shift the conversation back from online to physical.”

“And we wanted to show what lies behind those calm, effortless images: the testing, prototyping and production that I discovered when I visited her studio in Rotterdam.”

A mini-documentary and a book commissioned for the exhibition pull back the curtain on what it takes to create these perception-bending pieces with her team.

Over the years, these have become more ambitious in scale as well as sustainability, pivoting to 99 per cent biobased resin for her production and creating installations for the likes of Coachella and Apple HQ,

But no matter the size of the project, Marcelis says that materials remain her North Star.

“I wrote a one-sentence summary of what my studio does ten years ago,” she remembered. “‘A studio for material, installation and object design. Forever in search of magical moments within materiality and manufacturing processes to create unexpected experiences.'”

“I wouldn’t change that sentence today if I had to make the same summary again.”

Photography by Umberto Romito and Ivan Šuta

#9137. Trail Camera Photos of the First Coyotes to Use the World’s Largest Wildlife Crossing

Trail Camera Photos of the First Coyotes to Use the World’s Largest Wildlife Crossing

The world’s largest wildlife crossing, the $114 million Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing, hasn’t officially “opened,” but that hasn’t stopped the animals from using it above the extremely busy Highway 101 in Agoura Hills, California.

On October 28, a coyote became the first large mammal — a lizard was the first across the line, technically — to use the wildlife bridge. Yesterday, a second coyote went on it.

They were both caught on recently installed remote wildlife camera traps, an incredible tool for scientists and award-winning wildlife photographers alike.

As SFGate reports, the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing, which has been in the works since the National Wildlife Federation (NWF) and Santa Monica Mountains Fund began raising money for it in 2014, isn’t slated to have its ribbon-cutting ceremony until early December. Construction is ongoing, so it isn’t even technically a crossing yet.

Wildlife doesn’t wait. The project, which includes two bridges crossing the 10-lane Ventura Freeway, includes 13 acres of habitat restoration. Birds and bugs have already enjoyed the growing reclaimed habitat above the busy highway, while a western fence lizard was the first to go on the bridge’s surface itself.

The two coyotes were the first large mammals spotted on the structure itself, but a mountain lion and her two cubs, a mule deer, and bobcats have all been spied walking next to the wildlife crossing.

“To everyone who wondered how wildlife would know where to go without signs… apparently, they’ve figured it out,” writes the Facebook account for P22 Mountain Lion of Hollywood, an influential mountain lion that was tragically euthanized in 2022. The famous big cat made a lasting impact on California’s wildlife conservation efforts, inspiring many to get involved and help make projects like the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing possible.

For scientists, the new wildlife crossing bridge offers many interesting things to learn.

“This is more than just about whether animals use the crossing,” said Seth Riley from the National Park Service’s Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area team. “We want to understand how effective it is in reconnecting an ecosystem that has been divided by the freeway for decades. That is a much bigger scientific question and answering it will take years.”

Riley and other team members will learn a lot from cameras set up on and near the wildlife crossing, and the public will get to see many of these photos. For security reasons, there won’t be real-time public feeds from the site, though. Scientists will study how the wildlife crossing affects wildlife diversity, genetic diversity, habitat evolution, how light and sound affect animals, and more.

It’s an exciting time to be a wild animal near Highway 101. And a decidedly safer one.

#9136. Yinka Ilori reveals Tottenham Hotspur away shirt

Photography courtesy of Tottenham Hotspur Football Club

British-Nigerian designer Yinka Ilori has collaborated with Premier League football team Tottenham Hotspur to create a customised version of the club’s colourful away shirt.

Ilori reimagined the colourful away shirt, which was designed by Nike with a pattern of “never-before-seen visuals inspired by never-before-seen destinations”, by adding a graphic to the front and back.

On the front, in the position the sponsor logo is usually located, Ilori designed a circular motif combining the football club’s initials – THFC – with an abbreviation for London and the postcode for Tottenham, LDN17.

The lettering is bright orange with a white background.

On the rear of the shirt, Ilori created a graphic in his typical playful style around the letters COYS, which stands for Come On You Spurs.

Encircling the letters are the words “I know I am, I’m sure I am”, with the words “We are Tottenham wherever we go” around the whole graphic.

All of the lettering uses Ilori’s custom typeface, which was designed by type foundry British Standard Type for the designer in 2024.

According to the designer, who grew up in north London where the Populous-designed Tottenham Hotspur stadium is located, the collaboration aims to demonstrate the power of football to unite people.

“This project is a celebration of belonging and the power of football to bring people together,” said Ilori.

“For me, football is about the wider culture and the incredible sense of unity that comes from standing on the terraces, chanting alongside thousands of others,” he continued.

“I wanted the design to honour Tottenham Hotspur’s heritage while capturing that collective joy and spirit. The ‘Never Far From Home’ message really resonated with me, reflecting how football has the power to make you feel at home, wherever you are.”

The shirt is the latest design from the designer who has recently collaborated with brands including Brabantia and Veuve Clicquot.

Ilori also recently created a homeware and furniture collection for department store Dunelm.

Photography courtesy of Tottenham Hotspur Football Club

#9134. Bringing Back the Image Formats Apple Forgot

Bringing Back the Image Formats Apple Forgot

The 1990s brought Bill Clinton, The Simpsons, MP3s, Napster – and the age of personal digital photography and personal computer video.

The revolution began with digital cameras and Apple’s 1994 launch of the QuickTake 100. The path was pixelated at first, with heavily compressed, low-resolution photos that couldn’t begin to replace film. Still, the fuzzy handwriting was on the wall: the future was filmless.

As digital cameras were beginning to walk upright, a parallel evolution was taking place: personal computers gained the ability to play video clips, thanks to Apple’s QuickTime and, later, Microsoft’s Video for Windows. The quality was poor – grainy images and jerky motion within a saltine-sized frame. But it was sort-of TV…on a computer!

In the middle of these developments, Apple created an imaging technology that had no analog in the world of, well, analog. Introduced in 1995, QuickTime VR enabled photographers to produce a 360-degree panorama that appeared on a computer screen and that you could navigate with your mouse and keyboard.

This wasn’t the kind of VR we associate with today’s VR headsets – a 1995 Apple tech note called it “virtual reality for the rest of us.” You changed your vantage point by dragging within the panorama. Today, of course, this kind of panning is common (think Google Street View). But in the 1990s, it felt like something completely new, because it was.

Within ten years, it was all but abandoned. As Apple evolved the Mac’s operating system, the company left the QuickTime VR and QuickTake formats behind. This is the story of my efforts to bring them back.

I was a contributing editor and columnist for Macworld magazine during this era and was lucky to be able to cover digital cameras and QuickTime VR. I wrote a feature article on digital cameras in 1994 (PDF, 1.8MB) and led the magazine’s coverage of QuickTime VR in 1995 (PDF, 1.8MB). For a Macworld-branded book I wrote, I produced a CD-ROM containing an interview with the QuickTake 150 product manager.

In early 1995, I spent time with a team in Apple’s Advanced Technology Group, learning about QuickTime VR and what was initially a painful production process. It involved film! You’d mount a 35mm camera on a special tripod bracket, then shoot a series of overlapping images, then have the film processed, scanned, and transferred to Kodak PhotoCD discs. Finally, you’d stitch the images together with a $2000 software suite that required Apple’s MPW programming tool and lots of arcane typed commands.

Reminder: We shoot panos with our phones now.

Primitive as it was, QuickTime VR enchanted the amateur photographer in me. I’d been a technology journalist since the early 1980s, but computers and photography lived in disconnected circles of my life’s Venn diagram. In the 90s, those circles intersected and my job got a lot more fun.

In 1997, I took a QuickTake camera on a seven-week, 26-state road trip, shooting QuickTake photos and producing QuickTime VR movies along the way.

Between 1997 and 2001, I participated in a series of worldwide QuickTime VR celebrations called A Wrinkle in Time. Four times a year, dozens of QuickTime VR photographers around the world shot panoramas at the moment of the equinoxes and solstices.

Our work was published on the web, and visitors could revel in virtual views of each participant’s world – some shot at night, others by day, some in snow, others in Hawaii, but all taken at the same time. The project made the world feel smaller; it was a beautiful example of the promise of the web, where everyone had a voice that wasn’t drowned out by social networks and their ads and algorithms.

QuickTime VR was embraced by content creators of all kinds. Publishers produced commercial CD-ROMs whose panoramas enabled virtual travel – to other countries, to lost Mayan cities, to Star Trek’s USS Enterprise. On the web, museums and universities created virtual exhibits showcasing exotic places such as the pyramids of Giza and exotic objects such as primitive hearing aids. Architects and real estate agents created walkthroughs. Photographers took us to wilderness parks and Yosemite National Park. NBC News even published crime scene panoramas during the O.J. Simpson trial. And photographers, pro and amateur alike, explored this new way to capture the world around them.

Then Steve Jobs returned to Apple and everything began to change.

The Apple of 1997 had a broad product line that included multiple Mac models, numerous software initiatives (including QuickTime VR), and a family of peripherals – hard drives, printers, a scanner, and the QuickTake camera.

When Steve Jobs returned to Apple in 1997, he pruned that tree with a hatchet. Jobs cut 70 percent of the product line, chopping it down to four cornerstones: iMac, iBook, PowerBook, and Power Mac.

QuickTake cameras didn’t fit those quadrants. Apple introduced the QuickTake 200 in early 1997; by the end of that year, it had discontinued its entire camera line.

Over time, photos taken with the QuickTake 100 and 150 ended up in the file-format dustbin. Mac OS X couldn’t open them – you had to use the Classic environment, that stopgap compatibility layer that enabled Mac OS X to run the previous operating system.

When Classic went away in 2007, thousands – maybe millions – of photos became unreadable on anything other than an older computer. You could convert those photos using specialized utilities like Graphic Converter, but you couldn’t just open them in their native form.

QuickTime VR had a similar slow slide into obsolescence. Apple shipped its QuickTime VR Authoring Studio – an elegant software package for QTVR production – in November 1997. But the Advanced Technology Group where QTVR originated had already been shuttered a month prior.

Apple never developed an OS X version of Authoring Studio; QuickTime VR producers had to run it under the Classic environment. When Classic went away in 2007, it was either “use an old Mac” or switch to a third-party authoring tool.

By then, though, there was little reason. QuickTime VR was on its way to obscurity. The web killed the CD-ROM industry as publishers abandoned those silver platters in search of internet goldmines.

And the web itself changed. In the web’s early days, displaying rich-media content such as video required website visitors to download browser plug-ins. Messages like This website requires QuickTime or Download the Flash plug-in were common. This complicated life for web visitors and web designers alike.

Over time, the web community developed HTML standards that eliminated plug-ins. It was the right move – but it removed the ability to display QuickTime VR movies on a web page.

Apple continued to support QuickTime VR movies in its standalone QuickTime Player app, though even that viewing option wasn’t exactly obvious. You had to manually install QuickTime Player 7, which you either had to download or unearth from the macOS installation CD.

Then came 2019’s macOS Catalina. That version abandoned support for the 32-bit architecture of earlier Mac operating systems, and QuickTime Player 7 wouldn’t run. After that, attempting to open a QuickTime VR movie earned you an error message.

As for the web, many thousands of QuickTime VR movies were published during the format’s lifetime. Many still survive on old cobweb sites and on the Internet Archive. But they can’t be viewed with modern browsers or Apple’s current QuickTime Player.

Apple didn’t have to forsake these formats. It could have continued supporting the QuickTake photo format, and it could have adapted its QuickTime VR Authoring Studio software to run in Mac OS X and to export web panoramas that didn’t require browser plug-ins.

But business is business. Maintaining software isn’t free, and when the potential market is relatively small, spreadsheets are consulted and products die.

And so do those memories captured by the original QuickTake cameras. Does it matter? After all, the drives that held those photos can’t even be connected to a Mac made in this century. (Which illustrates the twin-bladed sword of digital preservation: file formats not only get abandoned, but files themselves get marooned on obsolete media.)

It isn’t up to us to say that the photos taken by the first mainstream digital cameras don’t matter. It was up to Apple, and Apple said they don’t.

Then there are the thousands of hours of QuickTime VR production effort expended by museums, educational institutions, photographers, and artists. A staff at Harvard University photographed and produced over 1200 QuickTime VR panoramas shot in and around the pyramids of Giza as part of its Digital Giza project. When Apple abandoned QuickTime VR – and when web browsers evolved beyond plug-ins – those movies became as inaccessible as a pharaoh’s tomb. (Happily, they’re being resurrected in HTML form in an updated website currently in development.)

It’s for these reasons that I created Vintage Viewer. It’s a free macOS app that lets you store, view, and export QuickTime VR movies and QuickTake photos.

I have a small but, to me, significant collection of QuickTake photos and QuickTime VR movies that I shot in the 1990s. I have an elderly PowerBook G4 where I can use the Classic environment to view them and to convert the QuickTake images into JPEG form. (There are a few modern macOS utilities that can convert QuickTake images, too.) But QuickTime VR movies are marooned in the past. I wanted to bring them into the present. I suspected I wasn’t alone.

I wasn’t wrong. As I explored Reddit and other online forums, I saw that others were also interested in these pioneering formats – including people who weren’t even alive when they debuted. (I saw phrases like “my dad had a QuickTake” more than once.) A tool that would enable vintage computing fans to explore and collect these forgotten formats – and that would enable the easy display and conversion of the VR movies created by nonprofits and others – would be my small contribution to the world of digital preservation.

Vintage Viewer converts QuickTake photos as well as QuickTime VR movies, but I don’t want to just convert them. I want to store them in their original formats to be first-class citizens on modern Macs.

You don’t have to create an HTML version of a QTVR movie in order to take it for a spin, or go through a conversion step to view a QuickTake photo. To Vintage Viewer, these formats are as fresh as an iPhone photo.

Rediscovering my vintage images rekindled my interest in these formats. By digging through a cabinet of old CD-ROMs and spending hours exploring the Internet Archive and other websites, I’ve built a collection of nearly 3,000 QuickTime VR movies.

I’ve also reconnected with some pioneering QTVR producers with whom I crossed paths thirty years ago. Photographers Richard Crowest, Doug Cope, and Erik Goetze generously tested Vintage Viewer and supplied some gorgeous movies that are included in a sample library that I include with Vintage Viewer. One of Doug Cope’s movies even has directional sound: as you pan, the soundscape moves between left and right speakers.

All three photographers embraced QuickTime VR in the 1990s and participated in the A Wrinkle in Time VR projects. Those projects, by the way, are all but lost. I did find one of them — the Winter Solstice 1997 edition — buried on a Macworld cover-mount CD-ROM that’s been uploaded to the Internet Archive. I retrieved their movies, but, lacking permission from each of its 80 participants, can’t publish them. My attempts to contact Robert Abbett, the projects’ producer, have been unsuccessful.

As for QuickTake images, I made contact through Reddit with a QuickTake fan in Australia who is only slightly older than the QuickTake cameras he collects. Dean Hucker has what he jokingly calls “a concerning amount of memorabilia surrounding” QuickTake cameras, including a collection of 16 of them. “There are a lot of people out there who do not want dead formats or their devices to disappear and that makes me very happy,” he told me. He’s building an app that can transfer photos from a QuickTake camera via a cable that enables a QuickTake 100 or 150 camera to connect to a USB port. His efforts inspired me to buy a QuickTake 100 on eBay and order the cable.

So I’ve not only rediscovered content made decades ago, I’ve also been inspired to create new content using those forgotten formats. My journey has come full circle – which, when you think about it, seems completely appropriate.

This weekend, Powerhouse Parramatta, a vast new arts and technology museum, opens in Sydney, Australia. Ben Luke speaks to The Art Newspaper’s Australian reporter, Elizabeth Fortescue, about the building and the scandal.

#9130. Biking and Hiking My Way Across Kyrgyzstan With a Fujifilm X-E5

Biking and Hiking My Way Across Kyrgyzstan With a Fujifilm X-E5

Sweating with labored breath, I push my fully loaded bicycle over Kyrgyzstan’s 12,400-foot Koi Dzolu Pass. The 23,000-foot peaks of the Pamir Mountains loom above while storms dance on either side, pelting me with occasional hail. In moments like this, I deeply appreciate every ounce shaved from my setup to stay mobile.

I am partway through a 25-day expedition traversing the third most mountainous country on Earth. On an unforgiving, remote route like this, you must haul everything: shelter, sleep systems, cold-weather clothing, repair parts, and rations. My primary role is documenting the journey through still photography.

Bikepacking is best described as multi-day bicycle touring taken off-road—navigating dirt tracks, gravel mountain passes, and singletrack trails rather than paved highways. Kyrgyzstan has quickly become a premier proving ground for world-class, high-altitude bikepacking routes.

Weight matters little on flat pavement, but it becomes everything when ascending. In Kyrgyzstan, gradients are often so steep that you end up pushing a heavy rig for miles at high elevation. Too much gear makes the expedition physically impossible; too little leaves you vulnerable to the unforgiving environment. Every piece of equipment must earn its place, especially the camera gear.

Adventure photography in this context is a dynamic hybrid of documentary, landscape, and action photography. There is no staging, no waiting for ideal light, and no stopping the team’s progress to set up a shot. Subjects move from your immediate foreground to a quarter-mile down the valley in seconds. You need immediate physical controls, sufficient dynamic range to save harsh mid-day contrast, and a gear setup that never slows you down.

Conventional wisdom suggests bringing a ruggedized, weather-sealed full-frame body or an ultra-tough Micro Four Thirds setup. Instead, I selected an unconventional combination for a backcountry traverse: a compact street-focused body paired with a motorized video lens.

The X-E5 provides a lightweight footprint — smaller and lighter than many Micro Four Thirds options — without sacrificing sensor resolution or shadow recovery. Its tactile dials allow instant on-the-fly adjustments to shutter speed, aperture, and focus zones.

Changing lenses on dusty, wind-swept high passes is a recipe for sensor contamination. I needed a single, versatile zoom with broad reach. The 18-120mm f/4 power zoom offered superior sharpness and reach compared to standard kit zooms, while staying significantly lighter than full-frame equivalents.

While power zooms are rarely the first choice for fast-paced still photography because of their electronic zoom response, the constant f/4 aperture provided adequate subject separation and allowed low ISO settings under shifting alpine light. And with practice, you learn to work around the zoom speed.

To add variety to the visual narrative, I packed two tiny specialty lenses:

The camera and three-lens setup weighed under three pounds and fit comfortably inside a compact waist pack worn while riding.

Pairing a rangefinder-style street camera with an electronically zoomed video lens might seem ill-suited for a rugged 1,000-kilometer crossing. Prior to the trip, I rigorously tested two bodies and three lenses on domestic shakedown rides to verify performance under load.

Modern camera gear is often pigeonholed into hyper-specific marketing categories. This expedition reinforced that understanding your gear’s nuances and tailoring its controls to your workflow matters far more than adhering to nominal camera genres.

After climbing the elevation equivalent of Mount Everest more than twice over 25 days, carrying a light, highly capable imaging system proved invaluable. Kyrgyzstan’s vast landscapes, nomadic culture, and dramatic passes demand respect — and an agile camera kit ready for every turn in the trail.

#9128. Strangers Raise $800,000 for Red Baron Worker Filmed Being Harassed by Prankster

Strangers Raise $800,000 for Red Baron Worker Filmed Being Harassed by Prankster

A Red Baron pizza worker who was filmed being harassed by a prankster pretending to steal $20 from him has paused donations on a GoFundMe page set up on his behalf after it neared $800,000.

The prank severely backfired on the young man filming the video after the Red Baron worker lost his temper with him.

Red Baron pizza stocker goes viral for going off on kid trying to prank him for a social media video. $400k has now been raised for him online & Red Baron says he’s employee of the month. Crazy this “pranker” uploaded this video at all. https://t.co/DYjhP4JvlQ

— Clay Travis (@ClayTravis) October 30, 2026

The wannabe influencer approaches the Red Baron worker, known only as Walt Z, as he was stacking shelves in a grocery store. In the video, he asks for the time, and when Walt gets out his phone, he plays the Apple Pay sound and says, “thanks for the $10.”

It appears the prankster is filming on Meta Ray-Bans and has at least one accomplice recording nearby.

Walt initially walks away, but the prankster comes back for more and says, “Thank you for the $20.” This causes Walt to snap.

“I don’t have time for this cr*p in my life; my life is hard enough as it is,” says Walt, visibly upset. “I got kids at home who went to bed without me… and I was supposed to be at home an hour ago, and I’m still out here working.”

“I’ve got to get up at five in the morning and do 10 more stores,” Walt continues. “So this is not a joke to me.”

“You’re probably making money off this, and I can’t even pay my goddamn mortgage,” Walt adds. “And I’ve got four kids at home.”

It’s a powerful tirade that caught many people’s attention. Fortune reports that the GoFundMe page was set up by a man called Luke Oakenshield who has never met Walt but wanted to track him down after watching the video, which was filmed back in August but only published recently.

The campaign raised $100,000 in three days, with former Republican presidential hopeful Vivek Ramaswamy donating $38,000. After it came close to $800,000, Walt posted a message on GoFundMe thanking people for their support and announcing that he is pausing donations and urging people to support other families in need. He adds that he won’t be giving any interviews.

Call them rage-bait pranks or clout-chasing harassment; these types of videos are a modern phenomenon that has its roots firmly in photography.

Meta’s smart glasses, which were apparently used to film the video of Walt, are just the latest tool in a long line of clandestine cameras. But with this kind of camera technology being made available to every Tom, Dick, and Harry, it’s becoming clear that society is losing its tolerance for such cruel pranksters.

#9127. Former workshop converted into contemporary Japanese home with "a sense of the passage of time"

Japanese studio Akio Isshiki Architects has transformed the home and workshop of a sheet-metal craftsperson in the castle town of Tatsuno into a modern house with a latticed wooden gate.

Architect Akio Isshiki, the founder of the eponymous studio, said he had to take a lot of different aspects into consideration when designing the project.

Among them was the location, as the two-storey home is located in a historic town known for being built around a medieval mountain castle.

“The project explores an architecture that responds naturally to the many contexts and conditions surrounding the house: the historic streetscape of the former castle town, traces of the former owner’s work as a sheet-metal craftsman, the client’s wishes, and practical constraints such as building regulations and structural requirements,” Isshiki told Dezeen.

For example, while the client had initially wanted a deck that would be connected to the dining room, the compact site made such a design difficult.

Instead, Isshiki removed part of the existing interior of the dining room to create a terrace space, which also includes a traditional-style engawa platform to connect the home with the garden.

Here, the studio added a sliding glass door that was designed so that its frame is hidden in the wall when it is closed, creating the impression of a fully open space.

Isshiki also wanted the 144-square-metre contemporary home to nod to more traditional Japanese houses.

“To sit comfortably within the townscape that retains the character of a former castle town, the spatial principles of traditional machiya – Japanese old townhouses – have been incorporated into this contemporary residence,” he explained.

“Examples include a long approach leading towards a bright garden at the back of the house, and an engawa, a narrow platform that connects the interior with the garden.”

The former workshop in front of the house was treated as a public-facing space. Where it looks onto the street, Isshiki added a large latticed, sliding gate, made from cedar, as well as a narrow entrance porch.

Inside, this multi-functional space becomes almost like an enclosed terrace. Here, Isshiki also added a small wooden toilet, inspired by those found in traditional machiya houses.

The studio kept a number of objects that were found in the old workshop, including a metal ring that now decorates a handrail next to the indoor staircase.

Isshiki relocated this staircase so that it sits at the front of the house, in the old workshop space – one of the biggest changes made to the layout of the house. A stone underneath the first step provides a space to remove footwear.

Isshiki’s studio used wood throughout the renovation, as the original building was made from timber and this material worked best with the existing neighbourhood, including a historic shrine that stands directly across from the house.

“The newly added wood, including the doors, is cedar, which is also the primary wood used in the original structure,” Isshiki said.

“Cedar is one of the most widely used types of wood in Japan and is readily available,” he continued.

“The contrast between the lighter new cedar and the existing cedar, which has darkened with age, brings a sense of the passage of time to the house.”

Akio Isshiki Architects also used earthen plasterwork in the home to create a tactile feel, while Tunisian tiles add decorative patterns in the kitchen. Here, the studio also created a built-in, combined wooden dining table and work surface.

On the top floor, which has a bedroom, living room and guest room, the studio mostly kept the original layout.

However, it added a sunken study space and a tokonoma, a recessed area used to display flowers and pieces of art.

“Through careful consideration of spatial dimensions, light, connections to the outdoors, materials, details, and relationships between spaces, the aim was to create a home that feels comfortable as a whole,” Isshiki concluded about the renovation.

His studio has previously designed a charred-cedar-clad house in Osaka and married old and new within a combined home and restaurant.
