The Intermedia and Digital Arts (IMDA) MFA Program at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County (UMBC) invites applications from interdisciplinary artists seeking to expand or reinvent their practice. IMDA is a three-year, 60-credit graduate program with private studios in Baltimore’s progressive art community. IMDA faculty are nationally and internationally recognized artists, filmmakers, designers, and scholars with active exhibition and publication records.

IMDA offers a multidisciplinary program with one on one feedback from world-renown visiting artists, independent teaching opportunities, professional exhibition venues, and dedicated fabrication, media, and physical computing labs. UMBC is a top-ranked R1 Research University with an inclusive culture that provides students with access to research centers and broad interdisciplinary opportunities. Graduate Assistantships that include full tuition remission, health insurance, stipends, and other merit based financial support are available.

IMDA supports a broad range of interdisciplinary creative practices including socially-engaged, community-based, interactive, and studio-based artworks made using cutting edge and traditional methods and technologies. Alumni present their work at distinguished venues around the world, receive prestigious grants and residency awards, and are academic leaders at internationally recognized art academies and universities.

"Is Social Security taxable?" is one of the most common tax questions retirees ask — and the answer frustrates almost everyone: it depends. Depending on your total income, anywhere from 0% to 85% of your Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax. The tax was introduced in 1983, originally affecting about 10% of recipients. Today, because the income thresholds were never indexed for inflation, roughly 56% of Social Security recipients pay tax on their benefits.

The good news: even in the worst case, you'll never pay tax on 100% of your Social Security. The bad news: the formula for calculating the taxable amount is one of the most convoluted in the entire tax code. In this guide, we'll break it down into plain English, show you exactly how to calculate what you owe, and — most importantly — share strategies the FI community uses to reduce or eliminate the tax entirely.

The IRS uses a special formula called "combined income" (also called "provisional income") to determine how much of your Social Security benefits are taxable. Here's the formula:

Combined Income = Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) + Nontaxable Interest + Half of Social Security Benefits

The resulting number determines which taxation tier you fall into. Notice that the thresholds haven't changed since 1993 — they are not adjusted for inflation, which means more retirees cross into taxable territory every year.

Important: "Up to 85% taxed" does not mean you pay an 85% tax rate. It means 85% of your benefits are added to your taxable income and taxed at your ordinary income rate. If you're in the 22% bracket and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you'd owe 22% on $25,500 — roughly $5,610.

This is the most common Social Security tax confusion. When the IRS says "up to 85% of benefits are taxable," it means 85% of your benefit amount gets added to your taxable income and taxed at your regular rate. If your marginal rate is 22% and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you owe about $5,610 — not $25,500. The effective tax rate on your full benefit in this example is about 18.7%.

Let's walk through a real example. Meet Sarah: she's 67, single, retired, and receives $24,000 per year in Social Security benefits. She also has $18,000 in IRA withdrawals and $2,000 in municipal bond interest.

Step 2: Determine the Tier Sarah is single with combined income of $32,000, which falls between $25,000 and $34,000. She's in the 50% tier — up to 50% of her benefits may be taxable.

Step 3: Calculate the Taxable Amount The actual calculation involves comparing two formulas and taking the lesser amount. For the 50% tier:

Sarah adds $3,500 to her other taxable income. At a 12% marginal rate, that's roughly $420 in additional federal tax on her Social Security.

Beyond federal taxes, 13 states also tax Social Security benefits to some degree as of 2026. Each state has its own thresholds and exemption amounts:

The remaining 37 states and Washington, D.C. do not tax Social Security benefits at all. If you're planning where to retire, this is a meaningful factor — especially if you have substantial SS benefits combined with other retirement income.

The FI community has identified several strategies that can significantly reduce the tax bite on Social Security benefits. The key insight: since taxation is based on combined income, controlling your income in retirement is the lever.

This is the single most powerful strategy. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula. If you retire early (before Social Security age), you have a window of low-income years to convert Traditional IRA/401(k) money to Roth.

Example: Between ages 55 and 67, you convert $500,000 from your Traditional IRA to a Roth — paying tax at rates as low as 10-12%. When you claim Social Security at 67, your Roth withdrawals don't push you into a higher SS taxation tier. Instead of 85% of your benefits being taxable, you might pay tax on 0-50%.

The math is dramatic over a 25+ year retirement. Converting at 12% during early retirement to avoid 22%+ taxation on Social Security for decades produces enormous tax savings.

Every dollar of AGI pushes you toward the 50% or 85% taxation tiers. Strategic levers include:

Once you reach age 70.5, you can donate up to $105,000 per year directly from your IRA to a qualified charity. This satisfies your Required Minimum Distribution (RMD) without the distribution being included in your AGI. Lower AGI means lower combined income, which means less Social Security is taxable.

For charitably inclined retirees, QCDs are one of the most tax-efficient giving strategies available — they simultaneously reduce your income tax AND reduce the tax on your Social Security benefits.

Delaying Social Security from 62 to 70 increases your benefit by roughly 77%. But there's a secondary benefit: during the delay years, you have more room to do Roth conversions at low tax rates without Social Security benefits adding to your combined income. The combination of larger benefits and lower taxation on those benefits makes delay doubly powerful for tax optimization.

If you retire before claiming Social Security, you have a golden window for Roth conversions. With little or no earned income and no SS benefits, you can convert Traditional IRA money to Roth at the lowest tax brackets of your lifetime. Every dollar you convert is a dollar that will never increase the tax on your Social Security benefits. This window closes permanently once you start claiming.

A step-by-step walkthrough for estimating what you owe.

List your AGI from all sources: IRA/401(k) withdrawals, pension income, wages, dividends, capital gains, rental income. Get your total Social Security benefit from your SSA-1099 form.

Pro tip: Don't forget nontaxable municipal bond interest — it counts in the combined income formula even though it's not on your 1040.

Add your AGI + nontaxable interest + half of your Social Security benefits. This "combined income" number determines your taxation tier.

Compare your combined income to the thresholds: Single — $25K (50% tier), $34K (85% tier). Married filing jointly — $32K (50% tier), $44K (85% tier).

For the 50% tier: take 50% of combined income above the lower threshold (capped at 50% of benefits). For the 85% tier: the calculation is more complex — use IRS Publication 915 worksheet or tax software.

Pro tip: Tax software handles this automatically. If doing it by hand, IRS Publication 915 has the complete worksheet.

The taxable portion of your Social Security gets added to your other taxable income and taxed at your marginal rate. Check if your state also taxes Social Security.

For single filers, Social Security becomes partially taxable when combined income exceeds $25,000 (50% tier) and up to 85% taxable above $34,000. For married filing jointly, the thresholds are $32,000 (50% tier) and $44,000 (85% tier). These thresholds have not changed since 1993 and are not indexed for inflation.

No. Social Security benefits are not earned income. They are classified as unearned income for tax purposes. This distinction matters for things like the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), IRA contribution eligibility, and the Social Security earnings test (which only applies to earned income like wages and self-employment).

No — and this is why Roth accounts are so powerful in retirement. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula used to determine Social Security taxation. Converting Traditional IRA money to Roth before claiming Social Security can dramatically reduce the tax on your benefits for life.

Yes. File Form W-4V with the Social Security Administration to have federal income tax withheld from your benefits. You can choose 7%, 10%, 12%, or 22% withholding. This avoids the surprise of a large tax bill at filing time. State tax withholding varies by state.

Social Security benefits are included in the Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) calculation that determines Medicare Part B and Part D premium surcharges (IRMAA). High-income retirees can pay significantly more for Medicare — up to 3.4 times the standard premium. Managing MAGI in retirement affects both Social Security taxation and Medicare costs.

There have been numerous proposals to reform Social Security taxation, including indexing the thresholds for inflation, raising the taxable percentage above 85%, or eliminating the tax entirely. As of 2026, no changes have been enacted. The thresholds have remained unchanged since 1993, meaning inflation automatically pushes more retirees into taxable territory each year.

Yes, Social Security benefits can be taxable — up to 85% of your benefits may be added to your taxable income depending on your combined income. The thresholds are low ($25,000 single, $32,000 married) and haven't been adjusted for inflation since 1993, catching more retirees every year. The single most powerful strategy is Roth conversions during early retirement years before claiming Social Security. Every dollar in a Roth account is a dollar that won't push your Social Security into the taxable zone. Plan your retirement income sources deliberately, and you can reduce or eliminate this tax entirely.

#9081. A View From the Easel: Natali Bravo-Barbee

“As a mother, there are so many spaces in my life that are organized around other people’s needs. The studio is a space where I get to return to myself.”

Welcome to the 362nd installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Natali Bravo-Barbee moves between modes of motherhood and making while testing the limits of what photography can be.

Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.

How long have you been working in this space?

Three years (the spaces change every year).

An average day in the studio is rarely average. As an artist and mother, I have learned to build flexibility into my studio practice. My days usually start once my children are in school, around 8:30 or 9am. I start by making a to-do list. There is an incredible amount of administrative work that is part of being an artist and maintaining a studio practice, so I usually try to get those tasks out of the way first.

Once I clear that list, I can pick up where I left off creatively. I usually have my mate and a thermos of hot water with me, and I sip as I settle back into whatever I was working on. Sometimes that means exposing cyanotypes that I coated the day before. Most recently, it has meant going through the photographs I selected to print and spending time with the images before deciding how I want to move forward with them. I’m constantly moving between making, looking, researching, and organizing. For me, all of those things are part of the studio practice.

The space affects my work quite a bit, particularly because I move between my home studio and my studio on Governors Island. They create two very different conditions for working.

When I’m working from home, the day is much more fragmented. I’m able to work around my family’s schedule, but I’m also surrounded by everything that comes with running a household: laundry, groceries, dinner, and the general visual noise of home. Sometimes I’ll be in the middle of something and realize I need to switch gears completely. There is always another task waiting for me.

#9080. OEB Architects channels 1980s interiors for London extension

Glossy ceramic tiles, a glass-block wall and a leafy garden were intended to evoke tropical modernism and 1980s interiors for London Tropical, an extension to a Victorian terrace designed by local practice OEB Architects.

OEB Architects was tasked with creating an open-plan kitchen and dining space at the rear of the three-storey terrace in Southwark that would feel “surrounded” by its garden.

“The project considers how an extension to a typical Victorian outrigger can connect to its modest urban garden,” Gabriel George, project architect at the studio, told Dezeen.

“It explores the layering and overlaying of translucent and reflective materials and bold, graphic objects to give a nuanced and varied space through all seasons, contributing to a feeling of living surrounded by the garden,” he added.

Instead of filling the width of the site, OEB Architects pulled the extension back from the southern boundary, allowing it to be lined with both a glass-block wall and full-height windows that address a courtyard and side return.

This openness continues around to an end wall with full-height sliding glass doors, not only framing the garden but allowing the space to be entirely opened up to a patio surrounded by leafy planting.

“The clients were keen not to have a conventional top-lit infill extension, with a roof light sloping down to the boundary, as is common among extensions to Victorian terraces,” George told Dezeen.

“This expansion is set back from the boundary, providing both a passage and a new outlook from inside,” he continued.

“This results in two new external spaces, a courtyard addressing the main house and the rear garden serving the extension. Each is wrapped in full-height glazing with a range of transparencies responding to each view.”

The extension’s interior is defined by a kitchen island clad in glossy green tiles and a column clad in shiny red tiles, acting as spatial anchors that contrast the otherwise minimalist, white-painted surfaces, stone floors and pale timber carpentry and ceilings.

Both the glossy tiles and translucent glass-block wall were used to create a changing quality of light throughout the day, with the south-facing courtyard able to be screened off via translucent curtains that further add to this effect.

“The material and spatial ideas were driven by conversations with the clients discussing architectural precedents along with art, graphic and design references, including mid-century West Coast American case study houses, 80s interiors and tropical modernism,” George said.

The extension’s floor level steps upwards to meet the back of the main home, where the connecting corridor has been flanked by a bathroom and pantry space.

OEB Architects was founded in 2018 by directors Tessa Baird and David Eland, and has offices in London and Brighton. The studio previously completed another extension for a home in Tottenham, which expanded a semi-detached home with a simple blockwork and timber structure.

#9079. Jordan Poorman Cocker’s Vision of Global Indigeneity

The curator, who just organized a major rehang of Indigenous art at Crystal Bridges, reflects on the ways institutions can create space for Native artists to flourish.

BENTONVILLE, Ark. — On October 16 and 17, before a room full of Indigenous artists, curators, and scholars at the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art’s symposium on contemporary Native art, Jordan Poorman Cocker opened with a land acknowledgment. Founded by Walmart heiress Alice Walton, the museum sits on the ancestral homelands of the Osage Nation, Quapaw Nation, and Caddo Nation, who were forcibly relocated in the 19th century. Poorman Cocker, a Kiowa and Tongan citizen, was hired as the museum’s Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA) officer and first full-time curator of Indigenous art in 2023. She makes the hour-and-a-half drive in from Tahlequah, Oklahoma, the Cherokee Nation’s capital and home to several nations coerced there during the removal era.

The two-day gathering coincided with the reinstallation of contemporary Native art in the museum, which Poorman Cocker spearheaded alongside Ashley Holland (Cherokee Nation) as a way to showcase the diversity of style, medium, and living Native artists across Indian Country, including works by citizens of the ancestral Tribes in Arkansas. Choctaw and Cherokee multi-disciplinary artist Jeffrey Gibson delivered a keynote address, and later spoke to an audience with Poorman Cocker while beading; Diné weaver Melissa Cody traced the lineage of her work in dialogue with her mother Lola Cody; and Lehuauakea delivered a workshop based in her traditional kapa practice.

Poorman Cocker’s own curatorial practice draws on her background in museum studies at Victoria University of Wellington in New Zealand and the global spirit of Indigeneity, which rejects the divisive borders of colonial nation-states. Like many Native curators, she cites the groundbreaking 2019 exhibition Hearts of Our People: Native Women Artists at the Minneapolis Institute of Art as a major source of inspiration. That sentiment was echoed by Kiowa beadwork artist Terri Greeves, who spoke at the symposium alongside other Kiowa Tribe members and matriarchs. Poorman Cocker is also a beadwork and textile artist herself, rooted in Kiowa and Tongan beadwork and textile conventions.

In an email correspondence with Hyperallergic, Poorman Cocker shared more about a recent landmark commission, telling a fuller history of Native art, and what it means to bring Kiowa voices into the museum. The interview has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity.

Hyperallergic: Tell me more about what the reinstallation at Crystal Bridges represents for Indigenous art in this moment. What is it trying to change? How did the 114,000-square-foot expansion inform the museum’s capacity to provide ongoing opportunities to collaborate with the featured artists?

JPC: The impetus is to recenter two primary areas: the Indigenous art collection and the craft collection. Native American and Indigenous art are foundational to every American art collection. Over the years, I have written acquisition proposals for artworks sourced from the gallery system and annual markets, with an emphasis on artist commissions.  Crystal Bridges is better positioned to nourish the art ecosystem, including many artists — particularly those whose work aligns with intergenerational art forms, who need financial support for artist apprenticeships, community classes, and other art education efforts that sustain artist communities and knowledge systems.

Indigenous and Native art makes up about 3% of Crystal Bridges’s permanent collection. The museum sector writ large has a long way to go to better present Indigenous artists and stories.

#9078. DC Protesters Slam Trump's Fascist Triumphal Arch

A group of 50 used puppets and a fake arch to deliver the point that Americans are against the "Arc de Trump."

WASHINGTON, DC — South of Memorial Circle, within eyeshot of the Lincoln Memorial and John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame, more than 50 protesters gathered yesterday, November 5, to oppose Trump’s proposed 250-foot Triumphal Arch ahead of the National Capital Planning Commission’s (NCPC) final meeting to vote on the project.

Hours after the NCPC approved the arch in an 8–4 vote, a district court judge granted the District of Columbia and Virginia a 14-day restraining order to halt construction.

At the event organized by Third Act DC, an environmental and pro-democracy action group for area residents aged 60 and up, two Virginia Congressional representatives, an Arlington County Board member, and Greg Werkheiser, an attorney with Cultural Heritage Partners, spoke about how the arch would infringe on the architectural and spiritual purpose of the space. He was one of two people associated with lawsuits that the District of Columbia and Virginia, the Arlington County Board, as well as Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian filed against the National Park Service and Department of the Interior in opposition to the arch.

Elon Musk is winding down production, and I won’t be shedding a tear.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Tesla is winding down Cybertruck production. Elon Musk has confirmed that manufacturing at the Texas Gigafactory will scale back around mid-2027 to make room for more Cybercab robotaxis. And so ends one of the strangest design experiments in automotive history, one riddled with ugly mistakes and design fails.

Okay, ‘ends’ might be jumping the gun a little. Elon Musk hasn’t said outright that the Cybertruck is being discontinued, and it’s not clear whether production could move elsewhere. But as posted on X, Texas is the only known facility equipped to build its rather specialised parts, so the writing is pretty clearly on the wall.

Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab productionNovember 6, 2026

It was always going to be a tough sell. When Musk unveiled the Cybertruck in 2019, he promised a revolution in pickup design. What we got looked like it had rolled straight out of a dystopian sci-fi movie: angular stainless steel, sharp edges and a comically oversized windscreen with one comically oversized, slow wiper. Different? Absolutely. I’ll give it that.

The reaction was instant, with designers and the internet having a field day. We covered the fallout in our 2019 look at the designers taking aim at Tesla’s Cybertruck, and the argument over whether it’s genius or a low-poly disaster has never really gone away.

The launch event set the tone for everything that followed. Tesla’s chief designer, Franz von Holzhausen, took a metal ball to the supposedly unbreakable windows, and they promptly shattered. Not exactly the show of strength Tesla was after, and a pretty cringe bit of live theatre for a truck sold on its toughness.

Then came the production delays, shifting specs, and a price that jumped from the original promises. Musk once talked about selling 250,000 Cybertrucks a year. According to Kelley Blue Book figures reported by Reuters, Tesla sold just 20,237 in the US during 2025, down 48% from the year before. Yikes.

We’ve been tracking the Cybertruck’s design misadventures since that first reveal, and it constantly surprised us for all the wrong reasons. We looked at early Cybertruck sketches that show how different the finished design could have been, and even imagined what happens when other carmakers go angular in our look at what every car would look like as a Cybertruck. The Mini Cooper, the first car I ever owned, in particular, wasn’t the looker it used to be.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

But the issues ran deeper than looks. In June 2023, we reported on leaked design and engineering flaws that made the Cybertruck sound even more terrifying, including problems with braking, handling, noise and water leaks. Then there’s the branding. In April 2024, we rounded up the six worst Cybertruck design fails, from that questionable logo to the accelerator pedal recall.

Then came the reports of bits falling off and the off-road truck getting stuck in mud – are you getting the picture? In March 2025, another Cybertruck design disaster emerged involving exterior panels coming loose. It’s quite something when a truck styled like an armoured tank can’t keep its own bodywork on.

To be fair, the Cybertruck was never meant to be universally loved, and ambition may have overtaken the practicalities of mass production. Musk wanted a vehicle that looked like nothing else on the road, and he got it. But good product design has to do more than turn heads. It has to work, make sense for the people buying it, and survive the rather less glamorous reality of everyday use, whether it's offroading or just driving to the shops without a bumper falling off. The Cybertruck struggled on all three counts.

That heavy, angular build also proved a barrier in Europe, where it failed to meet pedestrian-safety requirements. And the stainless-steel exterior may look suitably apocalyptic, but it brought its own manufacturing and finishing headaches.

Then there’s the branding. That huge angular silhouette was already shouting loud enough, and the aggressive typography and Cybertruck identity just pushed the whole thing further into concept-car territory. I love seeing designers take a big swing at something genuinely unusual. But there’s bold, and then there’s a design that seems to have skipped the bit where someone asks, ‘Is this actually a good idea?’

For contrast, check out some of the best car logos on the road today. Ferrari, Porsche and Mercedes have built enduring identities for a reason: they tell you something about the product and its heritage without yelling at you.

Tesla is now turning its attention to the Cybercab, its two-seat autonomous taxi, with the Texas factory being repurposed to ramp up production. The company is also pushing harder into AI and robotics, so the Cybertruck’s exit is part of a much bigger change of direction.

We’ve already had a glimpse of what that next chapter might look like, and Tesla’s Cybercab has its own rather silly design fail. Maybe the Cybertruck’s lessons haven’t quite sunk in yet.

So here’s to the end of the Cybertruck era, one that made us smile more than it had drivers, and to whatever the Cybercab era has in store.

#9076. Meg Onli and Zack Winokur to Curate 2028 Whitney Biennial

Having co-curated the 2024 Biennial, Onli returns to the next edition with Winokur, who founded the American Modern Opera Company.

Meg Onli, an organizer behind some of the Whitney Museum of American Art's signature exhibitions, and Zack Winokur, a performing arts director and co-founder, are the co-curators for the 2028 Whitney Biennial, the museum announced today, November 6.

“Meg is one of the most compelling curatorial voices working today, with an extraordinary ability to champion artists and bring fresh perspectives to the history of American art," Scott Rothkopf, director of the Whitney, said in a statement. "Zack is an equally inventive artistic programmer who has become one of the leading voices of his generation through groundbreaking work across opera, theater, dance, and the visual arts. Their partnership promises a radical new vision for the 2028 Biennial."

The news comes just two months after the 2026 Biennial closed and a month after unionized staff at the museum dodged a full-blown strike ahead of Roy Lichtenstein: Like New, a blockbuster retrospective co-curated by Onli. The Whitney union was one of four New York City museum unions under United Auto Workers 2110 — along with the Brooklyn Museum, the American Folk Art Museum, and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum — that voted to strike amid drawn-out contract negotiations over low compensation, benefits, and workplace conditions. Hours before the planned strike, unionized staffers ratified their second contract and secured a new wage floor, increased parental and bereavement leave, and stronger safety provisions, among other amendments.

First joining the museum as curator-at-large in 2023, Onli co-curated the 2024 Whitney Biennial, Even Better Than the Real Thing, with Chrissie Iles. That same year, Onli was promoted to Nancy and Fred Poses Curator to lead the Whitney’s painting and sculpture acquisition committee, bringing her previous experience as director and curator of the Underground Museum in Los Angeles and associate curator at the Institute of Contemporary Art at the University of Pennsylvania.

“From the Whitney’s early Annuals to its many subsequent iterations, the Biennial has a rich history of reinvention that is already giving us much to think about," Onli said in a statement. "I couldn’t be more excited to explore what the Biennial can be alongside Zack, who is such a dynamic thinker, and to see where our conversations with artists lead."

Winokur is the co-founder of the American Modern Opera Company, an interdisciplinary collective comprised of 17 singers, musicians, dancers, and other performing artists. He also served as artistic director for Little Island on Pier 55 and NYPopsUp, a statewide initiative aimed at opening performing arts spaces after COVID-19.

“I’m honored to be curating the Whitney Biennial with Meg,” Winokur added in a statement. “Our shared desire to center objects and people and the collision between them already echoes our collaboration. It’s that energy that makes the dialogue with her so fun and inspiring."

Dating back to 1932, the Whitney Biennial remains the longest-running survey of American art, with more than 3,600 artists participating in the exhibition to date. The 83rd edition is slated to open in March 2028.

#9075. Pablo Helguera to Helm the New School’s Vera List Center

Upon his appointment, the artist reflected on the urgency he feels to “make sense of rapidly unfolding events, question prevailing narratives, and imagine alternative futures.”

Artist, educator, and writer Pablo Helguera has been appointed as the new director of the New School's Vera List Center for Art and Politics (VLC), succeeding Senior Director and Chief Curator Carin Kuoni, who steered the arts-driven research center for 22 years. Helguera was also tapped as the director of the university's art collection, which consists of over 2,000 postwar and contemporary works.

Having entered the new role this Monday, November 2, Helguera takes the reins after six years of serving as an assistant professor and director of the Arts Management and Entrepreneurship graduate program at the New School's College of Performing Arts. Helguera was previously the director of adult and academic programs at the Museum of Modern Art for over a decade.

As an artist, Helguera centers social engagement through public performance and installation, archival findings, pedagogical practices, and traditional media. Among his most famous projects is “The School of Panamerican Unrest” (2006), a cross-continental road trip from Anchorage, Alaska, to Ushuaia, capital of Argentina's southernmost Tierra del Fuego province, that culminated in over 100 public engagement events across 25 cities in 20 countries. Helguera is also known for developing Librería Donceles, a traveling used bookstore with thousands of Spanish-language texts that visited 13 countries.

The social, ideological, and cultural frameworks of language are prominent themes that Helguera explores in his practice, which coalesces with his roles in education and public programming. He became a Guggenheim Fellow in 2008, and additional recognitions include support from the Franklin Furnace Archive, Art Matters, and Blade of Grass; a Creative Capital grant; and an honorary doctorate from the Kansas City Art Institute.

#9074. The Jewish Sisters in Renoir’s “Pink and Blue”

Author Catherine Ostler follows the lives of the two cherubic girls, whose rarefied lives in an elite, artistic French family would be toppled by the horrors of the Holocaust.

In 1881, at the dawn of the Belle Époque, Pierre-Auguste Renoir steps into the ritzy Parisian townhouse of the Cahen d’Anvers family to paint a double portrait of four-year-old Alice and six-year-old Elisabeth, daughters of the Antwerp-born Jewish banker Louis and salonnière Louise. In the finished canvas, “Pink and Blue, the Misses Cahen d’Anvers” (1881), the two cherubic girls with rosy cheeks and reddish-golden hair stand in a sumptuous salon, holding hands, enveloped in a cloud of lace and satin.

This “duet of sugared-almond-colored-sweetness,” as author Catherine Ostler puts it, and “La Petite Irène” (1880) — a portrait of their older sister, painted by the artist a year earlier — are the springboard for her book The Renoir Girls.

From the opening pages, Ostler’s exhaustively researched, deftly structured book conjures the gilded world of fin-de-siècle Paris, leading the reader through the brocade curtains of the Cahen d’Anvers family’s dazzling life as members of the Jewish elite to their tragic end in the Holocaust. At center stage is the art patron Louise; Marcel Proust was a close friend, and her famed salon drew artists, writers, and members of the conservative Catholic aristocracy alike. And there was her lover, the collector and art critic Charles Ephrussi, who had arranged for Renoir to paint the girls and was suspected of being Alice's biological father. But alongside this world of opulence and privilege, in which every ball and horse race the Cahen d’Anvers women attended made it into the newspaper columns, ran another Paris, one divided by inequality and political instability, which fueled antisemitism and punctured the sisters’ rarefied lives.

Ostler captures the collision of these two worlds with the dreadful inevitability of a train derailing in slow motion. Despite the French Revolution and the Napoleonic Code having ensured equal rights for France’s Jewish population, antisemitism was insidious across the country. It took the form of resentful grumbles “aligned with the times”: “I really give up with the Jews,” wrote Renoir to a friend complaining about Louis’s “stingy” payment. It took the form of the anti-Jewish venom of diarist and, perversely, frequent visitor to Louise’s salon, Edmond de Goncourt. And it reached its peak with the Dreyfus Affair of 1894 to 1906, in which a Jewish French army officer was framed for treason. While the Cahen d’Anvers and their close circle belonged to the Dreyfusard camp, some members of the Jewish elite — the haute Juiverie — seemed to waltz through this moral and political crisis, which polarized the nation. Amid political assassinations and anarchist bombs, Louise and Louis went on worshiping the 18th century and restoring Château Champs-sur-Marne to its ancient regime glory. Meanwhile, the girls continued on their path to assimilation, not without puzzling twists and heartbreaks.

In 1895, at the height of the Dreyfus Affair, a 21-year-old Elisabeth converts to Catholicism and marries a penniless aristocrat, whom she later divorces. In 1897, the adventurous, anglophile Alice meets the ambitious British Colonel Charles Townshend in Egypt and, a year later, ties the knot in an Anglican ceremony at her parents' chateau. And Irène, the only one to enter into an arranged marriage, leaves her husband, Moïse de Camondo, for the head of his stable. But in the 1930s, the glittering carousel comes to a screeching halt, and Ostler’s account of the Nazis’ occupation descends into a harrowing tale of persecution.

The Cahen d'Anvers’s love for France and desire to belong run deep throughout the book. Their forebears adapted their surname to sound more aristocratic; Irène’s son, Nissim de Camondo, fought for France and died in World War I. They gave generously to philanthropic causes, restored dilapidated historical properties, and later donated them to the French state. But neither their wealth nor their belief in the values of the Enlightenment could shield them from the catastrophe to come, and four members of the family perished in concentration camps, including Elisabeth, who, in 1944, old and infirm, was betrayed by the mayor of the village where she was hiding and died in or on the way to Auschwitz.

As for the paintings, “Pink and Blue” now hangs at the Museu de Arte de São Paulo Assis Chateaubriand, where it is one of the institution’s most popular works. “La Petite Irène,” on the other hand, was looted by the Nazis, restituted to Irène, and then was subsequently bought by the Swiss arms dealer and war profiteer Emil Georg Bührle. It is now on view at the Kunsthaus Zürich, its sweetness belying a story of devastation and betrayal amid one of the darkest chapters of European history — a story Ostler’s engrossing, kaleidoscopic chronicle vividly brings to life.

#9073. London’s National Gallery publishes recommendations of its citizens’ assembly

The recommendations comes as the museum plans for a major new extension

The National Gallery in London says in a new report that a new public body founded to advise the UK national museum on its future policy and direction has given it “a mandate to be brave”.

The new initiative, titled NG Citizens, was announced in July last year. The museum aims to transform its governance model by launching a citizens’ assembly made up of members of public from across the UK.

The accompanying report outlines the recommendations and shared vision developed by 55 participants who took part in five sessions between November 2025 and March 2026.

The new assembly recommended that the museum should “embrace and grow commercial opportunities” and also use technology to support personalised itineraries, especially for “under-represented” groups, among other objectives.

Other key recommendations for the museum include being more informative about its wider history, representation and context behind the art. The collection also urgently needs to be a true reflection of the UK, said the assembly members.

The overarching question put to the assembly members was: “What do you want from the UK’s National Gallery? How can it bring people and paintings together in authentic and meaningful ways, now and in the future?” A series of eight principles, defined as the “core values that guide how the gallery can move towards the vision”, were discussed at the sessions.

Core challenges on the agenda included: “How can the National Gallery balance its role as a free public gallery whilst being commercially minded? What is the social value of art? How can art galleries explain and support this? Can art ever be open to everyone?” Other issues discussed include “how to bring in new, diverse and loyal audiences.”

Over the next four years, a series of smaller panels, made up of assembly members, will work directly with the gallery to oversee the implementation of these ideas. “NG Citizens will now continue into its second phase: the Citizens’ Panel. The panel will consist of three separate cohorts between 2026 and 2030,” says the report.

Some issues were not up for discussion at the sessions says the report, such as ideas that would result in significant changes to existing buildings; ideas that involve buying or selling paintings; and ideas that might compromise the gallery’s role as an arm’s length body of the UK government.

The report concludes: “The National Gallery was the first of its kind to do this on this scale, in the world. We can accept it was never going to be perfect; it would present challenges, but we hope observers can learn from our experience… To have a group of people that we can work with over future years, who will maintain a critical and supportive perspective, presents opportunities far beyond the usual focus group approach.”

Maurice Davies, a UK culture consultant at Cultural Associates Oxford, says the report is “quite remarkable” but questions whether the National Gallery will be “bold and brave enough” to take forward the assembly’s recommendations.

He tells The Art Newspaper: “The panel have concluded that the gallery needs to be far more than it currently is; a collection of European paintings based in the centre of London. They say the collection ‘urgently’ needs to be far more diverse and to represent the diversity of the UK so it needs to change its collecting policy significantly.

And they say the gallery should share ‘paintings and resources’ throughout the UK which suggests the gallery might want to reconsider its current hugely expensive project to extend its building in central London in favour of using resources to work with museums and galleries in a wide range of locations.”

Last September, the National Gallery received pledges of £150m each (from Michael Moritz’s Crankstart foundation and the Julia Rausing Trust) for its planned major new extension scheduled for completion in the early 2030s.

#9072. Inaugural Walker Design Triennial features flesh-like speakers and post-apocalyptic scenes

A set of speakers with flesh-like exteriors was among the conceptual design work shown at the first Walker Design Triennial in Minneapolis, USA, which curator Joseph Grima said reflected on the meaning of design in a world fixated on optimisation.

Filling a series of galleries at the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis, Minnesota, the exhibition was called Beyond Materialism and featured numerous examples of conceptual design.

The pieces ranged from the historical works such as Italian radical designer Alessandro Mendini’s 1970s Lassù – paired with depictions of the performance of the chair on fire – to an international set of design studios representing the field today.

Grima, who has served as a curator and educator for several high-profile institutions including Design Academy Eindhoven and international exhibition series Alcova, said the show was meant to challenge mainstream conceptions of design.

“We live in an age that is conditioned to think that anything and everything can be designed, and often what is that everything can be optimised,” said Grima.

“And it’s precisely this association between design and optimisation that this exhibition intends to question.”

With objects of various scales on display, the Walker Design Triennial featured a room with large-scale conceptual installations. Many of the participants were international, with a cohort of contemporary US designers, including Germane Barnes and Theaster Gates.

Terracotta plinths were included as part of the exhibition design, supporting many of the small and large objects.

Some of the pieces were commissioned directly for the event, mainly in the large-scale section.

Among these was Spanish designer Lucas Muñoz Muñoz’s All Ears, a set of latex-covered speakers that were programmed to play sounds recorded in the months before in Minneapolis. A sleek soundboard allowed users to play the tracks, with multiple tracks routed through the amorphous, fleshy speakers all at once to cacophonic effect.

Muñoz told Dezeen that the installation was designed to be a “microphone” for the city itself and “make visible the act of listening”.

The broadcast from the soundboard was also projected out of the gallery as a radio sequence.

Also commissioned for the event was a work by Vessel, featuring two massive rolls of fabric spooled over a kiosk. The fabric was based on Vessel cofounder Navine G Dossos’s paintings of her and her partner James Bridle’s self-built home.

Also in the large-scale room was a series of post-apocalyptic appliances made from found objects by Brussels-based Espace Aygo, derived from the studio’s 2022 transformation of a derelict apartment building into a home and art space.

The themes of fleshy objects, post-apocalypticism, and reuse continued into the rooms with smaller objects.

Here, London-based studio Superflux showcased objects from its Relics of Abundance series, showing objects created by a future civilisation that may someday use our objects today in a time of scarcity, including a chair made from straw and rebar.

Austro-Canadian designer Christoph Wimmer Ruelland created a series of furniture pieces with found objects that are extraordinarily colour-matched, while Korean designer Jonghoo Jeong utilised jerrycans to create a fountain, a reference to his past practice of dumping the objects in his process.

Athens-based studio Astronauts showcased inflated metal works informed by the autobody shops, creating love seats, chairs and even a seesaw that are iridescent while still familiar.

Italian-German designer Maximilian Marchesani created a structural piece made of smartphone glass that refracts metal-coated leaves as well as a chandelier that combined LEDs with branches. South Korean studio Wknd Lab created a series of stools made from discarded shells.

Dozens of other designers took part in the installation, including Moon Seop Seo, Studio Ker, Objects of Common Interest, Stef Fusani, Kevin Quale and Kostas Lambridis, representing a who’s who of avant-garde design, refracted through the lens of Grima and the event’s artistic director, Asli Altay.

It was an “opportunity to stop, take stock for a moment, and reflect on what design is today,” said Grima.

Other recent design showcases include a show of wood furniture by Armadillo and furniture made from fragments of New York buildings by Rafael Prieto.

Beyond Materialism is on show at the Walker Art Center from 17 October 2026 to 14 February 2027. Find out more about design and architecture exhibitions, talks and fairs at Dezeen Events Guide.

#9071. Please Don’t Sit on the Flowers

Long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe landscape goes to auction, Brancusi gets lost at MoMA, interview with Doris Salcedo, and is showing at documenta worth it?

Sitting at September Cafe, I watch the autumn leaves separate from the trees and get carried away gently by the wind. They swirl and twirl, performing a merry little dance in the air before falling to their final resting place.

News has just come in about a sweeping Democratic victory in the midterm elections, as fierce and awesome as a Gustave Courbet wave. But I see nobody popping champagne bottles in the streets. A pregnant black cat with a hanging belly saunters by.

Lying back in the dentist’s chair, a TV screen in front of me shuffles picturesque views from exotic places. They're idyllic to the point of not looking real. My doctor, a Lebanese, shows me an X-ray of my mouth, which looks like Beirut at the height of the Civil War.

The sky over the Robert F. Kennedy Bridge is gray, and the Harlem River is brooding as I make my way to Taryn Simon’s exhibition Father Country I Do Love You at the Guggenheim Museum. The show tells the heroic tales of an FBI agent whose alleged career intersects with major events in American history. Cold, antiseptic photographs encased neatly in plexiglass make up a detective story linking the protagonist to the explosion of TWA Flight 800, the 9/11 attacks, the bombing of the United States embassy in Nairobi, Bill Clinton’s impeachment, and more. Trudging up the Guggenheim’s spiraling galleries, I wonder whether this patriotic show is organized and sponsored by the US State Department. Simon makes you read a lot, but all that reading is just meant to distract you from thinking.

Jodie Foster narrates the audio guide for those who don’t have the patience to read long-winded wall texts. At the cafeteria, while eating a bikini sandwich, I see a woman who looks exactly like Judi Dench, another actress. “I love storytelling,” she tells a friend before plunging her teeth into a chocolate croissant.

On my way out, I once again resent how this museum forces everyone to exit through the gift shop to encourage commerce, but I buy myself a $5 Guggenheim bag anyway. Outside, in one of the manicured gardens of the Upper East Side, a small sign pleads, “Please don’t sit on the flowers.”

I cross the street into Central Park through Engineers’ Gate, climb the steps past a gilded bust of John Purroy Mitchel, NYC mayor between 1914-1918, and look out over the Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis Reservoir. I think of the Kennedys, of Trump, and of Simon. A worker collects brown leaves in plastic bags and tosses them into a truck wrapped in a photo of green leaves. A mother tries to snap a photo of her child, but the unruly kid refuses to pose for the camera. He throws a fit, falls, and, to her shock, ends up sitting on the flowers.

Touch support and Spatial Preview will introduce new ways to create, sculpt and explore 3D work.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The new MacBook Pro PROLED XDR has the best display our design editor has seen on a laptop. It also introduces touch input to an Apple laptop for the first time, and that could change how creatives interact with their software.

Maxon sees a world of potential, announcing that Cinema 4D and ZBrush, long-time features in our guides to best 3D modelling software and the best animation software, will get touch support for the new MacBook in late November. And that's not all. Cinema 4D is also getting a new capability that allows artists to preview 3D creations with Apple Vision Pro.

Maxon believes the new MacBook Pro will introduce an "entirely new dimension to professional creative workflows" with its tandem OLED display, intuitive touch capabilities, and powerful M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. The touch display means artists will have new ways to explore interact directly with their 3D creations.

Whether building and animating complex 3D worlds in Cinema 4D or developing intricate digital sculptures in ZBrush, touch support is intended to bring the responsiveness of hands-on interaction to professional desktop workflows, complementing traditional mouse, keyboard, and trackpad workflows.

Maxon already has ZBrush for iPad, which made digital sculpting in the app more mobile and allowed artists to shape and refine their work with their fingers or Apple Pencil. Touch support on MacBook Pro extends that to the more familiar desktop experience.

While touchscreen displays on Windows laptops have been around for many years, Apple's PROLED XDR Display also delivers exceptional brightness, contrast, and color accuracy.

Meanwhile, upcoming Apple Vision Pro support for Cinema 4D will extend the creative process opening up collaborative, real-time three dimensional workflows. Through the new Spatial Preview API, artists using Mac Virtual Display on Apple Vision Pro will be able to explore, preview, and interact with Cinema 4D designs in immersive life-size detail, making it easier to evaluate proportions and composition before moving forward with production.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Rather than judging work based on a 2D image, artists and designers will be able to move through an interior, evaluate a proposed installation, or explore the layout of a space at real-world scale before anything is physically built. This could be particularly valuable for architectural visualisation, retail environments, exhibition spaces and experiential design.

The integration also aims to enable more seamless communication with clients and collaborators, allowing them to inhabit the same space at the same time, immersed in the scene or from a bird’s-eye view using Apple Vision Pro. For reviewers who may not be familiar with navigating 3D software, this could allow them to better understand the space, identify potential changes, and provide more informed feedback earlier in the creative process.

Cinema 4D and ZBrush will be immediately available on Apple's new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, which begins shipping 6 November, 2026. Touch support for Cinema 4D and ZBrush along with Open in Spatial Preview for Apple Vision Pro running visionOS 27 and Mac running macOS 27 will be available in late November.

A new Cinema 4D iPad app is also slated for release before the end of the year. You can learn more on the Maxon website.

An insult or tribute to the most-anticipated video game in history?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's under two weeks to go until the release of Grand Theft Auto VI for PS5 and Xbox, and the hype is approaching fever pitch. It was already the most-anticipated video game of all time. Now developer and publisher Rockstar Games is rolling out heavy digital and billboard advertising to cement the title's status as a global cultural event.

From Buenos Aires to Vienna, GTA VI ads have been appearing on the sides of buildings, at bus stops and in stadiums. At least one's already come in for a spot of artistic intervention after someone took advantage of game's visibility to make their own brand a household name, and it's sparked quite a debate.

The GTA 6 marketing has kicked off in more cities around the world: - Hamburg/Frankfurt/Leipzig, Germany 🇩🇪 - Buenos Aires, Argentina 🇦🇷 - London, UK 🇬🇧 - Paris, France 🇫🇷 - Singapore 🇸🇬 - Prague, Czech Republic 🇨🇿 - Taipei, Taiwan 🇹🇼 - Lisbon, Portugal 🇵🇹 - Santiago, Chile 🇨🇱 - Dubai, UAE 🇦🇪 - Rio de Janeiro, Brazil 🇧🇷 - Madrid, Spain 🇪🇸 The video also includes more footage from Cologne, Berlin, Munich, Vienna, Warsaw, São Paulo, New York, New Mexico, Tokyo, Osaka, Seoul, Hong Kong, Stockholm, Melbourne, Brisbane, Sydney, and Toronto. Enjoy!November 6, 2026

Sign painters Nick Birnie and Ian Potter spent over a week hand painting a huge GTA VI mural for Rockstar in Brooklyn, New York City. The artwork became an attraction, drawing fans who travelled to capture work in progress on the piece.

Within a month, the artwork had been tagged by a graffiti artist going by the name of Jelous, and the intervention has sparked quite a debate.

A post shared by jelous.ktd (@jelous.ktd)

Many people have expressed outrage at the desecration of the colossal tribute to Jason and Lucia from the upcoming game, with some saying the piece has been "ruined" by the graffiti artist.

"Hopefully they come and remove this crappy graffiti and fix the mural…. Also look on security cameras to find out where this guy lives and arrest him," one person writes on Instagram.

“As an Italian graffiti artist myself, I honestly think this is pretty disrespectful, even by graffiti standards,” someone writes over on Reddit.

A post shared by Nick Birnie (@birntoutstudio)

But some think fans are being overly precious about what is, after all, a huge advert installed by a subsidiary of a $39.06 billion corporation that's using public space to push an $80-$100 game, even if the artwork was hand painted.

Others point out that crime is a central feature of the GTA franchise. Players can commit everything from minor traffic offences to first degree murder. Some think that makes the tag a fitting response.

"There's nothing more GTA than tagging a giant GTA mural," one person reckons. Some even suggest that Rockstar should add it to the game.

#9067. Art Gallery of Ontario sets opening date for $73m new wing

Rendering of the Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery at the Art Gallery of Ontario, Toronto Courtesy of Art Gallery of Ontario, Diamond Schmitt, Selldorf Architects, Two Row Architect and Play-Time. Rendering courtesy of Art Gallery of Ontario, Diamond Schmitt, Selldorf Architects, Two Row Architect and Play-Time.

The Art Gallery of Ontario (AGO) in Toronto has announced that its new five-storey, C$100m ($73.4m), Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery, which will display around 400 modern and contemporary works, will open to the public on 25 September 2027. The expansion project was first made public in April 2022.

“The Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery is more than an expansion project—it is Toronto and Canada announcing its global position,” Stephan Jost, the AGO’s outgoing director and chief executive, said in a statement. “When this gallery opens in September 2027, the world will be made aware of the strength of the AGO collection and the degree to which it has evolved to be truly global.”

The new building is the result of a collaboration between three architecture firms: the Toronto-headquartered firm Diamond Schmitt (known for its revamp of Emily Carr University of Art + Design in Vancouver and the forthcoming New Brunswick Museum in Saint John); the New York-based firm Selldorf Architects (of the recent renovations of the National Gallery in London and the Frick Collection in Manhattan); and Two Row Architect, headquartered in Ohsweken, Ontario (known for the Perry Centre for Native American Art at the Shelburne Museum in Vermont).

“It’s not a small project,” Jost said at the time of the launch in 2022. The 40,000-sq.-ft expansion, which overlooks downtown Toronto’s Grange Park, increases the AGO’s display space by around 30%, including 5,000 sq. ft of gallery spaces with 23ft-tall ceilings.

Rendering of the Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery at the Art Gallery of Ontario, Toronto Courtesy of Art Gallery of Ontario, Diamond Schmitt, Selldorf Architects, Two Row Architect and Play-Time. Rendering courtesy of Art Gallery of Ontario, Diamond Schmitt, Selldorf Architects, Two Row Architect and Play-Time.

The gallery is certainly in need of additional space for its collection of modern and contemporary work, which has grown by around 18,000 pieces in the past decade. In 2024 it received a gift of 37 works from the estate of the telecoms executive Philip B. Lind, including pieces by Laurie Simmons, Stan Douglas, Jeff Wall, Ai Weiwei, William Kentridge, Rodney Graham, Philip Guston and others. Last year, the gallery acquired more than 200 photographs by Peter Hujar and received more than 450 works from the late collectors Carol and Morton Rapp—among them works by Robert Rauschenberg, Claes Oldenburg, Kara Walker, Rachel Whiteread, Jasper Johns, Roy Lichtenstein, Lee Bontecoue, David Hockney and others. (The gallery also found itself at the centre of a culture war debate after opting not to acquire a work by the US photo-based artist and activist Nan Goldin.)

The AGO also boasts the largest public collection of Henry Moore’s work outside the UK—so much so that two years ago, to mark the 50th anniversary of the gallery’s Henry Moore Sculpture Centre, the city of Toronto declared 13 November to be Henry Moore Day.

The project of building a new wing was sparked by a lead gift of C$35m ($25.7m) from Dani Reiss, an art collector, chairman and chief executive of Canada Goose and member of the Order of Canada. The Reiss Gallery project is now fully funded, thanks to contributions from a community of supporters and the governments of Ontario and Canada.

Speaking on behalf of the federal government, Gregor Robertson, the minister of housing and infrastructure, said: “The federal government is proud to support this sustainable, state-of-the-art gallery that will host some of the world’s best modern and contemporary art for generations to come.”

The lion’s share of the donated pieces, from the late collectors Carol and Morton Rapp, are prints and photographs

Philip B. Lind left the Toronto museum a trove of works by Stan Douglas, Jeff Wall, Ai Weiwei, William Kentridge, Laurie Simmons and others

During Stephan Jost’s tenure, the leading art museum in Toronto has launched construction of a new contemporary art gallery, added more than 18,000 pieces to its collection and navigated plenty of drama

Construction of the 40,000 sq. ft space, dubbed the Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery, is expected to begin in early 2024, with an opening scheduled in 2027

#9066. Lapalma presents a cross-section of its catalogue on Dezeen Showroom

From colour palettes and modular seating to outdoor furniture and tables, Italian brand Lapalma has listed a selection of its most recent products on our Showroom section.

The brand collaborated with architect and designer Raffaella Mangiarotti on a new palette of colourways that can be applied across its offering of products.

Nine new shades join seven rethought existing colours in what the brand describes as a “chromatic alphabet”, which can be mixed or matched across seating, tables and accessories.

When designing the collection, Mangiarotti considered each colour’s capacity to work seamlessly whether applied to metal, wood or plastic.

The brand’s Kipu Club outdoor chair presents a new iteration of Anderssen & Voll‘s original design and can withstand life outdoors.

A curvilinear backrest partially wraps a pebble-shaped seat, creating a comfortable and friendly seat for al fresco lounging.

A family of tables have been developed for the brand by designer Mario Ferrarini, who created and named the collection after the conical profile of Mount Kilimanjaro.

Aptly named Kili, the tables are designed to be sculptural as well as functional, coming in various sizes and tabletop shapes, with each element carefully aesthetically considered.

Snaking lengths of seating are created in this new modular system designed for the brand by Francesco Rota, who wanted to make “welcoming islands for meeting, working, waiting or simply taking a pause”.

The HUB modular system is reconfigurable, allowing users to reorder the modules to create evolving landscapes in open-plan spaces.

Designer Francesco Rota collaborated with Lapalma to extend the Plus modular outdoor seating system, which now comprises additional sun loungers and facilitates all-new combination options.

Round-cornered, lozenge-shaped modules available in various bright and neutral-coloured upholstery make up the range, which creates opportunity for open-air lounging and socialising.

Lapalma is an Italian furniture company with a forty-year history of designing and manufacturing tables, seating and other furnishings for both indoor and outdoor use.

It frequently collaborates with eminent designers, both fellow Italians and those from further afield, to develop cutting-edge furniture solutions for contemporary interiors.

Feeling frustrated on a Monday morning is not a reason to quit. But persistent patterns that affect your health, relationships, and long-term career growth are legitimate signals worth examining. The challenge is separating temporary frustration from genuine misalignment.

The FI community approaches this differently from mainstream career advice. Instead of asking "Am I happy at work?" — which fluctuates daily — we ask: "Is this role aligned with my long-term financial and personal goals?" That reframe turns an emotional decision into a strategic one.

Before you submit your resignation, your finances need to be ready regardless of how miserable you are. Quitting without financial preparation trades one source of stress for another.

The FI community has a massive advantage here. If you have been building toward financial independence — even if you are not there yet — your savings provide a runway that most people do not have. A $200,000 investment portfolio at a 4% safe withdrawal rate provides $8,000 per year in sustainable income, which dramatically reduces the pressure of a job search.

The worst time to make a career decision is when you are emotionally overwhelmed. A terrible meeting, a passed-over promotion, or a toxic interaction with a coworker can make quitting feel urgent when the situation may actually be temporary or fixable.

Use the 30-day test: if you have wanted to quit for fewer than 30 consecutive days, it is likely a temporary frustration. If the feeling has persisted — or intensified — for 30+ days, it is a pattern worth taking seriously.

How you leave a job matters as much as why you leave. Your professional reputation follows you for your entire career, and the people you work with today may be the hiring managers, clients, or references of tomorrow.

Two weeks notice: This is the minimum professional standard in the United States. For senior roles, three to four weeks is more appropriate. Check your employment contract — some roles require 30, 60, or 90 days notice.

The resignation conversation: Schedule a private meeting with your direct manager. Keep it brief and positive. Say: "I have decided to move on to a new opportunity. I want to thank you for [specific positive thing], and I am committed to making the transition as smooth as possible. My last day would be [date]."

The transition plan: Document your ongoing projects, key contacts, passwords, and processes. Offer to train your replacement. Complete as much outstanding work as possible. A strong exit creates goodwill that pays dividends for years.

What not to do: Do not badmouth the company, your boss, or your coworkers — not in the resignation meeting, not in your exit interview, not on social media. Even if your grievances are legitimate, airing them publicly hurts your reputation more than theirs.

Conventional advice says never quit without another job lined up. The FI community takes a more nuanced view: it depends on your financial position and the severity of the situation.

If you are leaving due to company changes — layoffs, restructuring, or role elimination — negotiate your severance package. Many employees accept the first offer without realizing severance is negotiable. Key leverage points include your tenure, difficulty of replacement, willingness to sign a non-compete or non-disparagement clause, and any outstanding commissions or bonuses.

Common severance components to negotiate: extended pay (push for 2-4 weeks per year of tenure), continued health insurance coverage, outplacement services, vesting acceleration for equity, and a positive reference commitment.

Health insurance is often the biggest financial concern when leaving a job. You have two primary options:

COBRA: Continues your employer plan for up to 18 months. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer was paying) plus a 2% administrative fee. COBRA typically costs $500-$700 per month for individual coverage and $1,400-$2,000+ for family coverage. It is expensive but familiar.

ACA Marketplace: Depending on your income after leaving, you may qualify for substantial subsidies. If your annual income drops below 400% of the federal poverty level, premium tax credits can reduce your monthly cost to $100-$400 for comprehensive coverage. FI seekers who leave jobs often qualify for significant subsidies because their earned income drops even if their net worth is high — ACA subsidies are based on income, not wealth.

Here is where financial independence changes everything. When you have significant savings — even if you have not reached full FI — you have leverage that most employees lack. You can negotiate from strength, take career risks, and walk away from toxic situations without financial desperation.

A $500,000 portfolio at a 4% withdrawal rate provides $20,000 per year indefinitely. That is not enough to live on for most people, but combined with a working spouse, reduced expenses, or part-time work, it transforms "should I quit my job" from a terrifying question into a strategic calculation. FI is not just about never working again — it is about having the financial security to make career decisions based on alignment and purpose rather than desperation and fear.

The FI community has a saying: financial independence is not about quitting your job — it is about having the freedom to choose whether to keep it. Every dollar you save and invest is a vote for your future autonomy. When you have 12-24 months of expenses saved, you negotiate from strength. When you reach Coast FI or beyond, a bad job becomes a choice, not a trap. Build your FI runway and the question changes from "Can I afford to quit?" to "Does this role still serve my goals?"

Work through these steps before making your decision.

Have you consistently wanted to leave for 30+ days? If no, wait. Temporary frustration is not a reason to upend your career. If yes, proceed to step two.

Pro tip: Keep a brief daily journal noting your satisfaction level 1-10. Data beats feelings for decision-making.

Is the issue your boss, your role, your compensation, the culture, or the industry? Some problems follow you to the next job. A bad manager is fixable by transferring. An industry you hate requires a bigger change.

Verify your emergency fund, health insurance options, debt situation, and FI runway. If you are not financially ready, keep working while you build your safety net and search for alternatives.

Before quitting, have you requested a transfer, a raise, a role change, or a conversation with HR? Many solvable problems go unaddressed because employees assume the answer will be no.

Pro tip: A direct conversation with your manager about your concerns resolves the issue 40% of the time.

If you decide to leave, secure your next opportunity (if possible), give appropriate notice, document your work for your successor, and maintain every professional relationship.

Pro tip: Never burn bridges. The colleague you leave today may be the hiring manager at your dream company in three years.

At minimum, 3-6 months of essential expenses in a liquid savings account. If you are quitting without another job lined up, aim for 6-12 months. The FI community recommends having your emergency fund fully funded, health insurance secured, and ideally some progress toward financial independence to provide a psychological safety net.

If your job is causing persistent anxiety, depression, or physical health symptoms that do not improve with coping strategies, therapy, or workplace changes — yes, your health must come first. But do it strategically: secure health insurance, build your financial runway, and consult a therapist or career coach before making the leap. Never make a permanent career decision during a temporary emotional crisis.

Generally, quitting gives you more control over the narrative, timing, and terms. Being fired can qualify you for unemployment benefits (quitting usually does not), but it can also create a negative reference. If you sense a termination is coming, consider whether negotiating a mutual separation with severance is an option. Document everything and consult an employment attorney if you believe the termination may be discriminatory or retaliatory.

Be honest and frame it positively. Acceptable explanations include: career transition (took time to retrain or earn a certification), personal development (traveled, volunteered, or cared for family), or strategic job search (took time to find the right fit rather than settling). Employers increasingly accept career gaps — especially post-2020 — as long as you can articulate what you did during the time off.

COBRA (Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act) lets you continue your employer health plan for up to 18 months after leaving. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer contributed) plus a 2% admin fee. Individual coverage typically costs $500-$700/month and family coverage runs $1,400-$2,000+/month. The ACA marketplace is often cheaper, especially if your income drops after leaving.

FI savings transform the equation entirely. With a substantial portfolio, you have a financial runway that removes the urgency and desperation from the decision. Even partial FI — having 2-5 years of expenses invested — means you can quit a toxic job, take time to find the right next role, or transition to lower-paying but more fulfilling work. FI is not just about retiring early; it is about having the leverage to make career decisions from a position of strength rather than fear.

The question "should I quit my job?" deserves a framework, not an impulse. Apply the 30-day test, diagnose the real problem, verify your financial readiness, explore internal solutions, and then make a deliberate decision. If you have been building toward financial independence, your savings give you something most people lack: the freedom to walk away from a bad situation without financial panic. FI is the ultimate career insurance — it turns "I have to stay" into "I choose to stay or go." Build your runway, protect your reputation, and make the decision from a position of strength.

I'm calling it. 2026 is the year of the movie title card. Also known as intertitles, these stylised film openers have existed since the silent movie era, showcasing a unique and iconic artistic legacy that rivals some of the best movie posters.

Title cards aren't just for aesthetics; they offer a narrative anchor, a beat to collect yourself before the action begins. But of course, it's. not empty imagery. The best movie title cards can be a storytelling device in themselves, and this year we've seen some stunning examples.

In contrast to the film's bold poster typography featuring sturdy sans serifs and clean composition, The Bone Temple's title card feels surprisingly organic. Created in a natural, hand-drawn scrawl, the imperfection of the lettering gives it an almost juvenile feel.

Appearing just after a particularly violent opening, the silent serenity of the title card scene regrounds the audience, offering a moment of respite from the chaos. But set against the temple of bones, there remains an eeriness to the blood-red hue of the title card typography,

A post shared by Warner Bros. Philippines (@warnerbrosph)

Championing hand-crafted design, Emerald Fennell's Wuthering Heights took a delightfully strange approach to title card creation. Made using hair (including some of the lead actors' real locks!), the stop-motion title card is equal parts whimsical and slightly disturbing, setting the tone for the madness that ensues.

"We wanted it to feel completely human", Fennell explains in a behind-the-scenes sneak peek. "It's really thrilling to show the hands that make something," she adds. Wonderfully tactile and hauntingly beautiful, the title card demonstrates how thoughtful design can effortlessly set the tone of a film.

A prime example of how simple title cards can create a sense of tension, The Drama's erratic opening plants a seed of anxiety amid the intimacy of the dance scene. Using a jumbled mix of script fonts, stately serifs and bold sans serifs, the chaotic nature of the title card signals a sense of chaos amid the calm.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Appearing only fleetingly, almost as if the screen is glitching, the random fonts create a sense of visual disharmony as they flash across the scene. Appearing in a conventional white colour scheme, the juxtaposition of order and disarray builds a perfect layer of discomfort.

Obsession demonstrates one of my favourite movie tropes – the integrated title card. After a particularly harrowing scene, protagonist Bear is seen weeping on his bed as a tense score begins to creep in. The camera pans down to reveal the Obsession title card woven into the duvet.

The simple visual effortlessly creates an eerie effect, as the viewer is thrown into the film's suffocatingly bleak universe. Purposefully domestic in nature, the tactile title card hints that the horror is not abstract or far away, but lingering under our noses.

Wildwood's beautiful title card was created by hand, using tactile design to breathe life into each letter form. With diverse natural wood textures, crawling ivy and powered pigment details, each human-made design has its own story woven between the branches.

With animation studio Laika heavily promoting its human-made artistry, it's no surprise this dedicated craft extends to its stunning title card. Demonstrating the beauty that comes from intricate, time-intensive work, Wildwood's title card shines as a rejection of the increasing quantity of AI slop taking over cinema.

Resident Evil title card. https://t.co/ZxxvIHJlthNovember 2, 2026

The Resident Evil title card is perhaps one of the most controversial on the list for an unexpected reason. With the franchise's origins stemming from the gaming world, many die-hard fans were anticipating the game's iconic title voice narration, something that director Zach Cregger opted against.

The tense, thumping score, paired with the rapid warping of the bold title card, creates an eerie effect that stands strong on its own (basically, doing away with the campiness of the game narrator was a good move). Grungy and terrifying, the title card perfectly encapsulates the film's decay into raw, unrelenting horror.
