The single biggest predictor of cheap airfare is not when you book or which tool you use — it is how flexible you are with dates and destinations. Google Flights date grid and Skyscanner everywhere search exist specifically to help flexible travelers find the cheapest options. Being willing to fly on a Tuesday instead of a Friday, or to visit Portugal instead of France, routinely saves 30-50% compared to fixed-date, fixed-destination searches. For FI-minded travelers, flexibility is a skill that pays dividends on every trip.

Tuesday and Wednesday are consistently the cheapest days to fly domestically, with fares typically 15-25% below Friday and Sunday prices. Saturday can also be a good value for departures. The savings are largest on popular leisure routes where weekend demand creates the biggest price swings.

No. The idea that booking on Tuesday at midnight gets you the best price is a myth. Airlines adjust prices thousands of times per day using dynamic pricing algorithms. What matters is booking within the optimal window (1-3 months out for domestic flights) and setting fare alerts to catch price drops.

For domestic flights, 1 to 3 months before departure is the sweet spot. For international flights, 2 to 8 months is optimal. Holiday travel should be booked 2 to 4 months ahead. Booking too early (6+ months for domestic) or too late (under 2 weeks) typically results in higher prices.

Sometimes. Spirit, Frontier, and other ultra-low-cost carriers advertise base fares 40-60% below major airlines but charge separately for carry-on bags ($35-$65), seat selection ($5-$50), and other extras. For a traveler with no checked bag and no seat preference, budget carriers save real money. For families or anyone checking bags, compare total cost including all fees — major airlines are often competitive.

Yes. The cheapest times to fly domestically are January (after the 7th), February (excluding Valentine week), early March, late April, September, October, and early November. The most expensive periods are the weeks around Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and the peak summer window from mid-June through mid-August.

Travel rewards cards earn points on everyday spending that can be redeemed for flights. A card earning 2x points on all purchases turns $25,000 in annual spending into enough points for 1-2 domestic round trips. The FI-aligned approach is to use a rewards card for purchases you would make anyway (groceries, gas, utilities) and let points accumulate passively — never spend more just to earn points.

Finding cheap flights comes down to three principles: be flexible with dates (fly Tuesday or Wednesday for 15-25% savings), book in the right window (1-3 months for domestic, 2-8 for international), and let technology do the searching (Google Flights fare alerts catch drops automatically). Combined with a travel rewards card that earns points on everyday spending, these strategies make air travel significantly more affordable without requiring hours of research. Set your alerts, stay flexible, and book when the price is right.

#9037. "Commitment of the design community remains strong" say Ukrainian design week founders

Photography courtesy of Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week

This year’s Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week went ahead despite Russian strikes affecting the local design community. The event’s founders share their top picks of exhibited brands that have continued production amid the war.

“The reality of operating in Ukraine remains extremely challenging,” Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week founders Anatolii and Kateryna Roskovshenko told Dezeen.

Ukraine has endured the constant threat of Russian bombardment for over four years, and recent months have been increasingly deadly for civilians, according to Human rights group Amnesty International.

Daily life for Ukrainians continues to be upended. Designers and manufacturers are navigating keeping operations running as Russian strikes damage their warehouses.

“Air raid alerts, power outages, disrupted logistics, rising costs, and damage to production facilities directly affect everyday operations,” said the husband-and-wife duo. “Several major Ukrainian furniture manufacturers have had their production facilities and warehouses hit by Russian strikes, causing significant damage and disrupting their work.”

“Businesses often have to adjust their schedules at short notice, reconsider investments, and find alternative ways to maintain production. Some have been forced to scale back operations or temporarily suspend projects,” they continued.

In the face of this, the design community came together for this year’s Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week, which took place in Kyiv from 5 to 11 October.

The flagship Design Hall exhibition gathered two hundred Ukrainian brands across interiors, furniture, decor, lighting and product design, showcasing their work to thousands of visitors.

Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week, which joined the international community of World Design Weeks in 2023, made changes to its planned programme to keep attendees safe. During the event, Kyiv experienced attacks that interrupted electricity and water supplies.

“Several planned events had to be cancelled for security reasons, while some furniture brands were unable to participate following earlier attacks on their facilities,” said the Roskovshenkos.

“We adapted Design Hall to take place entirely indoors, with changes to the original programme.”

“Yet the commitment of the design community remains strong,” they continued. “Thousands of people attended Design Hall, and hundreds of designers, manufacturers, and creative professionals came together to exchange ideas, establish new connections, and support each other’s work.”

Design brands in Ukraine are exploring new ways of developing products, testing materials and reaching customers, according to the Roskovshenkos.

“Despite the challenges of working during the war, Ukraine’s design industry continues to evolve,” they said. “Collaboration has become an essential part of how the industry operates, helping businesses share knowledge, find new opportunities, and adapt to uncertainty.”

“Particularly encouraging is the fact that new Ukrainian design brands continue to launch, even as existing businesses navigate difficult circumstances.”

“Over seven seasons of Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week, we have witnessed this evolution firsthand,” the pair continued. “Brands are becoming more confident in their identity, finding new niches, rethinking their production processes, and developing products that reflect their own creative vision.”

Read on for Anatolii and Kateryna Roskovshenko’s highlights from this year’s Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week:

“Juniper is a Ukrainian brand that combines traditional Carpathian craftsmanship with contemporary design, working with natural materials such as sheep’s wool and wood.

“In collaboration with KredoBank, the brand has created a collection of four wall panels inspired by Ukraine’s distinctive landscapes.

“Through natural textures and handcrafted techniques, each piece captures the character and atmosphere of these places, bringing elements of Ukraine’s cultural and natural heritage into contemporary interiors.”

“Gushka is a Ukrainian wool textile manufacturer [that] preserves traditional craftsmanship, creating its products on historic weaving looms using age-old techniques and natural wool from sheep that graze freely on the Carpathian slopes.

“Kint is a Kyiv-based furniture and object design brand [that] specialises in creating original furniture, decor, and accessories for residential and commercial spaces.

“The first collaboration between Kint x Gushka, initiated in 2024, brings together contemporary furniture design and traditional Ukrainian craftsmanship. The result is a limited-edition series of armchairs, reimagining kint’s signature design through natural Carpathian wool and Gushka’s traditional textile techniques.

“The two versions feature different handcrafted finishes – Stranded uses hand-applied wool strands layered over a smooth base to create a distinctive textured surface, and Brushed is made by hand-combing wool using a traditional smooth-weaving technique, resulting in a softer texture.”

“KosKa is a Ukrainian brand working with recycled paper-based biomass, combining traditional handcrafting techniques, material experimentation, and contemporary artistic expression.

“Founder Kateryna Kostevych creates each object by hand, exploring the possibilities of sustainable materials and bringing together natural textures, tactile qualities, contemporary forms, and functionality.

“The featured objects include Trypillian Bull, an original interpretation of ancient Trypillian ceramic figurines, and two lamps named Hat and Bright Eye.”

“Tiini is a Ukrainian brand that creates lighting, furniture, and accessories, born at the intersection of tradition and modernity.

“The brand breathes new life into authentic crafts, harnessing the richness of materials and their interaction with light to create unique pieces for the home.”

“Venko is a Ukrainian design and production workshop founded in 2014 in Radyvyliv.

“The brand specialises in creating three-dimensional wooden wall panels and decorative pieces, with a particular focus on textures and the expressive qualities of natural materials.”

“Yalanzhi Objects is a Ukrainian brand of lighting and decorative objects founded in 2019 by Yuliia and Yevhen Melnychenko. The brand approaches light as an artistic medium, not merely a functional element, but a way to shape spaces, establish rhythm, and create an emotional focal point within an interior.

“Many of its pieces are crafted from Zemletsvit, the brand’s signature biocomposite – a natural material characterised by tactile surfaces, earthy tones, and a distinct handmade quality.

“Yalanzhi Objects combines contemporary design language, sculptural forms, and a thoughtful connection to Ukrainian culture.”

#9036. A New Hudson Valley Art Space Promises to Be As Accessible as It Is In Flux

Less than two blocks from the Katonah train station stands a nondescript, gray two-story building on one of the main drags of this Hudson Valley town. Emblazoned in a kerned-out serif font, its name, Branchline, belies what awaits inside: a public-facing exhibition space for the Gochman Family Collection (GFC).

Established just five years ago, the GFC has already become one of the world’s leading collections of contemporary Indigenous art, with more than 850 works. Until now, works from the GFC have primarily hung in the New York apartment of Becky Gochman, the collection’s founder and custodian, and her family, though some 200 works are typically on loan to institutions around the world at any given time. The GFC has generously opened the home to museum groups, schools, and artists for tours and events as a way to bring more attention to Native artists, but the organization’s ambition has always been to make its holdings as accessible as possible. Related Articles Leah Ke Yi Zheng Joins Antenna Space, Pérez Art Museum Miami to Honor Nicolas Berggruen, and More: Industry Moves for October 28, 2026 Elisa Nuyten's Vega Foundation Is Quietly Reshaping the World of Moving-Image Art

“It’s one thing to articulate a mission, but what matters to me,” GFC creative director and curator Rachel Martin (Tlingít) said Thursday during a press preview, “is if I’m putting that language out into the world [then] I’m making sure that our organization is following that with action.” She added that she sees Branchline as a place for “bringing community together, which means making the Native community feel like they are very much a part of what the decision-making parts of this are, and then also inviting the community of Katonah to come in and learn about new artists that they might not have heard of.”

Anticipating that many visitors will arrive via Metro-North, the GFC named the space after the rail term “branch line,” or the place “where paths diverge and new paths begin,” as GFC director Laura Phipps put it. “We were excited about all the sort of ideas that ‘branch line’ conjures—both thinking about the metaphor of the train and the metaphor of trees—and what we can do to experiment and grow in this space.”

Free to the public, Branchline is taking its time to grow into its new digs, which will eventually total 10,000 square feet across four buildings. Friday evening’s inauguration will show off the first completed space, as well as plans for expansion in the coming months across an L-shaped plot that runs from the main building’s entrance on the Parkway to Katonah Avenue. The building houses a three-room gallery on the ground floor, two bedrooms upstairs for invited artists to determine how they want to spend the time, and a nearly operational ceramics studio downstairs.

Architectural renderings on view Thursday afternoon show that the building’s back door will open onto a small sculpture deck leading to a yet-to-be-built barn, where large-scale works will go on view. (The original barn was in such bad shape that it had to be torn down to make way for an exhibition space.) The barn will in turn lead to the Annex, which will take a more experimental approach (more on that later). From there, visitors will turn left onto a patio and eventually reach the back entrance of Twig, a retail store and café.

For now, visitors will get a taste of Branchline’s ambitions through a more traditional offering. Inaugurating the modest, nearly 2,000-square-foot gallery is “Line Break,” curated by GFC assistant curator Moonoka Begay (Ndee + Diné) with collection associate Nicole van Brugge. “Lines are a core facet of all visual language,” the exhibition’s introductory wall text begins, but Begay and van Brugge look past the formal qualities that a line and its breaks contribute to a work. Instead, they treat the line as a metaphor for lineage and bloodlines, borders and cartographic marks, horizons and sound barriers.

A tight show of 28 works by 18 Indigenous artists, “Line Break” offers visually compelling juxtapositions of artists from different generations working in a range of mediums and styles. Jaune Quick-to-See Smith’s The Spaniard (1988), a semi-abstract aerial view of the Flathead Indian Reservation in Montana, hangs next to Sara Flores’s Untitled (Shao Pei Maya Kené), 2024, a painting rendered in the geometric abstract visual language of the Shipibo-Conibo people, whose designs, according to an exhibition brochure, “map the community’s local worldview, environmental understanding, and cosmology.” Farther along are Teresa Baker’s Echoes (2024) and George Morrison’s Night Shadows. Red Rock Variation: Lake Superior Landscape (1994). Both are brightly colored abstract meditations on landscape made in very different mediums: acrylic, yarn, willow, and artificial sinew on AstroTurf for Baker; acrylic on canvas on board for Morrison.

Even the most seemingly formal works reveal their secrets as you delve deeper into how these artists use lines to make meaning. Across from the Quick-to-See Smith and Flores works are two pieces from Nadia Myre’s “Code of Construction” series, in which the artist arranges strung ceramic cylinders into squares depicting the ground-to-air distress signals for “Require Map and Compass” and “Not Understood.” Myre’s choice of medium draws on the tradition of wampum belts, used by Indigenous communities of the Northeast Woodlands to communicate political relationships. Myre’s work finds an analog in Faye HeavyShield’s the red line II (2025), a strand of red beads that the artist strung by hand. Here it is displayed in a coil, though its configuration is flexible—perhaps a metaphor countering the seeming immutability of shape, form, and even time.

The exhibition reaches its crescendo at its center with Raven Chacon’s Storm Pattern (2021–24), a handwoven wool textile accompanied by a multichannel sound piece whose low hum visitors have been hearing since entering the gallery. In 2016, Chacon noticed the sounds made by drones flying over the Oceti Sakowin camp at Standing Rock, where protesters had gathered to oppose the Dakota Access Pipeline. Ranging from loud and piercing to soft and soothing, the sounds of police surveillance drones mingled and merged with those of the protesters’ countersurveillance drones. In that harmonious dissonance, Chacon saw a score, which he recorded and also translated into the woven textile, charting the drones’ erratic flight patterns in a traditional Diné weaving style and structure.

Rounding out “Line Break” are two elements that will likely look drastically different in a few months. The GFC commissioned Matthew Kirk to make a site-specific work for an exterior wall of the building along an alleyway. Across three plywood panels, Kirk has collaged painted tar paper in various abstract forms and shapes. The work was already showing its ephemeral quality on Thursday morning, the paper having warped in the light rain.

A few steps down the alleyway is the Annex, which is still under construction: the plywood is exposed, and power cords run to jerry-rigged lightbulbs that illuminate its two floors. Rather than hide this rawness, the GFC team has decided to embrace it. For now, the Annex is home to a small show of drawings by Shuvinai Ashoona, who maps imagined scenes—ones that could perhaps one day come true—onto the Arctic landscape where she lives in Nunavut, Canada. The team acknowledged that it hasn’t quite figured out how the space will look in the near term, even once the build-out is complete. That will depend on how artists interpret a prompt that gives them the autonomy to do what they want.

“What GFC is doing is not trying to become an institution,” Martin said. “It’s trying to just meet where things are needed, and a space is definitely needed for art that is outside of the white box that you’re used to seeing, so that’s what we’re offering.”

#9035. What's Love Got to Do With It? The Relationship Cycle Explained

Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

From those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

Research shows that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

If the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of new love into a warm, enduring attachment.

Hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the issues head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

You know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

From design work to watching movies, these are the best laptops for every kind of pasttime.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you need to buy a laptop for creative work, it's so important to get it right. Prices have climbed sharply this year, so you don't want to be saddled with the wrong thing..

Our top pick for graphic design is the MacBook Pro 14-inch (M6). It’s a brilliant all-rounder for almost any creative job. However, depending on what you need it for, other laptops are worth investigating too.

So in this article, I've highlighted the best laptops for a range of different tasks, based on hands-on testing by our reviewers using real design software. For further options, see our guides to the best laptops for graphic design and the best laptops for CAD.

The MacBook Pro has been the default laptop for designers for years, and nothing has yet changed that. The M5 model came first by a clear margin in our Photoshop benchmarks. Its screen is sharp and colour-accurate, and the battery comfortably lasts a working day. Now Apple has replaced it with the M6 version, which went on sale on 6 November.

We haven’t tested it yet, but it’s a spec bump rather than a redesign. Apple claims up to 30% faster graphics, and it adds Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Crucially, it costs the same as the M5 model, which rose to $1,999 / £1,999 in Apple’s June price rises.

So my advice is: either buy the M6 at full price, or pick up the M5 if you find it heavily discounted over Black Friday. Alternatively if money’s no object, Apple’s new MacBook Pro with a PROLED XDR display starts at $2,899 / £2,899 and adds a touchscreen. Our writer Daniel John called its OLED panel “the best laptop screen I’ve ever seen”.

The ProArt P16 is the best Windows laptop we’ve tested for creative work, and it's our top pick in both our laptop for CAD and laptop for animation guides.

If you're using CAD, the fact that this laptop runs Windows really matters. Revit and SolidWorks don’t run natively on macOS, while the P16’s Nvidia graphics and 64GB of memory give you plenty of headroom for large models. The built-in dial is handy for zooming and rotating, too.

If you're an animator, meanwhile, the star is the screen. It’s a colour-accurate OLED touchscreen, and as our reviewer Erlingur Einarsson says: “The 120Hz refresh rate is a welcome upgrade too, especially for animators and video editors.” The RTX 5070 also speeds up rendering in GPU-heavy tools.

The ASUS ProArt P16, in short, is pretty much everything a creative professional could hope for However, if you need even more power, ASUS also sells a version with an RTX 5090 and a 4K screen for $3,999.99.

The 16-inch MacBook Pro is the top pick in our 3D modelling laptop guide. You get a big, sharp screen, plenty of memory and the kind of battery life that 3D-capable Windows laptops can only dream of.

When our reviewer Rob Redman tested the previous M4 Pro model in Blender, Cinema 4D and Maya, he was impressed by its rendering speed and smooth viewport. “Simple things like dragging and dropping materials, which can be a little laggy on some systems, are perfectly smooth,” he says. The M5 Pro builds on that with a faster chip and Apple’s latest GPU cores.

Two things to bear in mind, though. First, if your pipeline relies on Nvidia’s CUDA or Windows-only plugins, you’re better off with a Windows machine. In which case, the Acer Nitro 16S AI is our best-value pick, while the RTX 5090 inside the Alienware 16 Area-51 is ideal if you need maximum rendering power.

Second, the MacBook Pro 16-inch (M5 Pro) is a lot of money, and the price climbs quickly once you add memory. If you have a lot of money, though, there's a very nice PROLED XDR version with a touchscreen costing $3,399.

Looking for the best laptop for Cricut? Then here's some good news. Cricut Design Space isn’t a demanding app, so you don’t need to spend a fortune on a laptop to use it.

Cricut recommends a minimum of an Intel Core i3 and 4GB of RAM, but 8GB is a more comfortable starting point, and 16GB will help with complex, multi-layer projects. The IdeaPad 5 2-in-1 gives you 16GB as standard, which is why it tops our Cricut laptop guide.

The 360-degree hinge is the clincher. You can fold the screen back into tablet mode and tap, drag and resize your designs directly on the screen. It also has a good range of ports, including USB-A, which is handy if you’re plugging in your cutting machine or a USB stick full of SVG files.

It’s a bit heavier than a regular laptop, and the screen isn’t the brightest or most colourful, but neither matters much for crafting.

The PZ13 is a Windows tablet with a detachable keyboard, and it’s the top pick in our drawing laptop guide. The big selling point is that ASUS includes the stylus, keyboard, stand and sleeve in the box, so the price you see is the price you pay.

The 13.3-inch OLED screen is bright, sharp and very colour-accurate, with a Delta-E of 0.3 in our testing. Battery life is excellent too, lasting over 20 hours in our video streaming test. “It’s unique and ideal for creatives,” says our reviewer.

It’s not built for processing power, though. Its Snapdragon chip is better suited to drawing and photo editing than 3D, and some Windows software, including InDesign, isn’t fully compatible with Snapdragon chips. So check your favourite apps run well on it before you buy. The glossy screen can also be reflective.

For most students, and certainly for creative ones, the MacBook Air is the laptop to get. It’s thin, light and silent, the battery easily lasts all day, and it has enough power for design, photo editing and light video work. “A thin and light laptop that performs as well as this will always be attractive to a creative audience,” says our reviewer Ian Evenden.

That power is the reason to choose it over the cheaper MacBook Neo. In our testing, the Air M5 was much closer to the MacBook Pro than the Neo: it scored 17,091 for multi-core performance in Geekbench 6, against 17,897 for the M5 MacBook Pro. In Photoshop, it more than doubled the Neo’s scores.

It’s not so cheap any more, though. Apple raised the price by $200 / £200 in June, although students can get quite a lot of money off through Apple’s education store. If you want to save cash and your course doesn’t involve creative software, the MacBook Neo at $699 / £699 is a great-value alternative, as long as you can live with 8GB of memory.

The MacBook Pro 14-inch (M6). It’s fast, has a superb screen, lasts all day on a charge, and it handles everything from design and illustration to photo and video editing. If you prefer Windows, the ASUS ProArt P16 is the best alternative.

It depends mainly on your software. Most design, photo and video apps run on both, and Macs win on battery life and build quality. But if you work in CAD, Windows is the safer bet, as Revit and SolidWorks don’t run natively on macOS. Windows laptops are also the only option for Nvidia graphics, which many 3D and rendering tools rely on.

For creative work, 16GB is the minimum we’d recommend, and 32GB is the sweet spot if you work with large files. You’ll only need 64GB or more for heavy 3D, video or AI work. Note that RAM on Macs and many thin Windows laptops can’t be upgraded later, so buy what you’ll need.

Not for graphic design, illustration or Cricut crafting, where integrated graphics are fine. For 3D, CAD, animation and video editing, a powerful GPU will save you lots of time, which means either an Nvidia RTX graphics card or a MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro or Max chip.

For drawing and Cricut work, yes. Being able to tap, drag and sketch directly on the screen makes both much more natural. For most other creative work, it’s a nice extra rather than an essential.

Cricut says that Design Space isn’t supported on Chromebooks, so we’d recommend a Windows laptop or a Mac. Some users run the Android version of the app on a Chromebook, but you may lose some features.

#9033. How Going Blind Made Doris Salcedo’s Art Bigger and Better

Doris Salcedo is best known for her moving “anti-monuments,” gigantic artworks—or sometimes negative spaces—that propose new ways to commemorate atrocities. Always, she focuses on the victims’ perspectives. Her best-known work, Shibboleth (2007), installed in Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall, comprised one giant, scar-like crack in the concrete, rerouting foot traffic in a manner that evoked the jarring disruption of borders more broadly.

The Colombian artist began working at such a monumental scale only after she began losing her central vision. At age 31, Salcedo was diagnosed with Stargardt disease, a rare genetic condition, and today she is legally blind, with only peripheral sight. Related Articles Sophie Calle, Doris Salcedo Among Winners of $105,000 Praemium Imperiale Award Doris Salcedo Deserves Better Than Her Current Fondation Beyeler Survey

In November, at White Cube Gallery in New York, Salcedo will premiere a sculpture that is the culmination of decades of this collaborative way of working—and huge in a way that could never be accomplished by one person. A full-sized house—at nearly 30 feet—has been woven entirely from human hair. When I visited, dozens of assistants were working across her three studios, tying knots in individual strands, a painstaking process. The resulting pattern resembles chicken wire or a chain-link fence.

Even working with such a big team, the process took three years. “To be thankful is not enough,” Salcedo said of the collective effort, adding that it could have easily taken 20 years to make on her own—and that she couldn’t spare that kind of time at her age.

As Salcedo led me through her studio—her own iconic salt-and-pepper curls rhyming with the looping locks lining the space—she told me that all of her workspaces were designed by the architect Carlos Granada. The two have been working together for 25 years. He is also the architect behind Fragmentos, Salcedo’s 2018 “anti-monument” commissioned by her national government to commemorate the 2016 Colombian peace agreement. Visiting the building in the heart of Bogotá, what at first looks like a typical modernist, single-floor gallery takes on new weight in the feel of its flooring: The textured tiling is made from firearms that once belonged to the Colombian guerrilla group FARC and were later melted down. Visitors walk right on top of these instruments of violence and fear, on tiles Salcedo made in close collaboration with 20 Colombian women who survived sexual violence during the conflict.

The work has an undeniably chilling effect. School groups flock to it regularly. Some critics, though, have found its message misleading, since several splinter factions are still active and thousands of fighters rejected that 2016 agreement. But for Salcedo, Fragmentos is not a static space: She regularly invites other artists whose work resonates to exhibit within its walls. When I visited, a crew was de-installing a sound installation by Hajrah Waheed that filled the space with movingly hummed songs of resistance. The work, titled Hum II (2023), is surprisingly affecting, unifying: You’re made to feel something of the song’s sentiments even if they’re in languages you don’t understand. Fittingly, the title means “we” in Urdu, Waheed’s mother tongue.

Like Fragmentos, Salcedo’s studios boast high ceilings. Her workspaces also feature glass brick walls and floating staircases: These are sparse spaces that enable her and her team to see what they are working on. As she walked me through, magnifying glass in hand, she pointed out that one of her studios is the same shape as the home she is building—a triangle atop a square, as if a kid drew a house. Eventually, we came upon the net-like hair arranged in sections like a gradient, growing darker and denser at the bottom. She let me touch it, and I was surprised to find it so sturdy and lightweight at the same time.

THE WORK-IN-PROGRESS MARRIED a complicated process to a simple shape. As we spoke, I found myself wondering about the latter—why a house? I found a hint in two books sitting on the surface of her desk, both of them scanned so she can see them on a screen in large print: Domicide: The Global Destruction of Home and Dreamhouse: Stories of Art and Shelter.

House is not her first work on the subject of the devastating effects of the global housing crisis. Uprooted (2020–22), her prize-winning work in the 15th Sharjah Biennial (where, as it happens, she met Waheed, a fellow prize winner), repurposed 804 dead trees into a mesmerizing, if uninhabitable, home. At almost 1,000 feet long, the work is meant to speak to the predicament of climate refugees. Her newer work, which takes the same shape, is about more deliberate displacement: specifically, “domicide,” which the authors of one of the books on her desk, J. Douglas Porteous and Sandra E. Smith, describe as the calculated destruction of homes. Explaining the impetus for her piece, Salcedo pointed to current conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza, Syria, and Sudan, where people are being violently displaced en masse.

With House, Salcedo wanted to show that, while the dispossessed are of course vulnerable, they are also resilient. Her meshy nets are fragile and flexible, yet they are also much stronger than they seem. Hair may be ephemeral, but she makes it structural and sturdy. It’s all inspired, she told me, by the ways that spiders make webs of silk, material they take from their own bodies. Pairing hair and home, she evokes the ways that bodies and buildings—like dignity and domesticity—are tightly bound.

SALCEDO LEARNED TO WORK WITH human hair from earlier pieces: “Unland” (1995–98) comprises tables severed and then rearranged such that they depend on dissimilar tables for structural support. As if personifying the balancing act, the artist intricately threaded the surfaces with hair, drilling tiny holes in the tables to insert locks she gathered from a local salon. But for House, given its magnitude, she decided to source hair online, learning to look carefully for certain certificates, as there is a lot of violent crime in the human hair trade.

Hair is not the only tricky material that will feature in her fall show. On an upper floor of one of her studios, more assistants were at work on objects of a smaller scale, all destined for display alongside House at White Cube. They were wearing jeweler’s glasses and using X-Acto knives to meticulously remove the starch from individual grains of rice. A team of architects and engineers looked on, huddled around a computer on a lofted level as they worked out the structure of the sculpture’s shape. “I’ve never had such a large team,” she explained as I took in the scene. At one point, she tried working with a renowned engineer who eventually stepped down, saying the idea was too complicated.

When an artist uses sculpture’s most stalwart materials like wood or bronze—as Salcedo has in the past—“the tools are already designed for you,” she said. House required more trial and error than she’s ever needed before—so it also required her biggest team yet. “I had to fabricate new tools and new ways of working,” she explained as we watched assistants drill minuscule holes in starchless rice grains before passing them along to the next station, where still other assistants would thread individual hairs through those tiny openings. They were assembling a kind of mesh, then forming it around damaged cooking supplies—bowls and pots and pans—to form Grains of Sorrow (2023–26), a reminder of what is lost to domicide besides simple structure.

If this sounds like an incredibly elaborate—and surprisingly elegant—way to speak to tragedy, for Salcedo, both beauty and labor are part of her point. She is cognizant of how her studio might provide jobs to those who need them, employing, for instance, 150 women from the Colombian countryside, where it is difficult for them to find work.

The decision to both scale-up and work elaborately is as conceptual as it is material: “My work has always been labor-intensive because in the Global South, labor is intensive,” she said. “It’s completely different from industrialized countries.” She meant this not only as a way to shine a light on contemporary conditions, but also as a retort to art-historical tropes: Modernity is too often narrated, she said, as if “no single person from the Global South participated. But we know all the labor and all the suffering created modernity.” She wants to combine the forms and traditions of European sculpture with painstaking labor to show the two were always intertwined.

I asked her about the role beauty plays for her; she replied that she’s received a lot of criticism on this matter. She maintained, however, that “in all the violence and terror I’ve been researching all my life, I think the abject part belongs to the perpetrator,” adding that “beauty has a lot to do with dignity”—something she wants to restore as she tells the stories of victims. Elegance is also a way to get people to really look: The stories she’s telling are almost always in the newspapers, but that doesn’t mean everyone stops to soak them in. Salcedo doesn’t want you to divert your eyes from the world’s horrors, so she goes to extreme lengths to make sure you can’t look away.

#9032. Vibration Plate Benefits, According to a Weightlifting Coach

Vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he says.

As Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study showed that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe says this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he says.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

“Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe says. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”

Nobbe says WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he says.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe says.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he says.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

#9031. Six standout projects unveiled at Designart Tokyo 2026

As the 10th anniversary edition of Designart Tokyo gets underway, Jane Englefield reports on six highlights from the citywide festival of Japanese creativity.

Designart Tokyo opened on 30 October and will remain open across Tokyo until 8 November.

Around 150 projects by exhibitors from 13 countries are on display at various galleries and other pop-up locations throughout the city.

This year’s main exhibition venue is the former site of the Tokyo Expressway, also known as the KK Line, a portion of which is now an elevated park in the heart of Ginza.

Designart Tokyo’s first dedicated design store is also located on site, selling works from brands including Nendo and Alessi, as well as designers Ronan Bouroullec and Kwangho Lee.

Read on for six of our highlights from the event:

Pulling Apart is a novel adhesive on display as part of the Daikanyama exhibition Separation: Designed to Come Apart, which includes various products created to allow for fluid disassembly and recycling.

Tokyo studio Nomura created the project with the knowledge that, when glue-based adhesives are applied to timber or metal, they are often difficult or impossible to remove. This can mean that materials suffer indelible marks or cannot be recycled at the end of their life.

Nomura’s adhesive is a strong but flexible tape, which firmly holds heavy materials in place. But once the tape is tugged, it stretches and comes away easily.

“Leave one end within reach behind the plinth or under the tabletop, and when the time comes, a single pull undoes the whole thing,” said Nomura.

The tape was developed with easy-disassembly bonding technology developed by Aica Kogyo Company and is still in the prototype phase.

“Peco poco” is a common Japanese onomatopoeia describing a growling stomach.

Experimental design studio Howdunit used the phrase as its starting point for this table lamp, which can be manually unfolded like an accordion thanks to a small hook built into the top of the shade.

Made from delicate layers of gauzy textile, the light opens with a “rhythmic ‘peco poco’ motion” and can be set at various heights.

“By continually asking how things are made, we aim to discover new possibilities in design,” said Howdunit founders Haruto Kamijo and Sho Tasaki.

Forest: Perspectives by Oji Holdings and We+

Tokyo paper manufacturer Oji Holdings is presenting an exhibition in Ginza that meditates on our perspectives on forests.

The manufacturer asked nine professionals, from designers and wood specialists to a writer and a chef, to visit the network of forests it manages and share their individual responses to the landscape.

Among them are delicately whittled spoons made from fallen branches and wood sheets crafted out of bark using a process similar to making washi paper.

The exhibition was laid out in an encyclopedic display designed by local studio We+, founded by Toshiya Hayashi and Hokuto Ando.

Founded in 2021, Tokyo-based 21B Studio is presenting an exhibition at Shibuya’s brutalist-style Tiers Gallery.

Box is the first solo show by the young studio, conceived to demonstrate the myriad ways we can create the humble paper box through various folds and incisions.

The studio is giving out an intricately designed flatpack poster advertising the exhibition, which, once assembled, resembles the geometric architecture of Tiers Gallery itself.

Over in Tokyo Midtown, design master’s student Cecil Nabenashi is presenting a playful exhibition of vases and bowls made of deep-fried paper and fibres.

Nabenashi looked to tempura, Japanese food that is coated in batter and deep-fried in oil, when creating the project.

His goal was to experiment with his “tempura” technique to see if it could provide a long-lasting finish for design objects, using a “batter” he developed from a specially developed blend of non-edible ingredients.

The designer told Dezeen that he plans for his next challenge to be a deep-fried garment.

Industrial Romanticism is an exhibition on display at Minato’s Axis Gallery, Japan’s first dedicated design gallery founded in 1981.

The show is a group exhibition held by designers Yoshiki Matsuyama and Ryota Yokozeki, who asked eight leading Japanese companies to take part.

In-house designers at each of the companies, including bathroom brand Toto and camera maker Fujifilm, created prototypes of recognisable products with an imaginative twist.

Among the designs is a piano made by Ryusuke Baba of musical instrument maker Yamaha. Baba created the piano from pieces of timber that would normally be rejected for an instrument, creating a keyboard with an offbeat sound.

Designart Tokyo 2026 takes place from 30 October to 8 November 2026 at various locations across Tokyo, Japan. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

#9030. Death Row’s Last Meals Anchor a Museum-Wide Survey of Incarceration Art

Louisiana State Penitentiary, known as “Angola” for the slave plantation that once occupied its land, lies at the dead end of Highway 66.

Past the gate, the road continues—invitation permitting—through 18,000 acres of penal farmland punctuated by gun towers, barbed-wire enclosures, and incarcerated men picking crops on the so-called farm line. America’s largest maximum-security prison, long notorious for its reliance on solitary confinement, Angola runs on the forgotten.

Gary Tyler, a fiber artist and activist, remembers Angola. He arrived in 1974 at seventeen years old, wrongly convicted of shooting a white student during a segregationist mob’s attack on his school bus. The prison is bound on three sides by bayou, bluffs, and swamp; escaping into one’s mind was easier. His grandmother was a quilter, he said, and fabric could be found or bartered. Time was given. Over four decades inside, including two stints on death row, he got good, even renowned. Craftswomen from across the South came to Angola to find the man behind the textiles making rounds outside. Related Articles Art en Route: Museum of London Eyes Trump Baby Balloon, Art Institute of Chicago Deaccessions Chinese Artworks, and More Other Voices, Other Worlds

“All that time, I never thought of myself as an ‘artist,’” Tyler said at the opening of “Rebirth,” a solo show of his quilted and appliquéd works at the Grand Rapids Art Museum. “I said, ‘Call me a hobbyist.’ Artists were people in galleries, people with an audience.”

“Rebirth” is one of three solo presentations on view in Grand Rapids through January 2027 that showcase art by or about people once incarcerated within the United States. Ray Materson, whose show is subtitled “Metamorphosis,” works in a medium he invented during his prison sentence for a drug-fueled robbery with a toy gun: palm-sized embroideries stitched by hand from the threads of unraveled socks, Americana meets Renaissance miniature.

The third show is The Last Supper, a 1,000-piece ceramic installation by the artist Julie Green, shown in its entirety for only the second time. For twenty years, up until their death in 2021, Green illustrated final-meal choices on ceramic plates painted in cobalt blue and re-fired in her kiln. What does the condemned order on death row? An overflowing bucket of Kentucky Fried Chicken, lobster, steak, burgers and fries, pecan pie. Nothing, sometimes: inmates can refuse or be denied a selection. (Final meal selections are generally a matter of public records.) At a quick glance, these plates might pass for Staffordshire. A closer look could ruin your lunch.

“It’s not so much that these shows are timely,” said Jennifer Wcisel, curator of collections at the Grand Rapids Art Museum. “It’s that the question of what incarceration means to American life is never absent. It’s ongoing.”

But has punishment been so openly advertised since the pre-Civil Rights era? Tennessee’s botched attempt to execute Christa Pike, the only woman on its death row, was followed by a magazine interview with the physician on hand to pronounce her dead (he said the state should try again). The Defense Secretary called for the military’s first execution in six decades—by firing squad—to be livestreamed. The White House launched an online arcade, where in one game a pixelated Border Patrol agent, rounds up “border crossers.”

The art can’t hope to match the volume of cruelty. It aspires to empathy or at least empathy’s catalyst: curiosity. Whose aim does a public execution serve? Within the carceral system, how is dignity doled out?

The Last Supper argues that dignity is a fickle allowance. Texas ended special last meals in 2011, after white supremacist Lawrence Russell Brewer ordered a feast and left it untouched. Set against Green’s terrible, tender plates, the result is hard to defend. Bite-size biographies like “he never had a birthday cake so we ordered a birth-day cake for him” give way to row upon row of “Standard prison fare.” This is dinnerware for a haunted house.

It is also a map of America’s patchwork principles on capital punishment. The Supreme Court barred executing people with intellectual disabilities in 2002, then left the states to define who qualifies, within limits. One plate records an IQ of 61, well below the benchmark of about 70, and a request that the menu not be released to the media. Another records a request that their meal be saved until after the execution.

Everything on view is portraiture, if the word can stretch to cover a spirit given a recognizable shape, even one abridged to a birthday cake. Tyler and Materson work with representational directness in the opposite register from Green. We see faces. Their work can indulge fantasy, the province of the living. One of Tyler’s quilts depicts a former inmate known as Big Toe in the so-called Greek Alps, still wearing the armor from The Life of Jesus Christ, a play produced by the drama club Tyler founded. Portraiture at its best is said to reveal the heart. For centuries it was also a privilege of the powerful, who commissioned likenesses to control how they were seen. Prison inverts that arrangement: the powerful do the watching. But what does surveillance ever capture of its subjects? Insight can’t be taken, only given.

Materson’s intricate embroideries stray in their subjects from baseball to outer space, with the most striking blending imagination and documentation. In Self-Portrait (undated), he sits before a mirror, stitching the very piece the viewer is looking at. Down a receding tunnel, a smaller Materson stitches a smaller Materson, and so on: infinity, or its likeness. The thick black frame that cages his face is made of the same thread as the rest, not impossibly undone.

One quilt late in Tyler’s show features a great crane, the kind that roosted in the wetlands around Angola and sometimes landed in the prison yard. Tyler was released in 2016, after decades of campaigning by activists including Rosa Parks. The crane captures that moment. His soul, he said, sprang skyward on his first step outside. It has yet to descend.

Tyler’s Convict Poker (2025) unfolds at the Angola prison rodeo: a Black man hangs in midair, bucked from a bull. The last of its kind in the country, the event is held twice a year and open to a paying public. Spectators can’t legally bet; the gamble belongs to the prisoners who volunteer. In convict poker, a raging bull is loosed on a mock card game, and the last man still seated wins a prize. Posting this October’s rodeo to Facebook, an attendee wrote: “The announcer said they didn’t run that fast from the PoPo 🚓😂 Watch til the end, prisoners were flying…”

Tyler never rode in the rodeo. But he doesn’t judge. (One of his quilts were raffled at the rodeo and raised $30,000 for the hospice program.) The men who volunteer, he said, are willing “to jeopardize their lives or go through a sense of degradation just to entertain an audience because nobody wants to be forgotten.”

“These are men who may never go home. The announcer mentions their names, and that they are serving life sentences; understand?”

I will finally have to make peace with Camera Control, and I’m not happy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Whispers in the Appleverse suggest that the iPhone's Action Button could soon be a thing of the past, set to merge with Camera Control. As the tolerant yet unenthused owner of an iPhone 16 (the first line of models to include this feature), I must confess that the news has disturbed me. I can live without Cam Control, but the Action Button? She will be missed.

The iPhone 16 burst onto the scene with the promise that it was the latest and greatest iPhone for photography, and I lapped it right up. 2 years later, I have a confession. The Camera Control button and I rarely make contact, and when we do, we often fall out. My beloved Action Button could never.

I'll admit I was swept up in the initial glamour of the Camera Control button. Watching an Apple Genius effortlessly demo the tech had me fully indoctrinated. 'I will use that scroll feature every day', I naively thought. How efficient. How innovative.

Nowadays I tend to avoid the Camera Control button, having learned my lesson trying to use it at gigs. (Pro tip: balancing a drink under your chin while desperately trying to zoom using Cam Control can lead to major beer spillage if handled incorrectly). At times, I'll use it to make taking snaps a little easier, but on the whole, I scarcely employ the help of its various touch-sensitive capabilities.

But according to prolific leaker Instant Digital, I may have to get over my distaste for Cam Control, as future iPhone models will reportedly do away with the Action Button. Typically used to control the phone's silent mode, the Action Button can be set to an array of functions such as Focus, Voice Memo, Flashlight and more. Reports suggest this feature will soon be merged with Camera Control, supposedly streamlining these quick actions under one touch-sensitive roof.

Whether it's the simple functionality of the Action Button or the tactile haptic feedback of its gentle buzz, I find myself reaching for it far more than Cam Control. While I'll be sad to see it go, I'm intrigued to see how Apple will continue to evolve its iPhone models. It feels like the loss of the Home Button all over again, but I have mourned that and moved on. I'm sure I can do the same for the Action Button.

#9028. Toot Toot! 6 Tips to Prevent Protein Farts

Protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets. They happen because of how proteins are digested. But(t) don’t worry! We have some tips to help you say goodbye to those pungent protein toots without giving up your gains.

Protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant! They’re generally due to upping your protein intake from supplements like protein shakes.

And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.

Farts consist of different gases. The most stinky odors usually come from your gut bacteria, producing sulfur-containing compounds as they break down food. The main culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which gives off a characteristic rotten egg smell, yum!

But why do your protein choices lead to thunder from down under?

Well, there’s not much evidence that a high-protein diet causes protein farts. However, there’s some anecdotal evidence that supplementary protein — like protein bars, protein shakes, and powder powders — increases flatulence, but it’s likely due to non-protein ingredients like lactose.

Supplements containing whey protein or casein are derived from milk and are high in lactose, which can increase flatulence. If your body can’t properly digest lactose, it ends up in your colon, where bacteria feast on it, producing — you guessed it — more gas and cheek flapping.

So, whey protein can throw a curveball for those who are lactose intolerant or sensitive. Surprisingly, it might also stir up digestive drama even for folks who typically handle dairy like champs, potentially due to additives like fart-inducing sweeteners or thickeners.

Some people may also have more significant issues digesting protein. Proteins are big, complex molecules — breaking them down is no small task for your gut. Plant-based protein supplements, like those based on soya beans, may also worsen flatulence.

FYI: Another reason why flatulence is common with protein powders and supplements is due to the addition of artificial sweeteners in the powders and bars, like sugar alcohols, sucralose, sorbitol, xylitol, and stevia.

If you’re looking to continue your protein regimen without becoming a walking, talking whoopee cushion, here are some strategic adjustments you can make:

Don’t just dive into the deep end with your protein intake — wade in slowly. Gradually increasing the amount of protein you consume allows your digestive system to adjust without getting overwhelmed. This step-by-step approach can help minimize the likelihood of excessive gas.

Keep the water flowing. Drinking plenty of water is crucial as it helps your digestive system handle higher protein levels more efficiently. Proper hydration aids in the breakdown and absorption of nutrients, which can help prevent gas buildup.

Sometimes, your body needs a little extra help. Enzyme supplements like Beano or Lactaid can be game-changers, especially if you consume proteins that your body struggles with. These supplements help break down proteins and lactose, making digestion smoother and less gassy.

Variety isn’t just the spice of life — it can also be the solution to your protein fart problems. If whey protein tends to upset your stomach, explore other options like plant-based or animal-based proteins that might be easier to digest. Diversifying your protein sources can also ensure you get a broad range of nutrients.

What you blend your protein powder with can make a big difference. If you’re whipping up a protein shake, be mindful of adding high-fiber fruits and vegetables, as these can also increase gas production. Try to find a balance that allows you to enjoy the benefits of protein and fiber without the extra flatulence.

Introducing probiotics into your diet can improve your gut health, which can help manage and reduce gas production. Whether through supplements or probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, or sauerkraut, boosting your gut flora can aid in better overall digestion and less discomfort from gas.

Protein farts are a rather windy side effect of a high-protein diet, but they don’t have to knock you off course. Try easing into your protein consumption, staying hydrated, diversifying your protein sources, and integrating enzyme supplements or probiotics to max those gains, minus the stink bombs!

Last medically reviewed on June 30, 2024

#9027. Lagoons will weave through new Egyptian city masterplanned by SOM

International architecture studio SOM has unveiled plans for a new city in Egypt named Alam Al Roum, which will stretch 7.2 kilometres along the Mediterranean coastline.

Set to be built near Marsa Matrouh, the 20.6-square-kilometre masterplan features swimmable lagoons alongside 22 kilometres of seawater-connected lagoons, which will weave through the built environment to support stormwater management.

“The Mediterranean is home to some of the world’s great cities, shaped over centuries by climate, culture and economic forces,” said SOM principal Thomas Hussey.

“Alam Al Roum presents a rare opportunity to imagine a new city from the ground up, one that responds to the realities of climate change while offering an exceptional quality of life.”

SOM designed the masterplan around Egypt’s north coast landscape and climate, orienting buildings and public spaces to take advantage of coastal breezes and sunlight.

The development will be elevated to accommodate changing coastal conditions, while waterfront areas will be protected with natural interventions such as riparian buffers, stormwater wetlands, stabilised dunes and living shorelines.

Designed for developer Qatari Diar, Alam Al Roum will comprise beachfront and lagoon-side neighbourhoods, town centres, areas for hospitality and resorts, golfing facilities, an education district and a business hub.

A grand boulevard will form an urban spine connecting an international marina on the Mediterranean Sea with a mobility hub further inland.

Aiming to establish the city as a year-round cultural destination, Alam Al Roum’s waterfront downtown will contain a cultural pier, lighthouse, amphitheatre, yacht club, mosque, and markets.

The first phase of the city development is expected to commence in 2030, comprising a four-square-kilometre area with a beachfront stretch, open-sea-connected lagoons and a town-centre marina.

“Alam Al Roum represents our vision for a new generation of Mediterranean destinations – one that goes beyond the traditional seasonal resort to create a vibrant, year-round coastal city,” said Qatari Diar CEO Hamad bin Talal Al-Thani.

“We are bringing together nature, the sea, hospitality and everyday life within a carefully planned environment that reflects the unique character of Egypt’s north coast,” he continued.

“Through our partnership with SOM and our global network of experts, we are creating a destination that is rooted in its landscape and climate, while setting a new benchmark for integrated coastal development in the Mediterranean.”

In recent years, Egypt established a new capital city east of Cairo. The initial design concept for the city was designed by SOM and further developed by the international building consultancy Dar al-Handasah Shair & Partners.

#9026. The 13 Best London Museums to Visit

London’s numerous museums feature some of the best art, history, science, and cultural collections in the world. With many of these institutions free to enter, paying a visit to one or more can even be an inexpensive day out.

Many of the museums listed here have recently gone through major revamps, and over the coming year there will be even more destinations to visit, with the long-awaited London Museum coming to the historic Smithfield Market and the Museum of Shakespeare opening on the site of the Curtain Playhouse.

If you’re looking for extraordinary cultural objects from the dawn of civilization, head over to the venerable British Museum. There you’ll find such treasures as an impressive collection of ancient Mesopotamian items; the second-century BC Rosetta Stone, which provided the key to deciphering ancient Egyptian hieroglyphics; and the fifth-century BC ancient Greek Parthenon Marbles. Look up to see British starchitect Norman Foster’s amazing glass roof, completed in 2000. The British Museum holds more than eight million objects covering over two million years of human history, with about 80,000 objects on view at any given time. If you feel overwhelmed with the choice of what to see, book a tour and enjoy the luxury of being in the hands of a knowledgeable guide.

Right in the center of London on Trafalgar Square, the National Gallery offers artworks dating from 1260 right up to the 20th century—from Da Vinci to David, Canaletto to Constable, Michelangelo to Monet, Rousseau to Rubens, Cezanne to Seurat, Vermeer to Velazquez to Van Gogh, and that’s just a small fraction of its offerings. And it’s free to enter. For a fee, there are also larger exhibitions in the much acclaimed, recently renovated Sainsbury Wing. The Sainsbury Wing is quite the character itself, of course, ever since in 1984 King Charles III, while still Prince of Wales, described the initial proposed design for it as a “monstrous carbuncle on the face of a much-loved and elegant friend.” The plan was altered, and what opened in 1991 is what you see now: classical mannerism in a sensitively designed addition to the main gallery’s domed facade. After your visit, head to the St-Martin-in-the-Fields Crypt just over the road for a good-value hot canteen meal, and linger in this famous neoclassical church by 18th-century architect James Gibbs for one of its candlelight concerts.

The beating heart of the city, the Tower of London is steeped in so much history it’s dizzying—from the White Tower’s inception as a fortified palace by William the Conqueror on his invasion after the Battle of Hastings, in 1066, to its long-term use as a prison. King Henry VIII’s wife Anne Boleyn was imprisoned and executed there in 1536 after she was accused of adultery; Guy Fawkes, Robert Catesby, and the Gunpowder Plotters were kept in the Tower in 1605 after their failed plan to blow up the Houses of Parliament; and deputy Nazi Party leader Rudolf Hess was confined there in 1941. The Crown Jewels have been safeguarded at the Tower since 1661 and are immaculately displayed; other highlights include Anne Boleyn’s final resting place, an incredible collection of armor, twisted metal artifacts from the 1666 Great Fire of London, the Medieval Palace (in use until 1307) that recently opened to the public, and of course the Yeomen Warders, or Beefeaters, the retired military personnel who run the place. And if that isn’t enough, there’s also a fantastic immersive experience about the Gunpowder Plot in the old tunnels just outside the walls of the Tower, a superb addition that should be booked in advance.

A shrine to all things bright and beautiful and to creatures great and small, the Natural History Museum in South Kensington (around the corner from the Science Museum) was founded with proceeds from the Great Exhibition of 1851. Quite apart from what’s inside, this museum’s facade encapsulates its purpose: Stand in front of the building and see how many extinct and living species you can spot— there are saber-toothed cats, pterodactyls, ancient palaeotherium (stocky mammals with a beaklike snout), extinct and modern fish, lizards, goats, lions, and wolves. Opened in 1881, this museum was fast dubbed a “cathedral of nature,” and it still is, filled to the brim with flora and fauna, including a magnificent blue whale skeleton suspended from the ceiling. The museum holds an astonishing collection of specimens, 80 million in total, only a fraction of which can be displayed at any one time. Head to the all-time favorite Dinosaur galleries, complete with an animatronic Tyrannosaurus rex; then take your pick from volcanoes, fossils, human evolution, mammals, fish, amphibians, reptiles, minerals, and more. If the sheer amount of stuff is daunting, start with the Treasures gallery for the cream of the crop.

There is so much to see at the Victoria and Albert Museum in South Kensington that you just have to prioritize. With astonishing collections from Britain and across the world, the V&A holds examples of jewelry, design, fashion, art, and architecture, from medieval times to the modern era. One of the timeless highlights of this museum is the Cast Courts: The Victorians were mad about taking casts of classic sculptures, and we reap the rewards today. Built specifically to house the enormous reproductions of Trajan’s Column from ancient Rome, these monumental courts also hold an electrifying cast of Michelangelo’s David. Make sure you also see the Raphael Cartoons housed in their own gallery, and find out which William Morris works the museum currently has on show; his enduring Arts and Crafts textile and wallpaper designs are widely loved. And allow at least half an hour for a good browse of the V&A shop. It’s one of the best museum stores in existence.

Tate Modern has been a fixture of the art world since it was inaugurated in the year 2000 in an ex-power station, an ambitious undertaking by the Swiss starchitects Herzog and De Meuron. There’s a lot to see here; the best approach may be to concentrate on either the collections or the special exhibitions and not attempt to absorb it all in one sitting. Collection wise, don’t miss Surrealist Salvador Dalí’s 1938 Lobster Telephone; Unique Forms of Continuity in Space (1913, cast 1972) by Italian futurist Umberto Boccioni; Composition (1913) by British Vorticist Wyndham Lewis; the notorious Fountain by Marcel Duchamp (1917, replica 1964); the calming color fields of Mark Rothko’s Seagram murals (commissioned in 1958); and the classic Pop Art punch Whaam! (1963) by Roy Lichtenstein.

A treat for kids and adults alike, the Science Museum is always captivating. Wander into the Energy Hall for a hit of seductive steam-driven engines and then into the freshly reopened Space section to see space capsules from the 1960s to today. For those wanting a more interactive experience, there is the Wonderlab, for visitors 7 to 14 years old, and Power Up, a hands-on gaming experience for anyone over the age of 5, where guests can play on 160 consoles spanning five decades. (Be sure to book the interactive galleries ahead of time.) There’s an IMAX Cinema, too, with one of the biggest screens in Europe. The Science Museum has redone many of its galleries in recent years, including the excellent Energy Revolution, about the history of energy production, with examples of an antique electric car and offshore energy near the coast of Scotland; and the stunning Mathematics gallery, housed in a wickedly futuristic design by the late architect Zaha Hadid, showing objects such as intriguing handheld mathematical instruments, a 1929 experimental aircraft, early computers, and coding machines. There’s much more, covering such subjects as flight, clockmaking, science from 1550 to 1800, engineering, and medicine. And if you still want more, you can stay the night in the museum’s current season of Astronights, for space-obsessed children and their parents.

Founded by sugar magnate Henry Tate and opened in 1897, Tate Britain holds cornerstone works of the Victorian circle of Pre-Raphaelites, including Ophelia (1851–2) by John Everett Millais, John William Waterhouse’s 1888 portrayal of The Lady of Shalott, and lesser-known works by Dante Gabriel Rossetti, who exhumed his wife’s corpse just to recover an unpublished poetry manuscript with which she’d been buried. If you want to delve deeper into darkness, seek out the contorted forms of Francis Bacon’s 1944 work Three Studies for the Figures at the Base of a Crucifixion. Then recover by contemplating the gentle forms of British sculptor Henry Moore. Also in the collection are Torso in Metal from the Rock Drill (1913–15) by Jacob Epstein, a pivotal Vorticist work; Fall (1963) by Bridget Riley, one of her signature Op Art illusions; and the bright tones of A Bigger Splash (1967) by David Hockney.

Plunge into the decadent rococo interiors of the Wallace Collection with feel-good artworks and exquisitely crafted armor displayed in luxurious settings. Make sure you see The Swing (Les hasards heureux de l’escarpolette) (1767–68) by the Rococo hedonist Jean-Honoré Fragonard—it’s one of the sexiest paintings ever made—as well as the museum’s fabulously sumptuous collection of François Boucher paintings. The Laughing Cavalier (1624) by Dutch portraitist Frans Hals, enigmatic and engaging, also adorns the Wallace’s walls.

Entering the Courtauld’s permanent collection feels like getting together for a few beers with a bunch of old school friends—people you know, love, and will always relish the company of. With all the greats from the Renaissance masters to the Postimpressionists, the Courtauld shows you an old friend everywhere you look. There’s plenty to reacquaint yourself with, including Adam and Eve (1526) by Lucas Cranach the Elder, A Bar at the Folies-Bergère (1882) by Édouard Manet, Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear (1889) by Vincent van Gogh, and a strong array of works by Paul Cezanne, Edgar Degas, Paul Gauguin, Claude Monet, Auguste Renoir, Georges Seurat, and many more.

Within the concrete jungle of the Southbank Centre nestles the Hayward Gallery, which consistently delivers excellent contemporary works in its novel 1960s concrete environment. There is not permanent collection and all temporary shows are ticketed. Pop over to the British Film Institute afterwards for a movie, or to the Royal Festival Hall for a meal or a performance.

From 1512 until the mid-18th century, Greenwich was the headquarters for the British navy. First established under King Henry VIII, the Royal Navy became key to Britain’s success as a nation in trade and warfare alike, and its base was always Greenwich, now a UNESCO World Heritage site. Among the noteworthy attractions is the Queen’s House, built for Anne of Denmark (1574–1619) and designed by the so-called father of British architecture, Inigo Jones. (And if you approach from the river, you’ll see the remarkable symmetry in the buildings that flank the house, one of Christopher Wren’s classic feats of architectural wonder.) Once a royal residence, the Queen’s House now holds an excellent collection of art, including the 1588 Armada Portrait of Elizabeth I sitting in regal splendor before scenes showing the ruined Spanish Armada and the victorious British fleet. You can also see 19th-century master J.M.W. Turner’s largest canvas, The Battle of Trafalgar (1822), only recently put on display.

But that’s only one small part of the Greenwich complex. Don’t miss England’s answer to the Sistine Chapel at the Old Royal Naval College: the Painted Hall (1707–26), James Thornhill’s masterpiece, reopened to the public in 2019 after major conservation. For a comprehensive history of Britain’s maritime exploits, from sailing the seven seas and polar exploration to warfare and global trade, visit the National Maritime Museum, whose highlights include the Trafalgar Coat, the uniform that Admiral Horatio Nelson wore on his deathbed in 1805. Then visit the Cutty Sark, the fastest sailing ship of its time. Built in Scotland in 1869, she traded tea from China with a typical round trip taking just seven to nine months. And then, to tie the whole site together, head to the iconic onion dome of the Royal Observatory, where time was first standardized, in 1884. Step on the prime meridian line, gratis, or buy advance tickets to see the Great Equatorial Telescope, installed in 1893.

Complete with its own ride through the old underground tunnels used to transport mail, the Postal Museum tells the story of the Royal Mail, which might not sound immediately enticing, but this museum does it so well, it’s worth a visit. Its manageable size, brilliant story, and ride on the Mail Rail, with history explained via engaging projections on the tunnel walls, make this museum a gem and superb for visitors of all ages.
