Let's make this concrete. You and your partner want to celebrate a milestone — a sabbatical, a paid-off mortgage, financial independence itself — with a trip to Sydney. Here's exactly how this redemption plays out.

The Route: Los Angeles (LAX) → Hong Kong (HKG) → Sydney (SYD), on Cathay Pacific Business Class, with a 3-night stopover in Hong Kong.

Cash Price: A quick search on Google Flights confirms what you suspected — this itinerary in business class retails for approximately $8,000 per person during the shoulder season. During the Australian summer or holiday periods, it climbs closer to $11,000–$12,000.

Your Cost: 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles + approximately $85 in taxes and fees. Per person.

CPP Calculation: At $8,000 cash value, your 55,000 miles are worth 14.5 cents per point — more than seven times what you'd get redeeming Alaska miles for domestic economy. At $12,000, you're at 21.8 cents per point, which is among the highest CPP figures available anywhere in the U.S. loyalty ecosystem.

In Hong Kong, Cathay Pacific's The Pier Business Class Lounge awaits during your stopover travel. It's widely regarded as one of the finest airport lounges in the world — noodle bar, live cooking stations, a spa treatment center, and a wine selection that rivals dedicated restaurants.

After three days exploring Hong Kong, you reboard for the six-hour SYD leg, arriving in Sydney ready — genuinely ready, not depleted — to start your adventure.

Total cost for two: 110,000 Alaska miles + roughly $170 in fees. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: extraordinary experiences made nearly free through a system anyone can learn.

Alaska's booking window opens 331 days out. Cathay Pacific releases business class award space to partner programs in limited quantities, and the best dates disappear quickly. Set a calendar alert for 331 days before your target travel date and be ready to search — and call — that morning.

The single best technique for this redemption: run your search on ba.com before calling Alaska. BA's search engine is faster, more reliable for Cathay availability, and lets you visually scan a full month of dates. Identify two or three date options before you pick up the phone. This dramatically shortens your call time and reduces the chance of getting an agent who says "I'm not seeing anything."

Don't treat the Hong Kong stopover as a layover — treat it as a destination. Alaska's routing rules explicitly allow a free stopover on one-way awards. Two to four nights in Hong Kong costs you nothing extra in miles. Pair this with a cheap positioning flight or use it as an anchor for a broader Asia itinerary.

This is the most common and most painful mistake. Marriott-to-Alaska transfers are generally not reversible. If you transfer 165,000 Bonvoy points to Alaska and then discover no award space exists on your dates, you're stuck with miles you may not use optimally. Always confirm availability on ba.com before initiating any transfer.

Book two one-way redemptions rather than a round-trip. This gives you full flexibility on return routing — you might come back on Qantas through another city, or extend your trip without penalty.

Since there are no major flexible currency transfer paths into Alaska (no Chase, Amex, or Citi transfers), the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature from Bank of America is your most efficient earning vehicle. The welcome bonus alone can cover a significant portion of this redemption. Pair with everyday spending in categories that earn elevated miles.

If Cathay availability is closed on your dates, Qantas Business Class to Australia prices at the same 55,000 miles. Qantas' "The Business" product on their A380 Sydney routes is exceptional in its own right — and availability patterns differ from Cathay, so checking both genuinely doubles your options.

This redemption is purpose-built for the FI-minded couple or solo traveler who is willing to invest some effort in the booking process in exchange for an extraordinary, nearly free experience. If you've been dreaming about Australia and refuse to pay $8,000–$12,000 for a business class ticket — but you're also not willing to spend 20+ hours crammed in economy for a trip this significant — this is your answer.

Minimum requirements: You need 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles per person. For two travelers, that's 110,000 miles. If you're building from zero through the Alaska Visa, factor in 6–12 months of earning runway before booking.

Within a broader FI travel strategy, this redemption pairs well with a Marriott Bonvoy credit card for point accumulation and an Alaska Visa for direct mile earning. It's a medium-complexity move with a very high ceiling on value.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating** — and that rating is honest. It's not complicated in concept, but it has two specific friction points that trip up even experienced travel rewards enthusiasts. **Challenge 1: Earning the Miles** Alaska Mileage Plan's isolation from major flexible currency programs (no Chase Ultimate Rewards, no Amex Membership Rewards, no Citi ThankYou transfers directly) means you can't simply funnel points you already have into Alaska. The primary path is the Alaska Airlines Visa (Bank of America) or a Marriott Bonvoy conversion at an unfavorable 3:1 ratio. Plan your earning strategy well in advance. **Tip:** Prioritize the Alaska Visa signup bonus as your foundation, then supplement with Marriott points if needed. **Challenge 2: The Phone Booking Requirement** You cannot book this online. The call-in process intimidates people who've only ever booked travel digitally. **Tip:** Do your homework on ba.com first, have your dates ready, and approach the call as an informed customer — not someone asking for help finding availability. Agents respond well to specific, prepared callers. **Challenge 3: Cathay Award Availability** Cathay Pacific releases partner award space selectively and often in small quantities. Availability rated 3/5. **Tip:** Search exactly at the 331-day booking window, keep Qantas as your backup at the same price point, and be flexible with travel dates by even one or two days — a Tuesday departure often has inventory when Saturday doesn't. The good news: once you've done this once, you'll understand the system deeply enough to replicate it. The ChooseFI community has members who've booked this exact route multiple times. The first time takes effort. After that, it's a process you know cold.

The fastest path is the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card from Bank of America, which typically offers a 60,000 to 75,000-mile sign-up bonus. That alone nearly covers the 55,000 miles needed. You can also transfer Marriott Bonvoy points at 3:1 (165,000 Bonvoy points equals 55,000 Alaska miles) or earn miles through flying Alaska and its partners.

Yes. You would book two separate one-way awards at 55,000 miles each. You could fly Cathay Pacific one direction and Qantas the other, or mix carriers based on availability. Each one-way can include its own free stopover.

Cathay Pacific typically releases Business Class award space 90 to 330 days before departure. The sweet spot for finding availability is usually 90 to 120 days out, when airlines release unsold premium cabin seats. Check frequently, as availability can appear and disappear quickly.

Alaska allows one free stopover on one-way awards. On a routing from the US to Australia via Hong Kong, you can stop in Hong Kong for any number of days at no additional miles cost. Simply tell the agent when booking that you want a stopover in HKG. This effectively gives you two destinations for the price of one redemption.

The Alaska Mileage Plan redemption for Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class to Australia is one of the most extraordinary sweet spots in travel rewards. At 55,000 miles for a seat that costs $5,000 to $12,000 in cash — with zero fuel surcharges and a free stopover in Hong Kong — this redemption delivers 9 to 22 cents per point. It requires more planning and effort than a simple hotel booking, but the payoff is a genuine luxury travel experience that proves the asymmetric value the FI community builds its travel rewards strategy around.

#8991. What Does Dark Green Poop Mean? Causes, Diet, and When to See a Doctor

Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.

Most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down. But if the green becomes a recurring (fecal) matter, it might be something else.

Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.

Spotting green or another unexpected color in the toilet can be startling, but it’s more common than you might think. From dietary influences to your body’s digestion speed, several factors can change poop from earthy tones to other shades. Let’s check some out.

Are you chowing down on lots of green leafy veggies like spinach, kale, or broccoli? These foods are high in chlorophyll, which can dye your doodles green. Chlorophyll doesn’t always break down entirely before reaching your intestines, meaning it passes through your system and colors your stool green.

Have you ever had a St. Paddy’s Day-themed milkshake or a brightly colored cake? Artificial colors in foods and drinks can change poop from brown to green. It’s not magic! It’s just the dye in green food passing through your gut unchanged.

When your digestive system processes food too rapidly, it doesn’t allow for the full breakdown of bile, a yellow-green fluid that aids digestion. This often results in a greenish stool, especially during fast-moving episodes of diarrhea.

Have you recently been taking antibiotics? These meds can reset your gut’s bacterial crew. Since these tiny critters play a big part in the shade of your stool, introducing antibiotics might cause green poop sometimes.

If you’ve had certain medical treatments, it can affect digestion and cause bright green poop. One example is graft-versus-host disease, which may occur with bone marrow transplants. This tricky condition can bring about less-than-welcome guests, like diarrhea and green stool. It’s a clear signal from your body that things are out of sync.

Some uninvited microscopic guests like Salmonella bacteria, the water-loving mini parasite Giardia, and norovirus can also be a reason for your poop turning green. These critters can hustle your digestion at an unnaturally quick pace, turning your stool green as they disrupt your gut’s usual rhythm.

Babies can surprise you with a whole crayon box of poop colors, and green is definitely in the mix.

For infants, green stool might stem from the same factors as adults, like dietary changes. This includes adjustments when they start eating solids or changes in a parent’s diet if chestfeeding.

Another harmless cause could be ingesting a small amount of amniotic fluid in the womb. So, if you notice your little one sporting some spring grass-colored diapers, it’s usually no biggie.

If the green theme park in your toilet isn’t closing down, or if it’s accompanied by other symptoms like severe stomach pain, nausea, or diarrhea, it might be time to call in the pros. Persistent changes in stool color may signal underlying health issues that need medical attention.

Dark green poop can result from eating lots of leafy greens or foods with green coloring. However, it can also indicate that food travels quickly through the digestive system.

While liver issues can change stool color, they usually turn it pale or dark, not green. If you’re worried about liver health, look for pale or clay-colored stools instead.

If you haven’t been on a kale-eating spree, dark green poop might be from iron supplements or constipation remedies, which can also give poop a greenish tint.

Dark poop could be a sign of your diet or medications. However, if it’s black and tar-like, it might mean bleeding in your upper gastrointestinal tract. In that case, chatting with a healthcare professional is a must.

While green poop can def throw you through a loop, it’s usually not a sign of anything serious. It’s often your body’s way of dealing with what you eat or how fast you digest. So, unless it’s paired with other worrying symptoms, there’s probably no need to panic.

#8990. pearce+ co-builds guerrilla shading pavilion from salvaged timber and canvas sails in camden

architecture practice pearce+ completes the guerrilla shading pavilion for the camden inspire festival, an open, mobile cooling structure.

EE17 edited by christina vergopoulou November 9, 2026 3 min

Commissioned by Camden Town Unlimited and Euston Town BIDs for the Camden Inspire festival, architecture practice PEARCE+ collaborated with advocacy group Shade The UK and local volunteers to co-build the Guerrilla Shading pavilion. Sited at Camden Collective in London, the structure responds to escalating urban temperatures and the urban heat island effect, functioning as reusable, mobile shade infrastructure designed for continuous reassembly rather than single-event use.

The primary framework comprises five prefabricated panels sized for transport in a standard transit van. Engineered with a tapering profile to counter wind loads transferred by cantilevered tensile canopies, the structure utilizes structural timber salvaged from previous PEARCE+ installations. The lower register of the frame is intentionally left open, enabling visitors to manually weave an enclosure using reclaimed balloon fabric supplied by Cameron Hot Air Balloons and Inflate Studio. Tensioned naturally dyed canvas sails, developed in collaboration with artist Auda Sakho, project outward from the core frame to expand the shaded footprint over the surrounding garden. Complementing the physical pavilion, Camden Inspire and PEARCE+ Studio published Guerrilla Shading Our City, an open-source guide detailing low-cost shading tactics, ranging from DIY external shutters and tensile sails to urban tree planting and municipal planning permissions.

Guerrilla Shading pavilion is a co-built urban cooling structure designed by PEARCE+the structural skeleton is formed by five prefabricated modular timber panelsthe installation functions as reusable, demountable infrastructure

#8989. Nothing but a single joint holds together Dado furniture

Berlin studio Allen Kaufmann Architekten has adapted a traditional woodworking joint to create a flat-pack range that can be assembled completely without tools – and it’s been voted furniture design of the year by Dezeen readers.

No glue, screws, brackets or other fasteners are used in the Dado tables and shelves.

Instead, their solid-timber construction is held together using only one deceptively simple type of joint: a narrow trench cut across the length of one piece of wood so another can slot into it.

Known as a dado or housing joint, it has been a fixture of woodworking for thousands of years.

But Allen Kaufmann Architekten has reimagined this traditional technique as the only thing holding up an entire self-supporting furniture range that can be easily flat-packed, assembled, demounted and repaired.

“I started with the traditional dado cut, a simple groove cut into timber, and asked whether that basic operation could become an entire structural system rather than simply a joint,” explained studio co-founder Justin Allen.

His patented joint, developed over several years of prototyping, turns dado cuts on their head – or more precisely, at a 45-degree angle – so they can be used to join not just two pieces of wood but four.

This allows a vertical element, a horizontal element and two diagonal braces to lock together at a single point through simple geometry.

“Visually, it has something of a post-and-beam construction, with intersecting diagonal bracing, almost like the inside of a timber barn,” the architect explained. “But the geometry and the way all four elements meet are specific to Dado, giving the joint its own distinct appearance.”

So far, Allen has used this same logic to create a table and a modular shelving system, using a limited set of repeated parts.

As Allen sees it, this offers a more elegant solution to current joinery systems. Furniture with permanent fixings is cumbersome, expensive and emissions-intensive to transport, he argues, while traditional flat-pack systems rely on different screws, brackets and fittings that can be lost or damaged.

In both cases, the joints limit how often and how easily the furniture can be disassembled and reused, which can lead to an otherwise functional piece being abandoned.

With Dado, Allen has avoided the need for fixings and left the joints themselves exposed, in the hope that the furniture’s owner will be able to understand how it works and how it might be maintained.

“The connection remains visible, so the joint becomes the detail, the structure, the assembly and ultimately the design,” he explained.

Each of the range’s standard components is CNC milled with machine precision. This allows the whole range to be produced by a single workshop anywhere in the world – another win in the transport department.

Dado was named furniture design of the year in this year’s Dezeen Awards public vote and is now in the running to be crowned overall winner by a jury of leading industry figures including Norman Foster, Michael Anastassiades and Jaime Hayon.

There, it is up against projects from Tom Fereday, Yabu Pushelberg, String Furniture and more.

#8987. How to Calculate Your Rising and Moon Sign: A Beginner’s Guide

The sun sign is the *it girlie* of the “big three” elements in astrology.

But do you know about your moon sign and rising sign?

We chatted with an astrologer to understand what they are and how to calculate them.

According to Olga Verkhotina — astrologer and personal coach — the big three in astrology are your three most significant chart elements:

“While a natal chart contains so many more intricate details beyond just three elements, the big three is a way to determine the main highlights that make up your personality and overall temperament,” Verkhotina says.

Verkhotina explains that a rising sign is the zodiac sign that falls at the beginning of your First House — basically, the beginning of your natal chart.

“The First House in astrology is associated with a person’s identity, individual activity, even their appearance, and the sign that houses that theme gives its characteristics,” she says.

“Knowing your rising sign describes the way others may perceive you, the way your behavior comes across, as well as how you approach new situations in life.”

You’ll need: date, time and place of birth.

“Knowing the accurate time is important here because even 10 minutes can make a difference in the sign,” Verkhotina explains.

“Once you have the data, you can trust astrology software to calculate it for you. There are a lot of natal chart calculators online, so you can just search ‘rising sign calculator,'” Verkhotina says.

Pro tip: Verkhotina suggests reading horoscopes from your rising sign instead of your sun sign, saying it will likely give more personalized insights on which areas of your life might be impacted by current cosmic events.

“A moon sign describes the position of the moon on the zodiac wheel at the moment of your birth,” Verkhotina says.

She explains that the moon in astrology symbolizes:

“The moon sign helps you better understand how these themes demonstrate themselves in your life,” Verkhotina says.

Unlike the rising sign, you don’t have to have the precise time of birth to know your moon sign, although Verkhotina says it’s still recommended.

You can also use an online calculator to find your moon sign or refer to the ephemeris — a table showing the daily positions of planets.

Verkhotina describes the sun sign as the most important planet in your chart.

“It’s the center of your vitality, your ego, consciousness, and individuality at its core. That’s why it’s the most commonly known element in astrology,” she says.

It represents the zodiac sign the sun was in at the time of your birth, which Verkhotina says gives your individuality certain qualities associated with its specific sign.

“It’s important to understand that although the sun is a huge element in astrology, it doesn’t cover the nuances of one’s character,” Verkhotina explains.

Instead, she says it just represents overall traits.

Verkhotina adds that the specifics of your character are covered in the rest of your astrological chart. “This is why sometimes no two leos are the same,” she says.

This one is easy peasy — you don’t have to have your time or place of birth.

“The sun cycle is very similar every year, so you can look it up by the date, month and year of your birth. Each sign corresponds to a calendar date that year,” Verkhotina says.

Here’s each astro sign, in a nutshell, according to Verkhotina.

Your sun sign is important, but your moon and rising signs add extra details.

Your rising sign reflects your identity and how others see you, while your moon sign reveals your emotions and behavior.

To find these signs, you can use online birth chart calculators. Just make sure you have your birth date and time handy for accurate results.

#8986. inside mikoü architecture and its search for meaning in craft and construction

from the intimacy of the traditional riad to the engineering of contemporary buildings, the french-moroccan twin architects explore how cultural memory, craftsmanship, and industrialization can inform a more holistic approach to architecture.

In We Are Building Ourselves, a film by Louisiana Channel, Salwa and Selma Mikoü describe architecture as a process that extends beyond the production of buildings. ‘As architects, we are building also our own personality, our own culture, our own way to see the world. And project after project, we push boundaries that could be also our own boundaries as women,’ the architects share. For the Paris-based twin sisters, every project is a way to establish their position in the world and negotiate the cultural, professional, and personal experiences that shape their work.

That idea is reflected in a practice that brings together seemingly opposing forms of knowledge. The founders of Mikoü Architecture draw on Moroccan traditions of craft and ornament while exploring prefabrication, industrialization, and the technical logic of construction. They are interested in how engineering can become part of architectural expression, how industrial processes can coexist with craftsmanship, and how cultural memory can inform buildings without becoming a superficial visual reference.

In the Louisiana Channel film, the sisters discuss architecture through the language of making: the assembly of materials, the relationship between structure and ornament, the social qualities of space, and the knowledge carried across generations.

Before establishing Mikoü Architecture in Paris in 2008, the sisters each worked at Ateliers Jean Nouvel and Renzo Piano Building Workshop. These experiences exposed them to different approaches to architectural thinking and making, from the development of a strong conceptual position to the practical knowledge involved in realizing a building. For the sisters, engineering is the skeleton of a building, an underlying system that can inform its spatial and visual character. Their interest in prefabrication and industrialization comes from this understanding of construction as an integral part of design. They describe industrialization as a ‘progress gesture’, while acknowledging that these methods are ‘still not standard at all’.

The architects bring craftsmanship and industrial production into the same conversation. They are interested in prefabrication and what it makes possible, but also in the knowledge that comes from working with materials and understanding how things are made. One does not have to come at the expense of the other.

They also speak about ornament in relation to structure and how it can occur from the construction process itself. In the film, they discuss the tension between what is exposed and what is hidden, comparing it to archaeology and ruins, where the remains of a structure offer clues to what once existed.

Born in Fez, Morocco, Salwa and Selma Mikoü draw on their relationship with the country as part of their thinking. They speak about Marrakech as an ‘immersive city’ and about the strong impressions that places leave on them. These experiences shape how they think about space, particularly the relationship between private life and the outside world. They point to the traditional riad, with its terraces and inward-facing spaces, where neighbors can see and speak to one another.

Speaking about Art de Rives, their project in Bordeaux, they describe it as ‘a kind of urban millefeuille’, combining housing, artist residencies, and student accommodation. Its relationship with the Garonne is central to the project, which seeks to open the development toward the river and the surrounding city. The architects’ experience of growing up in Morocco and building their careers in France brings two different architectural cultures into their work. Moroccan craft traditions, particularly the use of ornament, remain an important reference, while their years working within the French architectural scene have shaped their understanding of contemporary practice.

Working together has shaped the way Salwa and Selma Mikoü think and work. They describe a process that involves a lot of talking and drawing, with collage becoming one of the tools they return to when developing ideas. They call it part of their DNA. Being twins also means that their professional and personal lives are closely connected, something they reflect on in the film when discussing how people often see them as one person.

The sisters speak about architecture as a way of shaping who they are, not only as architects but as women finding their place in a profession that has its own expectations and established hierarchies. Every project gives them another opportunity to question those limits.

#8985. Library by Collective Architecture breathes new life into Scottish high street

Film and photography by Jim Stephenson

The conversion of a dilapidated high-street building into a public library in Paisley, Scotland, shortlisted for the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award, features in this video by photographer Jim Stephenson.

The film forms part of a series being published by Dezeen in collaboration with the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) to highlight the annual award’s 2026 shortlist.

In the video, viewers are introduced to Paisley Central Library, designed by Scottish studio Collective Architecture to serve as a welcoming community space with reading areas, event spaces and a study room.

According to studio director Ewan Imrie, Paisley Central Library was conceived as a civic space for “people to dwell”.

“The client was very clear from the outset that the building had to be as welcoming to all different types of people from all aspects of society,” Imrie said.

“Encouraging people to dwell was the most important thing and if they pick up a book and read it then that’s a bonus.”

Established in 2002, the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual award that highlights Scottish projects, with this year’s winner set to be announced on 26 November.

Comprising three reuse projects, RIAS said this year’s shortlisted projects tap into “important conversations around community, collaboration, retrofit and reuse”. Shortlisted alongside the Paisley Central Library is the Edinburgh Futures Institute by Bennetts Associates and the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion by Studio Octopi.

Last year’s winner was a public park renewed by studios Stallan-Brand and LDA Design.

The film and photography is courtesy of Jim Stephenson.

#8984. Yoga and Overweight: Health Benefits and Tips for Getting Started

Part of the beauty of yoga is its accessibility for everyone. Yoga practitioners come in all shapes and sizes and are hella modifiable. If you have overweight, there’s 100% a place for you in the world of downward dogs, crescent lunges, and resting pigeons.

Check out these benefits of yoga for overweight.

For wellness, you’d be hard-pressed to find a more holistic practice than yoga. Your physical and mental health can get a boost from busting out your mat.

The limb-stretching, muscle-engaging, bodyweight-bearing nature of yoga has many physical benefits.

For starters, yoga may enhance your metabolism. An older study found that people who practiced had greater metabolic efficiency and lower weight than non-yogis.

It’s clear, too, that yoga’s combo of cardio and strength torches calories. A 160-pound person can burn around 180 calories per hour, popping in and out of poses. A 2021 study revealed that both Hatha and vinyasa yoga led to weight loss, with an average of 3.4 kilograms (7.5 pounds) lost over a 6-month.

Extra strength and flexibility are two other well-known upsides of the practice. Research shows that even sedentary folks can build these elements of fitness by taking up yoga. One study showed that, after 8 weeks of practicing at least twice a week (180 minutes), people with no prior yoga experience had greater muscle strength, endurance, flexibility, and cardio-respiratory fitness.

On the surface, yoga might look like mere stretching — but the practice goes far beyond the physical. Yoga engages the mind in all sorts of ways that may have benefits for overweight.

By training your brain toward calm and focus, yoga sessions encourage mindfulness. A mindful outlook can have far-reaching effects in multiple areas of life, like promoting mindful eating and greater body awareness.

As a form of self-care, yoga can also promote a healthier body image. In a 2018 study, young adults who made it a habit reported higher satisfaction levels with their bodies. Better self-esteem and motivation have also been linked to the practice.

Then, too, yoga’s stress-relieving effects might follow you off the mat and into the dining room. Some research has found that people who do yoga binge eat less often.

Wanna get started with yoga but aren’t sure how? We got you.

It all starts with setting realistic goals and expectations. If you’ve never practiced before, you won’t be pretzel-ing yourself into challenging poses like scorpion or crow overnight — and that’s OK. Consider setting smaller, step-wise goals, such as attending a 30-minute class twice a week or mastering a few basic poses. Little by little, you’ll work your way up to a more advanced practice.

It’s also wise to select a class (or video) for beginners. Check your gym or yoga studio’s schedule for introductory sessions, and don’t be afraid to let an instructor know before class that you may need some modifications. Most are happy to provide adaptations to make the class a better experience for beginners.

Meanwhile, if you’re pursuing a yoga practice for weight loss, remember to pair it with other healthy lifestyle practices for best results. Though stretching and holding poses burn calories, yoga might not take you to your weight loss goal alone. A balanced diet, cardio exercise, and sufficient sleep are other keys to achieving a healthy weight.

Yoga stereotypes of scantily clad gym babes in impossible contortions might make you feel somewhat intimidated about in-person classes. If you’re concerned that a gym session will make you self-conscious, start with an at-home practice. (YouTube is a treasure trove of classes and instructors explicitly geared for people with overweight.) All by yourself in your living room, there’s no one to impress.

Or, if you’re up for in-person yoga, let your instructor know your needs again. Modifications are always possible.

No matter where you practice, credit yourself for showing up for your health. And, at the beginning of your session, don’t forget to set an intention you find motivating or encouraging, such as “I am caring for my body” or “I am worthy of love and respect.”

Overweight doesn’t have to be a barrier to taking up yoga. Start small, knowing that you’ll get more comfortable with each session. With all the physical and mental health benefits a yoga practice provides — and all the modifications that make it more accessible — it’s worth a try, regardless of weight.

#8983. Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?

By now you’ve probably heard about GLP-1s, sold under brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy. This class of medications mimics naturally occurring hormones involved in appetite control and blood sugar regulation to treat type 2 diabetes and aid weight-loss efforts. It should be no surprise, then, that conversations around these popular drugs have largely centered on the scale. However, some scientists are starting to look more closely into how they may impact something perhaps even more personal: our sex lives.

At present roughly one in five Americans reports taking or having taken a GLP-1, according to a recent poll. As the number of people using these medications has soared, so have anecdotal reports about how they’re impacting users’ day-to-day—and yes, this includes things like pleasure and sex drive. Though there hasn’t been a ton of research into the relationship between sexual health and GLP-1s yet, more scientists are starting to investigate potential impacts.

In a review published in Obesity Pillars in March 2026, for example, researchers propose that GLP-1s may influence desire by impacting brain chemistry. But how exactly might these drugs impact sex drive? And is there a way to remain engaged in your sex life while on a GLP-1? We tapped experts to find out.

To understand how GLP-1s might influence libido, it helps to walk through how they work more broadly.

Some options, like Wegovy and Ozempic, contain semaglutide, which is a synthetic version of a naturally occurring hormone, glucagon-like peptide-1, or GLP-1. Semaglutide binds to GLP-1 receptors throughout the brain and body, helping regulate appetite, blood sugar, and feelings of satiety, James Simon, MD, an ob-gyn and reproductive endocrinologist and one of the researchers behind the Obesity Pillars study, tells SELF.

Other options, like Zepbound and Mounjaro, contain a different active ingredient called tirzepatide, which mimics both GLP-1 and a related hormone, and thus impacts the body in similar ways to semaglutide.

On top of reporting reduced appetite and increased satiety, a number of patients have also found that these weight-loss medications quiet what they call “food noise.” But as it turns out, the same parts of the brain that control appetite are also responsible for other reward-seeking behaviors, according to Dr. Simon. He says this could help explain why taking GLP-1s may have the auxiliary impact of decreasing appetite for another pleasurable activity: sex.

On top of that, early research suggests that GLP-1s may affect certain serotonin receptors, including one called 5-HT2C. This is thought to be a key player in the sexual side effects often experienced by those taking selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as reduced libido and delayed orgasm.

“We know that, while SSRIs are fantastic options for anxiety and depression, they can have a significant impact on sexual desire and orgasmic function in both men and women,” says Dr. Simon. “It makes sense that other medications that also impact serotonin pathways might have similar impacts on sexual desire in some individuals.”

Sexual function isn’t just about hormones and brain chemistry. It also depends on the pelvic floor, a group of muscles that support the bladder and bowel, among other organs, and play an active role in arousal and orgasm, explains pelvic-health physical therapist Iris Xu, PT, DPT, of Fusion Wellness & Femina Physical Therapy.

“During arousal the pelvic-floor muscles increase blood flow to the genitals,” Dr. Xu says. During penetration the muscles lengthen and relax to allow for comfortable insertion and boost sensation. And during orgasm they contract rhythmically, creating the pulsing feeling associated with climax, she says.

In general, weight loss—from GLP-1s or other methods—can improve pelvic-floor function because reduced abdominal pressure means the muscles don’t have to work as hard to support the pelvic organs, Dr. Xu says. A 2024 study published in Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics found that women carrying more fat, particularly in the pelvic area, had weaker pelvic floor muscles than those with less.

But GLP-1s don’t just encourage fat loss. Because these medications can lead to relatively rapid weight loss, preserving lean muscle mass can be challenging—especially without adequate protein intake or resistance training, says Dr. Xu. “[GLP-1s] can also cause loss of lean body mass and strength, especially when used in isolation without exercise or diet modifications,” she adds. In extreme cases this can lead to a condition called sarcopenia, which some studies have linked to reduced pelvic floor function. (FWIW, muscle loss can occur no matter how you lose weight. But by accelerating the weight-loss process, GLP-1s may speed up muscle loss as well.)

At the time of writing, research specifically examining GLP-1 medications and pelvic-floor outcomes remains limited. There is also little data on these drugs’ impact on muscle loss. But the research we do have points to this being a likely outcome, and Dr. Xu says losing too much lean mass may weaken pelvic floor support. This, in turn, can affect arousal, orgasm intensity, or overall sexual function.

As mentioned earlier, part of the notoriety of these medications is the speed at which many patients lose weight. Research has shown that, on average, people who are overweight or living with obesity can lose anywhere from roughly 10% to 20% of their total body weight on a GLP-1, depending on factors like which drug they use, what dose they take, and how long they continue treatment.

However, despite cultural messages to the contrary, weight loss does not automatically translate to increased body confidence and desire, Joy Berkheimer, PhD, LMFT, a sex and relationship therapist, tells SELF.

“Particularly if you have a long history of having your body policed against external beauty standards—as most women and people assigned female at birth do—the rapidity of the physical changes can lead you to feel unfamiliar in your body,” she says. Sexual desire and pleasure are often closely tied to embodiment, so a lack of embodiment can impact intimacy, she says.

It’s not all bad news; for some people the broader health changes associated with these drugs may actually improve aspects of sexual well-being. People go on GLP-1s for help with a variety of health conditions, such as obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), to name just a few. Addressing these sorts of underlying issues may benefit sexual health.

That means even if the medications dial down some of the brain signals tied to desire, other changes happening in the body (e.g., improved energy, hormone balance, and physical comfort) may help support a healthier sex life, Dr. Simon tells SELF.

“Fat cells are highly inflammatory and impede our well-being far beyond their impact on our weight, leading to things such as joint pain and muscle fatigue,” he says. Feeling weak and achy can reduce interest in any physical activity—sex included!—as well as decrease pleasure during them. But as fat mass decreases and inflammation drops, people may feel more comfortable, energetic, and ultimately sexier. Additionally, as body composition improves, hormone levels may shift in ways that boost sexual desire and function, particularly in those with dysfunction, Dr. Simon says. (Body fat contains enzymes that can convert testosterone into estrogen. When levels of these hormones are unbalanced, it can impact sexual health.)

GLP-1 medications have also been shown to improve markers associated with vascular health, including blood pressure. Healthy blood flow is essential to arousal in people of all genders, says Dr. Simon. For those with vaginas it supports clitoral engorgement, lubrication, and vaginal expansion.

Finally, as metabolic health improves some people will see an increase in their energy levels and feel more comfortable in their bodies, says board-certified bariatric surgeon and obesity medicine specialist Betsy Dovec, MD, FACS, DBOM. For some—particularly those navigating postpartum body changes or the menopause transition—that renewed energy and groundedness can translate into increased confidence and desire, she says.

Taken altogether these physiological shifts can enhance sexual function for some people, even as the medications potentially continue to lower the volume on certain reward pathways.

Of course, our sex lives aren’t driven by biology alone. They are mediated by culture and society, the relationships we’re in, our sense of self and self-confidence, and more. The broader life changes that can accompany weight loss may shift libido north or south.

In a society that often equates thinness with desirability, people who don’t fall into the narrow confines of “thin” may feel undesirable, unsexy, or even undeserving of pleasure. For some individuals changes in body composition toward that supposed ideal may lead to increased confidence.

A 2025 survey from the Kinsey Institute and DatingAdvice.com found that 59% of GLP-1 agonist users said the medication had an impact on their dating life, with a number saying it boosted their confidence. Justin Lehmiller, PhD, a social psychologist, research fellow at the Kinsey Institute, and host of the Sex and Psychology podcast, tells SELF that confidence can have huge impacts on our sexual satisfaction.

“Feeling confident makes it easier to surrender to pleasure and facilitates communicating about our sexual needs and desires, which helps to ensure that we’re getting more of what we want in bed,” he says. “By contrast, when we aren’t feeling confident, it’s easy to get stuck in our heads during intimacy and start worrying about things like how we look.”

For those who are single, increased self-confidence may inspire someone who previously didn’t use dating apps or go out to bars because of body image hang-ups to start putting themselves in situations where connection feels more possible, Dr. Simon says. Meanwhile, in long-term relationships that confidence could translate into greater willingness to initiate sex or say yes to a partner’s advances, he adds. It may also mean someone feels more comfortable experimenting with positions they once shied away from—potentially even discovering ones that bring them more pleasure.

In these cases the reward pathways are still muted. However, because other things that shape sexual desire and enjoyment (like confidence) have increased, patients on these drugs may be experiencing better and/or more sex overall.

“Changes in libido are among the most common concerns people bring into sex therapy,” Dr. Berkheimer says. “But often they are a completely normal response to life transitions or physiological shifts, rather than a sign that something is wrong.”

Desire isn’t static, she explains. Rather, it fluctuates across the lifespan in response to factors like stress, sleep quality, exercise routine, medication, illness, hormones, relationship dynamics, and more. That means any shifts you notice after starting a GLP-1 medication aren’t necessarily a sign that something is off—your body might just need time to adjust, Dr. Berkheimer says. Still, if the change feels distressing or different enough to affect your well-being or relationships, it’s worth bringing up with your doctor.

Sexual health, Dr. Dovec says, isn’t a frivolous concern. “Pleasure matters. Intimacy matters. Feeling sexy matters. These are at the core of quality of life,” she says. Shifts in sexual desire and function can offer useful information about what’s happening in your body more broadly. So if sexual changes happen, talk to your provider. As frustrating or unwelcome as these shifts can be, they’re often temporary or solvable with a provider’s help, according to Dr. Dovec.

Sometimes the solution is as simple as adjusting GLP-1 dosage or timing; other times a clinician may suggest lifestyle changes, like adjusting your diet or exercise routine, or additional treatments that support hormone balance.

Not sure how to start the conversation? Dr. Dovec suggests keeping it simple: “You can just say, ‘Something feels different,’ or ‘I don’t feel like myself sexually.’ You’re not going to shock or embarrass your doctor.”

If you find yourself missing pleasure during this season of libidinal lull, Dr. Berkheimer encourages approaching your body with curiosity rather than pressure and expanding intimacy beyond intercourse. “That can look like slowing down and focusing on sensation instead of performance, exploring non-goal-oriented touch like massage or extended skin-to-skin contact, [or experimenting with] sex toys or pleasure aids,” she tells SELF.

Working with a body-neutral or Health at Every Size (HAES) sex therapist can also help you navigate medication effects, physical changes, identity, cultural conditioning, and more so you can erect an updated pleasure practice that honors the body you’re in now, Dr. Berkheimer adds.

#8982. Starvation Mode: How Caloric Restriction Affects Your Body

Cutting back on calories but not losing weight? You might wonder if you’ve gotten stuck in the twilight zone of so-called “starvation mode.”

Everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight. But is starvation mode really a thing — or just an urban legend?

The concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response. To prevent you from losing weight rapidly, your metabolism slows, conserving energy by reducing the calories it burns.

Research shows starvation mode — formally called adaptive thermogenesis or metabolic adaptation — is a legit phenomenon. It’s well documented that sometimes, the more weight you lose (and the more rapidly you do so), the more your body resists the process.

Evolutionarily speaking, this may be a holdover from when humans faced food scarcity and needed a mechanism for self-preservation. But in today’s world, starvation mode can be a frustrating roadblock to weight loss.

What does this metabolic hiccup look like? These symptoms may indicate that starvation mode is becoming a problem for your health:

Starvation mode isn’t the same thing as actual starving. In today’s modern food environment, true starvation is rare. If you’re eating regularly, you won’t experience life-threatening starvation.

However, your body might exhibit some of the same early signs as real starvation. These include the symptoms listed above.

Most commonly, though, starvation mode involves stalled weight loss. You may have hit the wall of adaptive thermogenesis when restricting calories and increasing physical activity without losing weight.

Getting into starvation mode can take just a few days, especially if those days involve severe calorie restriction.

So what counts as severe calorie restriction? Many experts advise not going below 1,200 calories per day for women and 1,500 calories per day for men unless supervised by a doctor. Anything below these numbers could land you in starvation mode faster.

Fortunately, getting your body out of starvation mode isn’t complicated.

First, there’s the obvious solution: Eat a few more calories. But we don’t mean just any calories. By adding a few more nutrient-dense foods (especially those with fiber and protein), you may find weight loss becomes easier, not harder. Both of these nutrients have links to weight loss — so they might help you get out of starvation mode without gaining weight.

If you’re feeling extremely depleted, you might take a temporary break from a weight loss diet to replenish your nutrient stores.

Choosing the proper exercise could also bump you out of starvation mode. Resistance exercises like weightlifting, yoga, push-ups, squats, and others build muscle, which increases your metabolic rate.

According to a 2014 study, people who participated in a 9-month resistance exercise program increased their resting metabolic rate — aka how many calories they burned at rest — by an average of 5%.

Weight loss is a balancing act. It’s normal to experience physical and emotional ups and downs.

That said, it’s time to see a doctor if you’re noticing symptoms like extreme fatigue or lethargy, constipation that lasts more than a few days, sensitivity to cold, or unusual mood changes. Your healthcare team can help you hit the sweet spot of weight loss without lingering in starvation mode.

Despite its name, being in starvation mode doesn’t mean you’ll starve. Instead, it’s a state in which your body has adapted to your weight loss efforts, giving you pushback on how many calories it burns. With strategies like tweaking your calorie intake and adding strength training, you can get out of this mode and back on the path to sustained weight loss.

#8981. SMALLrevolution’s traceable recycling takes second in designboom special prize at seoul design award

recycled aircraft safety strips become furniture that retains its glow, making the material’s previous life visible.

One of the major social concerns of the 21st century is the environment and the future that awaits it. Against this backdrop, recycling systems deserve closer attention. Cue SMALLrevolution, second-place winner of the designboom special prize at the Seoul Design Award 2026, whose traceable circular systems give objects new life without discarding their material history.

While there is a global consensus on the need to repurpose existing materials and avoid overexploiting fossil resources, Eurostat reports that only 42% of the waste treated in the European Union in 2024 was recycled, while around 30% ended up in landfills.

This is the context in which SMALLrevolution operates. The Danish circular design and manufacturing company proposes treating recycling as an overarching approach considered from the design stage, rather than simply a way to manage a product at the end of its life.

SMALLrevolution designs and manufactures products from waste, documenting the materials’ previous lives. This allows users to understand the journey those materials have taken before becoming the finished product.

As part of this philosophy of traceability and its commitment to sustainability, SMALLrevolution makes preserving the original colors, textures, and characteristics of the plastics it uses an aesthetic principle.

Rather than relying on chemical additives, pigments, or virgin plastic to create uniformity, SMALLrevolution embraces the raw aesthetic of its materials. The resulting furniture, decorative pieces, and architectural installations serve as a constant visual reminder of their previous lives.

One example is its work with Lufthansa Technik’s GuideU emergency floor markings. These strips are transformed into furniture and interior products that retain the original material’s photoluminescent properties, carrying their former function into a new setting.

One of SMALLrevolution’s defining features is its involvement across multiple product life cycles. The approach encompasses waste collection, material processing, design, manufacturing, procurement, and end use, maintaining traceability throughout and supporting individual and corporate accountability.

Today, SMALLrevolution works across sectors including healthcare, aviation, infrastructure, events, and consumer products. Since 2021, it has reintegrated more than 66 metric tons of plastic into commercial value chains, including 16 metric tons in 2025 alone. This has been achieved through collaborations with partners such as Novo Nordisk, Lufthansa Technik, Airbus, Clever, Roskilde Festival, and Danish hospitals. Business partnerships account for 98% of its revenue.

For the creators, working with these partners provides tangible proof that circular systems are not a utopian idea, but can become an operational model capable of functioning under real market conditions.

This approach connects with the values of the designboom Special Prize at the Seoul Design Award 2026, in which SMALLrevolution was awarded second place. Making the history of materials visible brings a creative dimension to recycling, while traceability and commercial results demonstrate the practical impact of its vision.

See how SMALLrevolution is reshaping sustainable design and stay tuned for the grand prize winner announcement on November 11th.

#8979. What Is ‘Nonnamaxxing’? The Italian Grandma Lifestyle Might Be the Secret to Longevity

When I moved to Italy in 2024, one of the first things I noticed was the very particular way Italian nonne, or grandmas, live. They walk everywhere, frequently across the city, without any assistance. Many of them are dressed to the nines, but they also don’t try to hide their age.

I was then delighted—and unsurprised—when I came across a new wellness trend making the rounds on social media. “Nonnamaxxing” is the idea that anyone can maximize their life if they just embrace the habits of Italian grandmas. It happens to be sensible guidance.

There’s certainly a lot to learn from Italian grandmothers. Italy leads the European Union in life expectancy, and it’s a country where the number of centenarians is growing. A cluster of villages in Sardinia is one of the world’s five Blue Zones. Online guidance includes ditching social media, eating homemade everything, wearing cotton nightgowns, and welcoming unhurried lunches with friends. Some of these suggestions line up with how I’ve seen Italian grandmas live. But as a health and science journalist, I’ve noticed there’s more to it than what looks good on Instagram or TikTok. In fact, Licia Fertz, a 96-year-old Italian nonna based in Viterbo, Italy, tells SELF, quite the opposite is true.

“I put on my makeup and dress in cheerful colors, even if I’m not leaving the house, because presenting yourself well is an act of self-love,” Fertz says.

It seems that Italian nonne are the health gurus we all need. Read on to learn their secrets to a happier, healthier, and longer life.

I rarely see Italian nonne who don’t look their age. In fact, it’s one of the first things I noticed when I moved here. At the pools and beaches, it doesn’t matter how old they are; women, nonne included, frequently wear bikinis. Honestly, it’s refreshing and emphasizes a cultural mindset that aging is a natural part of life.

Fertz tells SELF that this mindset is key to her living a long and healthy life. “Never think of yourself as old,” says Fertz. “You are born young.”

It turns out that as you age, having a more positive attitude about getting older could help you live longer too. A recent study found an association between how women view aging and the actual pace at which they age.

Sonja Lyubomirsky, a distinguished professor of psychology at the University of California, Riverside, and author of How To Feel Loved, tells SELF that a mindset is like putting on a pair of glasses or a coat. “It certainly matters very much what our mindset is when we think about aging,” Lyubomirsky says. “Is it a gift? Is it about wisdom, maturity, and the richness of life, or is it about deterioration and loss?” Both can be true, she says. “But you can choose.”

At school pick-up for my daughter, I don’t only see other parents. I also see Italian nonne. That’s because Italian grandmas are very involved in their grandkids’ lives and take an active role in caregiving. In fact, for better or worse, the Italian economy is supported by the unpaid labor of Italian grandmothers—and this is well-known and discussed in local mom groups.

Research shows that caregiving later in life may lead to better aging and act as a buffer against cognitive decline. One recent study found that grandparents who provided childcare—ranging from caring for sick grandkids, helping with homework, or driving them to school—scored higher on memory and verbal fluency tests compared with those who didn’t help with childcare.

“I live with my grandson,” Fertz tells SELF. “I’m a great-grandmother, and every day spent with my great-granddaughter is a gift that never ceases to amaze me.”

Even if you’re not a grandparent, helping others can yield similar health benefits. According to research published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine, people who volunteered more than 100 hours a year—versus those who volunteered zero hours a year—had a reduced risk of mortality, more optimism, and purpose in their lives.

Italian cities and villages are highly walkable, meaning walking isn’t something people do for exercise; it’s just a way of life. Even if someone has a car, sometimes a destination is only reachable by foot because Italy’s infamously narrow streets. Gas is also more expensive in Italy. While this might be inconvenient for some, a walking-first lifestyle happens to be associated with longevity.

“Walking is the most fundamental form of human physical activity and many, many hundreds of studies confirm that walking helps people age slower and better,” Daniel Lieberman, a professor of Human Evolutionary Biology at Harvard University, tells SELF. “Walking helps you age well.”

Paola Mariotti, a pediatrician and nonna based in Florence, Italy, tells SELF that walking is very important to her, and was very important to her own grandparents, who didn’t have a car and walked everywhere. Today, as a more modern nonna, Mariotti focuses on walking at least 5,000 steps a day—which she tracks on her phone—but strives to get 10,000 steps or more, if possible, each day.

Much of America isn’t walkable, but a 2025 study published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine found that even 15 minutes of fast walking a day can reduce premature death.

At cafés in Italy, I’m always struck by how Italian nonne drink un caffè. Usually, she is just enjoying her coffee and watching people walk by, rather than scrolling on her phone or sending emails on her laptop. Some might call this the dolce far niente, which means the sweetness of doing nothing. While it’s true that these moments of pause and presence are more common in Italy, there’s something deeper to them. They reflect how, as a culture, Italians are content to live more mindfully. They appreciate quality over quantity and don’t feel the need to constantly multitask for the sake of being productive.

In fact, Jonathan Alpert, a psychotherapist in New York, tells SELF that he thinks nonnamaxxing has less to do with actual Italian grandmothers and more about Gen Z’s desire to escape hustle culture. “The appeal here is the fantasy of a life that feels grounded, warm, and unhurried,” Alpert says. “A lot of younger people are burned out by the pressure to constantly optimize themselves, be productive, and turn their lives into content.”

While in the moment, multitasking can feel like you’re being more efficient, researchers say that it actually does the opposite and can lead to increased stress levels.

The antidote to hustle culture is a mindful one. This can be as simple as just enjoying a coffee without much else, as it’s been found that people who stay in the present moment age better and with more resilience.

In Italy, there’s an emphasis on eating what’s in season. In fact, my local market provides customers with a chart that identifies exactly what fruits and vegetables are in season each month. This lifestyle isn’t exactly optional—produce that’s out-of-season is harder to come by. Antonino De Lorenzo, professor emeritus of human nutrition at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, tells SELF that the value isn’t in the variety of food, but in what’s gained when you choose seasonal produce, which is food that is less likely to have preservatives and industrial products.

“Freshness, variety, ripeness, and preparation methods can all exert a significant influence on a food’s nutritional profile,” De Lorenzo says. “A high-quality diet, maintained over time, promotes healthier aging, characterized by better preservation of physical, mental, and cognitive functions, as well as reduced exposure to major chronic diseases.”

Indeed, the Mediterranean diet, which focuses on olive oil, vegetables, fruits, whole grains and legumes—all popular in Italy—has been linked to longevity. As researchers tend to emphasize, the Mediterranean diet isn’t a fad diet. It’s a way of life.

Italian grandmas are stereotypically known for being connected to their communities and neighbors—maybe even a bit too much, in the sense that it can veer into nosiness. Viral videos on social media have joked that Italian nonne are Italy’s security systems.

“The most important thing for living a long and happy life? Don’t isolate yourself,” Fertz says. “Always stay in touch with people, travel, plan outings, and get out of the house.”

According to a study in The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry, having a sense of purpose can help preserve cognitive function as you age. A separate study found that people with a higher sense of purpose had a reduced risk for depression and loneliness. Whether that is being in-the-know in your community, or finding a hobby to keep you busy, the key is to feel connected and busy.

Because boredom, Fertz says, is “the one thing that truly makes you old.”

#8978. Hyatt Luxury — Park Hyatt for 25,000-30,000 Points

Savings rate, FI number, and the path to freedom.

Withdrawal plans, Roth ladders, and early access.

Imagine stepping off a long-haul flight, exhausted and slightly rumpled, and walking into the Park Hyatt Tokyo — the hotel made iconic by *Lost in Translation* — and being handed a room key to a suite with floor-to-ceiling views of Mount Fuji. Or picture arriving at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme, where Haussmann architecture frames your every view and the concierge greets you by name. Or standing in the Park Hyatt New York, 25 floors above Midtown, watching the city sprawl in every direction from a room that costs more per night than most people's monthly car payment. Now imagine paying nearly nothing for it. That's the power of the World of Hyatt award chart — and the Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community's collective jaw drop: a single night at the Park Hyatt New York regularly retails for **$1,200–$2,000**. The Park Hyatt Tokyo commands **$800–$1,500** per night. The Park Hyatt Paris? Easily **$1,000+** in peak seasons. Yet every one of these properties sits at **Category 7**, bookable for just **25,000–30,000 World of Hyatt points** per night. At 30,000 points for a $1,500 room, you're extracting **5 cents per point (cpp)** — in a world where most loyalty programs are engineered to deliver 1–1.5 cpp if you're lucky. The CPP range for this sweet spot runs from **2.7 cpp all the way to 6.7 cpp**, meaning even a modest redemption delivers 2–3x the value of a typical points transaction. Why does this gap exist? Because Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** anchored to categories, not real-time cash pricing. When demand spikes — New Year's Eve in New York, cherry blossom season in Tokyo, Paris Fashion Week — cash rates explode upward while your points cost stays locked. The hotel's revenue management team can't touch your award rate. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community is built to exploit. This isn't aspirational travel for the ultra-wealthy. This is FI-minded travel: understanding the system, earning points intentionally, and converting them into experiences that would otherwise require an extra year of saving. A two-night stay at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for 60,000 points — points you can earn from a single credit card welcome bonus — is the kind of redemption that reframes what financial independence actually looks like in practice.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt prices its awards on a fixed category chart, while Park Hyatt properties punch dramatically above their category ceiling in cash value.

Here's how the Hyatt award chart works: properties are assigned to Categories 1 through 8, with standard award nights running from 3,500 points (Cat 1) up to 45,000 points (Cat 8). Park Hyatt properties — the absolute pinnacle of the Hyatt portfolio, a collection of ultra-luxury city hotels that competes directly with Four Seasons and Ritz-Carlton — fall predominantly into Category 7 (25,000 points/night) and Category 8 (40,000 points/night). But unlike Four Seasons or Ritz-Carlton, which have largely abandoned fixed award charts in favor of dynamic pricing that tracks cash rates, Hyatt has held the line on fixed pricing. This is a rare and increasingly endangered feature in hotel loyalty, which is exactly why the ChooseFI community should be actively using it now.

The transfer path that makes this accessible is Chase Ultimate Rewards. Chase transfers to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant — meaning you can spot availability, transfer your points, and book within minutes. Bilt Rewards also transfers to World of Hyatt at 1:1, also instantly, giving you two powerful earning pipelines into the same program.

This matters enormously for strategy. Chase Ultimate Rewards is arguably the most flexible points currency in travel rewards — earned through cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve — and the fact that it flows directly into Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio without any degradation is a genuine gift. 30,000 Chase UR points become exactly 30,000 Hyatt points. No conversion fees, no waiting period, no surprises.

Another critical mechanism: World of Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award redemptions. With hotel awards this is less of an issue than with airline programs, but it reflects Hyatt's broader philosophy of clean, predictable award pricing. What you see is what you pay — taxes and fees on hotel awards are typically minimal.

Now layer in Globalist status, and the value compounds further. World of Hyatt's top-tier elite status (earned at 60 qualifying nights per year) unlocks complimentary suite upgrades at check-in (space available) and free breakfast for two guests daily. If you're a Globalist checking into the Park Hyatt New York and you receive a suite upgrade, you've just added hundreds of dollars of daily value to an already exceptional redemption — and free breakfast at a Park Hyatt can easily run $60–$90 per person.

The booking window is 395 days out, which matters for high-demand dates. The Park Hyatt Tokyo during cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or the Park Hyatt New York around major events will see award availability evaporate quickly. Understanding that you can search and book nearly 13 months in advance is your single biggest tactical advantage for locking in prime dates.

Finally, it's worth understanding what you're getting at the property level. Park Hyatt is not Hyatt Regency or even Andaz — it's Hyatt's true ultra-luxury tier, with butler service, marble bathrooms, curated art collections, and some of the best city-view room designs in the world. The points-to-experience ratio here is genuinely exceptional.

Before anything else, inventory what you have. Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards account and note your balance. You need a minimum of 25,000 points for a Category 7 Park Hyatt night or 40,000 points for a Category 8 property. If you're planning a multi-night stay, multiply accordingly — 30,000 points per night at a Category 7 is a reasonable planning number that covers most Park Hyatt sweet spots.

Decide which property you're targeting. The flagship three for this redemption are:

Go to hyatt.com and use the hotel search. Enter your destination city and dates. In the rate filter, select "Use Points" to display award availability. The site will show you the points cost per night — if you see the Category rate (25,000 or 40,000), availability exists. Note that peak and off-peak pricing can adjust these numbers slightly, so check a few date combinations.

Search flexibly. If your first-choice dates show no availability, shift by a day or two — award inventory at Park Hyatt properties is released in small blocks and replenished irregularly. Use the calendar view to scan multiple dates at once.

This is critical: do not transfer points until you've confirmed award availability exists on your target dates. Point transfers to Hyatt are irreversible. Once you've found open award space, note the exact dates and room type, then move immediately to Step 4.

If you're using Chase Ultimate Rewards: Log into your Chase account, navigate to "Pay Yourself Back" → "Transfer to Travel Partners" → select World of Hyatt. Enter the amount (in increments matching your need) and confirm. The transfer is instant — your Hyatt account will reflect the points within minutes.

If you're using Bilt Rewards: Navigate to the "Rewards" tab, select "Transfer Points," choose World of Hyatt, and confirm. Also instant.

Return to hyatt.com immediately after the transfer confirms. Search your target dates again, select the award rate, and complete the booking. You'll pay any applicable taxes (typically modest for hotel awards) and your points will be deducted. Print or screenshot your confirmation.

Award inventory at Park Hyatt properties is genuinely limited. If you lose availability between searching and transferring (rare, but possible), call the World of Hyatt member line (1-800-304-9288) — agents sometimes have access to inventory not visible online. Alternatively, set calendar reminders to check again; properties occasionally release additional award space within 30 days of arrival as booking patterns clarify. Remember: the booking window opens 395 days out, so planning ahead dramatically expands your options.

Let's walk through a real booking that illustrates exactly why this redemption has earned its place in the ChooseFI community's hall of fame.

The Setup: Two Nights at the Park Hyatt Tokyo

You're planning a trip to Japan in early April — a shoulder period just after peak cherry blossom season, when the city is still spectacular but the crowds have thinned slightly. You pull up hyatt.com and find award availability at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for two nights at 25,000 points per night.

The Cash Cost: A quick search on the Park Hyatt Tokyo's direct booking page for the same dates shows standard King rooms starting at $1,100/night. For two nights, that's $2,200 in cash — before resort fees or any extras.

The Points Cost: 50,000 World of Hyatt points (25,000 × 2 nights), transferred instantly from Chase Ultimate Rewards.

The CPP Calculation: $2,200 cash value ÷ 50,000 points = 4.4 cents per point — well above the program's already-impressive baseline and squarely in the sweet spot's 2.7–6.7 cpp range.

What You Actually Experience: The Park Hyatt Tokyo occupies floors 39–52 of the Shinjuku Park Tower skyscraper. Your King Deluxe room on the 42nd floor has floor-to-ceiling windows framing the Tokyo skyline — on a clear morning, Mount Fuji appears in the distance like a postcard. The bathroom features a deep soaking tub, Aesop amenities, and heated floors. Breakfast in the Club on the 41st floor is an exquisite affair — if you hold Globalist status, it's included for both guests, adding roughly $60–$80 per person per day in value.

If you've achieved Globalist status, a complimentary suite upgrade at check-in (space available) could place you in a room with panoramic corner views that would retail for $1,800+ per night.

This is the kind of redemption that makes the FI math click in a visceral way. You earned 50,000 Chase UR points — achievable through a single premium travel card welcome bonus — and converted them into nearly $2,500 of genuine luxury. That's the system working exactly as it should.

The Park Hyatt category properties — especially Tokyo and New York — have notoriously limited award availability. The booking window opens 395 days in advance, and for high-demand dates (cherry blossom season in Japan, summer in Paris, New Year's in New York), competitive award inventory can disappear within days of opening. Set a calendar reminder for 395 days before your target date and be ready to search and transfer the same day.

The 1:1 instant transfer from Chase Ultimate Rewards makes the Chase ecosystem your most efficient pipeline into World of Hyatt. The Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve both transfer to Hyatt at 1:1, instantly. Pair either with the Chase Freedom Unlimited or Chase Freedom Flex to funnel everyday spending into the UR ecosystem before converting to Hyatt points when you have a target booking.

Cash prices at Park Hyatt properties fluctuate dramatically — your points cost does not. A room at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme during Paris Fashion Week might run $2,000/night while your award costs the same 25,000 points as a Tuesday in November. The bigger the cash premium on your dates, the higher your effective CPP. Research when local demand spikes and target those windows deliberately.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. This is activity-based expiration — any earning or redemption resets the clock. Don't let a large balance sit dormant. A small hotel stay, a points transfer, or earning through a Hyatt credit card all count as qualifying activity.

This is the cardinal mistake. Chase UR → Hyatt transfers are irreversible. If you transfer 60,000 points and then discover your target dates are unavailable, those points are now stranded in Hyatt — useful for Hyatt redemptions, but no longer flexible. Always confirm award space first, then transfer.

While 40,000 points/night for a Cat 8 property sounds steep, certain Park Hyatt properties in this tier — like the Park Hyatt Maldives Hadahaa — can retail for $2,000+/night, delivering CPP values that rival the best airline redemptions. Don't automatically limit your search to Category 7.

Hyatt does use peak and off-peak pricing tiers that can push Category 7 awards from 25,000 to 30,000 points on high-demand dates. Always check the actual points cost displayed during your specific date search rather than assuming the standard rate applies.
