Park Hyatt is Hyatt's top-tier luxury brand, competing directly with Four Seasons, Ritz-Carlton, and Aman resorts. What makes this a travel rewards sweet spot is the disconnect between cash prices and points cost. While competitors like Marriott Bonvoy may charge 85,000-100,000 points for comparable luxury, Hyatt keeps Park Hyatt redemptions at Category 7-8 (25,000-30,000 points). Combined with the 1:1 transfer ratio from Chase Ultimate Rewards, a single Chase Sapphire Preferred sign-up bonus can fund multiple nights of genuine luxury.

Earn Chase Ultimate Rewards through the Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, or business cards like the Ink Preferred. A single sign-up bonus often covers 2-3 Park Hyatt nights. Alternatively, earn directly with the World of Hyatt credit card.

Log into your Chase account and transfer Ultimate Rewards to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio. Transfers are typically instant, so you can transfer right before booking. Only transfer what you need for confirmed availability.

Use the World of Hyatt website or app to search your desired Park Hyatt property and dates. Filter by "Points" to see award availability. Check flexible date ranges to find the best redemption opportunities.

Complete the booking using your Hyatt points. Make sure you are logged into your World of Hyatt account so elite benefits apply. Consider booking a standard room and requesting a suite upgrade at check-in if you have Globalist status.

If you have Globalist status, contact the hotel before arrival to request suite upgrades and confirm breakfast inclusion. Even without top-tier status, joining World of Hyatt (free) earns you base-level benefits and points on incidental spend.

The fastest path is through Chase Ultimate Rewards. Cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve earn Ultimate Rewards that transfer 1:1 to World of Hyatt. A single sign-up bonus of 60,000-75,000 points can cover 2-3 nights at a Park Hyatt. You can also earn directly with the World of Hyatt credit card.

Compared to other luxury hotel chains, Park Hyatt availability is relatively good. Booking 3-6 months in advance for popular properties like Park Hyatt Tokyo or Park Hyatt Maldives improves your chances. Off-peak and shoulder season dates often have wide-open availability.

Yes. Globalist elite status works at all Park Hyatt properties and unlocks suite upgrades (subject to availability), free breakfast, late checkout, and waived resort fees. This dramatically increases the total value of a points stay.

Properties in high-cost destinations like Tokyo, New York, Paris, Sydney, and the Maldives typically deliver the highest cents-per-point value because their cash rates are so expensive. A Park Hyatt Tokyo stay worth $600-$800/night for 25,000 points is a standout redemption.

This redemption is purpose-built for the intentional luxury traveler in the ChooseFI community — someone who has been systematically accumulating Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards points and wants to convert that discipline into a genuinely extraordinary hotel experience, not just a free night at a mid-tier property.

The minimum to play: You need at least 25,000 World of Hyatt points for a single night — ideally 50,000–75,000 for a meaningful multi-night stay. This is achievable through a single Chase Sapphire welcome bonus plus modest everyday spending.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating**, and it's worth being specific about where the friction lives — because once you understand it, most of the difficulty evaporates. **The earning is easy.** Chase Ultimate Rewards points flow into World of Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, and Chase is one of the most accessible premium rewards ecosystems for new-to-intermediate travel rewards participants. The points pipeline is well-established and reliable. **The transfer and booking mechanics are easy.** The actual process — confirm availability, transfer points, complete booking — is straightforward if you follow the correct sequence. The Hyatt website is functional and the award search is transparent. **The hard part is availability.** Park Hyatt properties are genuinely popular, the award inventory is limited, and the most desirable dates (cherry blossom season, major holidays, Fashion Week) book out fast. This is where most people hit a wall — they discover the sweet spot, feel excited, and then find no availability for their dates. **Three tips to overcome the availability challenge:** 1. **Use the full 395-day booking window.** Plan further ahead than feels natural. If you want Tokyo in April of next year, you should be searching in late March or early April of the current year. 2. **Be flexible by 3–5 days on either side.** Award inventory often opens mid-week when demand is lower. Shifting from a Saturday check-in to a Thursday can unlock availability that doesn't exist on peak nights. 3. **Check repeatedly near the 30-day mark.** Properties occasionally release additional award space as the date approaches. Setting a weekly reminder to re-check your target dates costs nothing. If you're willing to plan ahead and stay flexible on exact dates, moderate difficulty becomes very manageable — and the reward on the other side is worth every bit of the effort.

The Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most compelling redemptions in the entire travel rewards landscape. Booking a genuine ultra-luxury hotel experience for 25,000-30,000 points — points that transfer 1:1 from Chase Ultimate Rewards — delivers 2-4 cents per point in value. Whether it is the iconic Park Hyatt Tokyo, the beachfront Park Hyatt Maldives, or the classic Park Hyatt New York, this sweet spot consistently delivers outsized value. For anyone building a Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy, Park Hyatt should be at the top of the aspiration list.

#8977. Text Neck Exercises: Simple Moves to Ease Digital Strain

Whether you’re caught up in doomscrolling or just checking your work emails, chances are you’re spending a lot of time on your phone. But all that screen time can lead to a pesky condition called “text neck.” Hunching over your device can leave you with some severe aches and pains.

So, hold your phone up to eye level and check out these easy tips to get rid of text neck fast!

Also known as “tech neck,” text neck is a term coined by a chiropractor to describe the neck pain you might feel after spending too much time looking down at your phone.

Most of us check our phones with our heads tilted forward and down. When you do this for too long, the muscles in your neck get strained. The muscles in the back are overstretched, while the ones in the front are compressed.

If you have text neck, here’s what you might be dealing with:

But don’t get bent out of shape about overusing your favorite device. There’s no solid proof that your phone habits are to blame for your neck woes. Several studies found no connection between using your device and having neck or shoulder pain.

You could get a sore neck from overusing your muscles for many other reasons, like genetic factors, weight issues, or bad posture. “Text neck” might be a term concocted by a chiropractor to get your business. But, hey, we’re not judging.

To help ease text neck pain, try these simple exercises.

Aside from these cubicle-friendly exercises, here are some ideas to help keep text neck from being a regular pain in the y’know:

“Text neck” is the popular term for the head and neck pain caused by hunching over your device for too long. But don’t throw away your beloved device just yet. More research is needed to link “text neck” to your tech time.

In the meantime, sit up straight and do gentle exercises like neck rolls, chin tucks, and shoulder rolls. To prevent text neck from hitting you up on the reg, take regular breaks from your phone and seek out habits that help lengthen and strengthen your body. Your neck will thank you!

#8976. podcast: architecture that refuses signature styles for spaces shaped by instinct

the room for utopias podcast continues with indian architects and designers exploring how to dismantle signature styles to create spaces rooted in human instinct.

Challenging the impulse to package buildings into neat aesthetic categories, the Room for Utopias podcast series returns with Indian architects and designers interrogating the tension between enduring human rituals and the myth of signature style. Realized in partnership with INDX|GLOBAL during designboom.paris, this edition, themed A Future Without Formula, investigates what happens when practices step away from recognizable branding. Across two panel debates, hosted by designboom’s Managing Editor, Iñaki Laguardia, the series frames architectural identity not as a static visual stamp, but as an evolving narrative rooted in environmental responsibility and a fluid way of thinking.

The fifth episode of Room for Utopias brings together Ankit Gupta of Ankit Gupta & Ridhima Sogani Architects, Shalini Ganguli of Shalini Ganguli Interiors, and Kshitiz Manu of K Manu & Associates to examine how architecture can balance fast-evolving lifestyles with persistent biological instincts. The conversation moves past superficial trends to identify what built spaces must preserve and what they must urgently reinvent.

Kshitiz Manu of K Manu & Associates distinguishes between daily habits and human nature through a computational metaphor. ‘Ritual is a software and instinct is an operating system. Rituals can be changed… but our instinct stays the same. To maintain that balance is architecture,’ Manu explains. He critiques hermetic, high-tech interiors that disconnect occupants from nature, warning against what he terms ‘2:00 p.m. building’ where static artificial lighting and perpetual climate control freeze the perception of time. Instead, he advocates for spaces that let moving sunlight and lengthening shadows reveal the day’s progression, emphasizing that a building’s real life only begins once the designer departs and daily chaos takes over.

Shalini Ganguli of Shalini Ganguli Interiors addresses domestic fragmentation caused by private screens and self-contained bedrooms, urging designers to safeguard areas of unstructured shared presence. Ganguli argues that rooms must intuitively enable families to coexist without forced interaction. ‘In many rooms you have your own television, you can completely lock yourself out… but what happens is that your life goes unwitnessed. It is our moral responsibility to not ever get rid of areas in the house which enable the family to interact with each other,’ Ganguli states, calling for homes that accommodate human connection and layered memories over sterile, picture-perfect staging.

The sixth conversation dismantles the commodification of architectural aesthetics. Moderator Iñaki Laguardia sits down with Sonali Bhagwati of Designplus Architects (DPA), Priyanka Mehra of PS Design, Manish Gulati of MOFA Studio, and Ajay Arya of A Square Designs to interrogate whether signature styles limit creative evolution and contextual responsiveness.

Sonali Bhagwati of Designplus Architects (DPA) differentiates between superficial packaging and genuine practice identity. ‘When you look at identity, you are actually looking at the core values that a firm or a practice wants to imbibe. You don’t have to try and superimpose a particular style which is trending onto everything,’ Bhagwati states. For her, design s anchored in a deep narrative rather than aesthetic imitation: ‘The moment your narrative is strong, your architecture will always have a place.’

Manish Gulati of MOFA Studio challenges the historical obsession with stylistic signatures, arguing that styles are retrospective constructs invented by critics to sell architecture. ‘Style is only useful for critics and journalists… It’s the packaging. If you have to sell something and you don’t package it well, it won’t sell,’ Gulati remarks. Describing his studio as’’optimistic non-conformists,’ Gulati asserts that architecture should respond to personal aspirations, user memory, and pressing planetary urgencies rather than dogmatic stylistic rules. ‘Future is not about style. Future is about what is important at the moment  — like climate change — that’s the most important factor when it comes to architecture,’ he notes.

Priyanka Mehra of PS Design defends contextual belonging, balancing client aspirations with geographic rootedness. ‘The house must sit where it belongs. A design has to be rooted in identity, in context where it is sitting,’ Mehra emphasizes. She argues that individual stories should drive spatial concepts. ‘No two individuals are alike. Why do the houses need to be the same?’

Ajay Arya of A Square Designs reflects on the evolving nature of urban living, noting that major cities are experiencing a transitional phase where rigid stylistic dogma is giving way to fluid expression. Arya argues that an architect’s identity should not be bound to reproducing the same look repeatedly, but should instead manifest in how materials are combined and softened to reflect the personality of the inhabitant. ‘I feel creativity should be fluid… and also they should have freedom of thought, and how new things would just come our way in the future,’ Arya shares, emphasizing that spaces must balance modern trends with enduring personal resonance.

From domestic thresholds that allow natural light and time to mark the day, to studios actively unlearning signature aesthetics in pursuit of ecological and public responsibility, both conversations advocate for an architecture unburdened by dogma. These practitioners show that utopias in contemporary practice do not require inventing a novel aesthetic stamp. By prioritizing core values over trending formulas, they point toward an architecture that remains grounded, adaptable, and genuinely alive long after construction ends.

guests: Ankit Gupta (Ankit Gupta & Ridhima Sogani Architects | @ankitguptaarchitects), Shalini Ganguli (Shalini Ganguli Interiors | @shaliniganguliinteriors), Kshitiz Manu (K Manu & Associates | @kshitizmanu), Sonali Bhagwati (Designplus Architects | @dpa_designplusarchitecture), Priyanka Mehra (PS Design | @psdesign.co.in), Manish Gulati (MOFA Studio | @mofa_studio), and Ajay Arya (A Square Designs | @asquaredesigns)

#8975. 6 Supplements Doctors Actually Take

These days, it seems like everyone is taking a supplement—to look better, think better, sleep better, relax better, poop better, or work out better. And you’re not imagining things: Half of adults and one-third of children in the United States take supplements regularly, according to the Office of Dietary Supplements.

Supplements may be ubiquitous, but many experts have serious reservations about their rise. First, most physicians recommend obtaining nutrients directly from food rather than a pill or capsule. Second, supplements aren’t reviewed for safety and effectiveness by the FDA before they hit shelves. Because of all the concerns surrounding supplements, Jeffrey Linder, MD, MPH, a general internist and professor of medicine at the Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, takes a dim view of the category overall: In fact, “a vast majority of supplements are probably worthless,” he tells SELF.

Still, there are exceptions to every rule—and supplements are no different. Many experts, as it turns out, do take some type of supplement, but they are choosy about which ones they select. Read on to learn more about six they actually use.

How it works: Vitamin D plays key roles in bone health and immune function. In fact, low vitamin D is associated with a wide swath of medical conditions, according to Dr. Linder—including cancer, autoimmune diseases, infectious diseases, and cardiovascular issues (and, famously, seasonal affective disorder, or SAD).

Why some docs like it: Vitamin D deficiency is widespread, especially among people who live at northern latitudes that don’t see as much sun during the winter, and people with darker skin. What’s more, few foods contain significant amounts of vitamin D, so it’s tough to source enough from your diet. Lawrence Green, MD, a dermatologist and clinical professor at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences, tells SELF that these two factors make vitamin D a rare nutrient “we do need to take supplements for.” Nearly every single one of the eight doctors who spoke with SELF for this article said they take a vitamin D supplement, especially in the winter, though the frequency and dosage varied.

What to keep in mind: Most docs recommend vitamin D3 (also known as cholecalciferol) over vitamin D2 (also known as ergocalciferol), as studies have shown that D3 is more effective at raising vitamin D levels in your blood. Whichever option you decide on, try to take it with food—specifically, an item that contains fat. Because vitamin D is a fat-soluble nutrient, it “absorbs better that way,” Sara Velayati, MD, an obesity medicine specialist at Montefiore Einstein and an assistant professor at Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York City, tells SELF. For this reason, Dr. Green makes a point of taking his supplements with breakfast or dinner. “The fattier and thicker the meal,” the better, he says.

What it does: Calcium is a mineral that helps build and maintain strong bones and teeth. Women in their 40s approaching menopausal age should make it a particular priority to ensure their intake is adequate, Rachel Pessah-Pollack, MD, an endocrinologist at NYU Langone Health and a clinical professor at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, tells SELF, as the physical changes that come with perimenopause and menopause can heighten bone loss and downstream health conditions like osteoporosis.

Who takes it: Like the other supplements on this list, calcium is best sourced from your diet, Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. “But if you’re not able to (I try to get dairy products but often come up short), a supplement is needed.” She takes a combined calcium and vitamin D tablet daily, as vitamin D helps calcium absorb.

How to take it: “The type of calcium supplements you are taking matters,” Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. Calcium carbonate and calcium citrate are the two most common. “Calcium carbonate should be taken with food because it requires gastric acid to be absorbed,” Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. Calcium citrate is an alternative that can be taken with or without food.

How it works: Magnesium is a mineral that can enhance sleep and muscle recovery. Research has also shown that it’s effective at preventing migraines, Raquel Zemtsov, MD, MPH, a family medicine doctor and assistant professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, tells SELF.

Why some docs like it: In addition to Dr. Zemtsov, who takes magnesium to stave off migraine symptoms, Dr. Velayati takes magnesium for the sleep benefits. Likewise, Sheeva Talebian, MD, a reproductive endocrinologist at CCRM Fertility of New York, and Kathleen Jordan, MD, an internal medicine physician and chief medical officer at Midi Health, also turn to it at bedtime to boost their shut-eye.

What to keep in mind: Some types of magnesium are better tolerated, says Dr. Velayati—something to note if you’re especially sensitive to side effects. Magnesium glycinate “avoids the gastrointestinal upset caused by magnesium oxides and magnesium citrates,” for example, Dr. Jordan says. Depending on your needs, however, magnesium glycinate might not be the best option: Magnesium oxide is the recommended magnesium type for migraines, so that’s the one Dr. Zemtsov keeps on hand, for example. Taking magnesium with food can also help prevent GI distress, according to Dr. Velayati.

How it works: Omega-3 fatty acids are polyunsaturated fats that are important for cardiovascular health. Common omega-3 supplements include fish oil and krill oil.

Why some docs like it: Dr. Jordan, Dr. Talebian, and Dr. Velayati all take omega-3s. “With their anti-inflammatory properties and association with improved brain health, this is a popular supplement among physicians, myself included,” Dr. Jordan, who takes krill oil, says. Similarly, Dr. Velayati dabbles in fish oil, but takes it selectively. “The right dose really depends on the goal, but I don’t think it’s necessary for everyone,” she says.

What to keep in mind: Fish oil supplements can have a characteristic fishy aftertaste, so it might take some trial and error to find one that works for you (read: doesn’t leave you gagging). What’s more, absorption and bioavailability can be a challenge, according to Dr. Jordan. Because omega-3s, like vitamin D, are fat-soluble, taking fish oil with a meal that contains fat can help skirt this problem. Some claim krill oil doesn’t cause the dreaded aftertaste as much as fish oil, and evidence suggests it’s also better absorbed by the body.

How it works: Iron, a mineral, acts as an essential ingredient in hemoglobin, a protein found in your red blood cells. Without enough iron, your blood won’t be able to carry out its core task of delivering oxygen to organs and tissues, resulting in anemia.

Why some docs like it: Iron deficiency is common in women due to the loss of blood during menstruation every month. “Occasionally, despite trying my hardest to seek out iron-rich foods, I still develop an iron deficiency,” Dr. Zemtsov says. When that happens, she takes ferrous gluconate (a particular type of iron supplement) every other day to treat or prevent anemia, since research shows iron supplements are better absorbed and cause fewer side effects that way. Dr. Jordan also takes iron supplements, citing the advantages for sleep, hair health, and overall energy.

What to keep in mind: Iron absorption is enhanced by vitamin C, so pairing your iron supplement with a food that contains vitamin C or even a vitamin C supplement—as Dr. Zemtsov does—can be helpful.

How it works: Fiber, a type of carb, boosts digestion in a variety of ways: It keeps you full, helps prevent constipation, and supports bowel health. Besides the GI stuff, it also serves other functions in your body, including stabilizing your blood sugar and lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol.

Why some docs like it: “Unless you are that rare woman who regularly gets in her 25 to 30 grams per day, extra fiber intake is beneficial for almost everyone, and addresses multiple issues for me personally, including prediabetes and a rising cholesterol level,” Dr. Jordan says. She takes a fiber supplement as needed, on days when she doesn’t manage to hit her goal.

What to keep in mind: If your body isn’t acclimated to a high fiber intake, suddenly bombarding it could cause some digestive distress (think gas and bloating), so start slow to ease the transition. You’ll also need to increase your water intake simultaneously, since fiber requires water to work.

“When someone is considering a supplement, I usually recommend having a specific reason for taking it”—like a confirmed nutritional deficiency, Dr. Velayati says. “Overall, I view supplements as a way to fill a gap, not a substitute for good nutrition, sleep, exercise, and evidence-based medical care.” The bottom line: Supplements are really meant for plugging holes in your diet.
